docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure your system has the following installed:

  • Rust 1.85+: Check with rustc --version. If not installed, download from rustup.rs.
  • Cargo: Comes bundled with Rust. Verify with cargo --version.
  • Git: Required for cloning the repository and integration features. Verify with git --version.
  • macOS or Linux: Hone is tested on macOS 12+ and Linux (Ubuntu 20.04+). Windows support is in progress.

docs.title: Platform-Specific Dependencies
docs.text:
macOS: 

xcode-select --install

Linux (Ubuntu/Debian): 

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install build-essential pkg-config libssl-dev

Optional: - Docker (for running SWE-bench or containerized workloads) - Node.js 18+ (for MCP JavaScript extensions)

docs.title: Clone and Build from Source
docs.text:
Clone the Hone repository and build the release binary:

git clone https://github.com/wojciechkpl/hone.git
cd hone
cargo build --release

The binary is located at target/release/hone. Copy it to your PATH:

# Option 1: Copy to a directory already in PATH
sudo cp target/release/hone /usr/local/bin/

# Option 2: Add the build directory to your shell profile
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/path/to/hone/target/release:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
hone --version

Expected output: 

hone 0.1.0

If you also intend to run the daemon server:

cargo build --release --bin honed
hone --version
honed --version

Both hone and honed should now be available in your PATH.

docs.title: 3. First-Time Setup (hone configure)
docs.text:
Before running your first session, complete the interactive configuration wizard:

hone configure

This command guides you through provider selection, API key entry, and model selection, writing everything to ~/.config/hone/config.toml.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Walkthrough
docs.text:
Here's what the wizard looks like:

Welcome to the Hone configuration wizard.

Step 1: Select a provider

  1. Anthropic (Claude)
  2. OpenAI
  3. DeepSeek
  4. OpenRouter
  5. Ollama (local)
  6. Claude CLI (claude binary)

Enter your choice (1-6): 1

After selecting Anthropic (option 1):

Step 2: Enter your API key

Note: Your key is read from stdin and not echoed. It will be stored
securely in ~/.config/hone/config.toml.

Hint: sk-ant-...
API key: [hidden input]

Step 3: Select a default model

  1. claude-sonnet-4-5
  2. claude-opus-4-5
  3. claude-haiku-4-5
  4. claude-3-7-sonnet-latest

Enter your choice (1-4): 2

After model selection:

Configuration written to ~/.config/hone/config.toml
Provider: Anthropic
Model: claude-opus-4-5

Ready to use hone! Start with:
  hone

docs.title: What Gets Written to config.toml
docs.text:
After completing the wizard, your configuration file at ~/.config/hone/config.toml looks like:

[agent]
default_model = "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5"
context_window_tokens = 200000
max_iterations = 50
temperature = 0.3

[memory]
enabled = true
encrypted = false

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "sk-ant-..."
base_url = "https://api.anthropic.com"
timeout_secs = 30

[sandbox]
enforce = true
platform = "auto"

docs.title: Configuration Hierarchy (Priority Order)
docs.text:
Hone applies configuration in this order (top wins):

  1. CLI Flags: hone --model openai:gpt-4o --budget 10.00
  2. Environment Variables: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
  3. Config File: ~/.config/hone/config.toml
  4. Defaults: Built-in defaults

Example: If both a CLI flag and env var are set, the CLI flag takes precedence.

docs.title: 4. Provider Setup
docs.text: Hone supports multiple providers. Choose based on your needs: capability, cost, and privacy.

docs.title: Provider Comparison
docs.text: Provider Tool Calling Cost Best For Setup Time Anthropic (Claude) Yes $$ Production, full features 2 min OpenAI Yes $ Budget teams 2 min DeepSeek Yes $ Cheap alternatives 2 min OpenRouter Yes $ Multi-model access 2 min Ollama No Free Local/offline work 5 min Claude CLI No Varies Existing users 1 min Gemini CLI No Free tier No setup needed 1 min

docs.title: Provider Auto-Detection Order
docs.text:
If no provider is explicitly specified, Hone checks in this order:

  1. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable → Anthropic
  2. OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable → OpenAI
  3. claude command in PATH → Claude CLI
  4. gemini command in PATH → Gemini CLI
  5. OLLAMA_HOST environment variable → Ollama
  6. Fallback → Mock provider (testing only)

docs.title: Anthropic (Recommended)
docs.text:
Full feature set including advanced tool calling and the 200K context window.

Get your API key:

  1. Visit https://console.anthropic.com
  2. Click "API Keys" → "Create Key"
  3. Copy the key (starts with sk-ant-)

Configure:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-abc123def456ghi789"
hone "hello"

Or using the configure wizard:

hone configure
# Choose: 1 (Anthropic)
# Paste API key when prompted
# Choose model: 2 (claude-opus-4-5)

Verify it works:

hone "What is 2 + 2?"

Expected output: 

[Model: anthropic:claude-opus-4-5]
2 + 2 equals 4.

Usage: 34 input tokens, 12 output tokens
Cost: $0.001 USD

Available models:

  • claude-opus-4-5 — 200K context, best for complex reasoning
  • claude-sonnet-4 — 200K context, fast, balanced
  • claude-haiku-4-5 — 200K context, cheapest

Pricing (per million tokens):

  • Opus 4-5: $3 input / $15 output
  • Sonnet 4: $3 input / $15 output
  • Haiku 4-5: $0.80 input / $4 output

docs.title: OpenAI
docs.text:
Cost-effective alternative with gpt-4o and gpt-4-turbo.

Get your API key:

  1. Visit https://platform.openai.com
  2. Go to "API Keys" → "Create new secret key"
  3. Copy the key (starts with sk-)

Configure:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-proj-abc123..."
hone --model openai:gpt-4o "hello"

Or via configure wizard:

hone configure
# Choose: 2 (OpenAI)
# Paste API key
# Choose model: 1 (gpt-4o)

Available models:

  • gpt-4o — Latest, most capable
  • gpt-4o-mini — Fast and cheap
  • gpt-4-turbo — Previous generation
  • gpt-3.5-turbo — Budget option

docs.title: DeepSeek (Cheapest)
docs.text:
Great for development and cost-conscious teams. ~90% cheaper than Anthropic.

Get your API key:

  1. Visit https://platform.deepseek.com
  2. Create API key

Configure:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
export HONE_OPENAI_BASE_URL="https://api.deepseek.com"
export HONE_OPENAI_MODEL="deepseek-chat"
hone "hello"

Or in config file:

[providers.openai]
api_key = "sk-..."
base_url = "https://api.deepseek.com"
model_override = "deepseek-chat"

Available models:

  • deepseek-chat — General-purpose
  • deepseek-coder — Code generation and analysis
  • deepseek-reasoner — Extended reasoning

Pricing: ~$0.14 input / $0.28 output per million tokens (vs $3/$15 for Claude)

docs.title: OpenRouter (Multi-Model, Single Key)
docs.text:
Access 100+ models from a single API key. Great for comparing models.

Get your API key:

  1. Visit https://openrouter.ai
  2. Sign up and copy your API key

Configure:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-or-abc123..."
export HONE_OPENAI_BASE_URL="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
export HONE_OPENAI_MODEL="anthropic/claude-opus-4-5"
hone "hello"

Available models (examples):

anthropic/claude-opus-4-5
openai/gpt-4o
google/gemini-2.5-pro
meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct
mistralai/mistral-large

See the full list at https://openrouter.ai/models

docs.title: Ollama (Free, Local)
docs.text:
Run open-source models locally. No internet, no API key, completely free.

Install and start Ollama:

# Download from https://ollama.ai

# Start the server (runs on localhost:11434)
ollama serve

In another terminal, pull and test a model:

ollama pull llama3.2

Configure Hone:

hone --model ollama:llama3.2 "hello"

Or add to config:

[providers.ollama]
base_url = "http://localhost:11434"
timeout_secs = 300

Available models:

  • llama3.2 — Latest, 8B
  • llama3.1 — Previous, 8B
  • mistral — Fast, 7B
  • neural-chat — Conversational
  • qwen2.5-coder — Code generation

List installed models:

ollama list

Pros:

  • Completely free
  • Runs locally (privacy)
  • No API key needed
  • Works offline

Cons:

  • Slower than cloud (depends on your GPU/CPU)
  • Less capable than Claude Opus
  • No tool calling support (yet)

docs.title: Claude CLI (Pass-Through)
docs.text:
Use your existing Claude CLI binary if you have it installed.

Install Claude CLI first:

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install anthropic/brew/claude-cli

# Or download from https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python

Verify Claude CLI is on PATH:

claude --version

Configure Hone:

hone --model claude-cli:claude-opus "hello"

Or via configure wizard:

hone configure
# Choose: 6 (Claude CLI)

Pros:

  • Uses your existing Claude CLI credentials
  • No extra API key setup

Cons:

  • No tool calling support
  • Generation 1 models only
  • Slower than API calls

docs.title: Gemini CLI (Pass-Through)
docs.text:
Use Google's Gemini CLI if you have it installed.

Install Gemini CLI:

# macOS
brew install google-cloud-sdk
gcloud init

# Or download: https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install

Verify installation:

gemini --version

Configure Hone:

hone --model gemini-cli:gemini-pro "hello"

Pros:

  • Free tier available
  • No paid API setup needed

Cons:

  • No tool calling support
  • Less capable than Claude

docs.title: Provider Detection Flow
docs.text:
Hone automatically selects a provider unless you override it. Here's the decision tree:

┌─ Start hone session
│
├─ Is --model flag set?
│  ├─ YES → Use that provider
│  └─ NO → Check config.toml
│
├─ Is default_model in config.toml?
│  ├─ YES → Use that provider
│  └─ NO → Auto-detect
│
├─ Auto-detect flow:
│  ├─ Check ANTHROPIC_API_KEY env var?
│  │  ├─ YES → Use Anthropic
│  │  └─ NO → Continue
│  │
│  ├─ Check OPENAI_API_KEY env var?
│  │  ├─ YES → Use OpenAI
│  │  └─ NO → Continue
│  │
│  ├─ Check 'claude' command exists?
│  │  ├─ YES → Use Claude CLI
│  │  └─ NO → Continue
│  │
│  ├─ Check 'gemini' command exists?
│  │  ├─ YES → Use Gemini CLI
│  │  └─ NO → Continue
│  │
│  ├─ Check OLLAMA_HOST env var?
│  │  ├─ YES → Use Ollama
│  │  └─ NO → Fallback
│  │
│  └─ Fallback → Mock provider (testing)
│
└─ Session starts with selected provider

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
All environment variables in one place. CLI flags and config file override these.

Variable Purpose Example ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Anthropic API authentication sk-ant-abc123... OPENAI_API_KEY OpenAI/compatible endpoint key sk-proj-abc123... HONE_OPENAI_BASE_URL Override OpenAI endpoint https://api.deepseek.com HONE_OPENAI_MODEL Override OpenAI model name deepseek-chat OLLAMA_HOST Ollama server URL http://localhost:11434 RUST_LOG Logging verbosity debug, info, warn, error HONE_CONFIG Override config file path ~/.config/hone/config.toml

docs.title: Config File Format
docs.text:
Full annotated example at ~/.config/hone/config.toml:

# ── Agent settings ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

[agent]
# Default model to use when no --model flag is provided
default_model = "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5"

# Total context window in tokens (model-dependent)
context_window_tokens = 200000

# Tokens reserved for model output
reserved_output_tokens = 4000

# Tokens reserved for system prompt
reserved_system_prompt_tokens = 2000

# Temperature (0.0 = deterministic, 1.0 = creative)
temperature = 0.3

# Maximum iterations per session (prevents infinite loops)
max_iterations = 50

# Maximum tool calls per turn
max_tool_calls_per_turn = 10


# ── Provider configuration ────────────────────────────────────────────────

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}"  # or hardcoded: "sk-ant-..."
base_url = "https://api.anthropic.com"
timeout_secs = 30

[providers.openai]
api_key = "${OPENAI_API_KEY}"
base_url = "https://api.openai.com/v1"
timeout_secs = 30

[providers.ollama]
base_url = "http://localhost:11434"
timeout_secs = 300  # local models may be slow


# ── Memory and session persistence ────────────────────────────────────────

[memory]
enabled = true
db_path = "~/.local/share/hone/memory.db"
encrypted = false
decay_days = 90
max_items = 10000


# ── Sandbox security ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

[sandbox]
enforce = true
platform = "auto"  # "seatbelt" (macOS), "landlock" (Linux), "seccomp"

[sandbox.defaults]
allow_read = ["{project_root}"]
allow_write = ["/tmp"]
allow_network = false

[sandbox.tools.shell]
allow_read = ["{project_root}", "/usr/lib"]
allow_write = ["/tmp", "{project_root}/target"]
allow_exec = ["/bin", "/usr/bin", "/usr/local/bin"]

docs.title: HONE.md Project Config
docs.text:
Create a HONE.md file in your project root to configure Hone per-project:

# HONE.md
project_name: my-app
default_model: anthropic:claude-opus-4-5
context_window_tokens: 150000

# Tools to enable/disable
tools:
  shell: true
  git: true
  file: true
  lsp: true

# Sandbox policy
sandbox:
  enforce: true
  allow_read:
    - src/
    - tests/
    - Cargo.toml
  allow_write:
    - src/
    - tests/
    - target/

# Agent-specific instructions
agent_instructions: |
  You are a senior Rust engineer.
  - Always use 2-space indentation
  - Write tests alongside implementation
  - Check clippy warnings

# Cost budget for this project
budget_usd: 50.0

Place this in your repository root. Hone reads it on session start.

docs.title: 6. Your First Task
docs.text: Now let's run Hone on a real task. We'll fix a simple bug and add a feature.

docs.title: Example 1: One-Shot (Quick Question)
docs.text:
Ask Hone a one-shot question without starting interactive mode:

hone "What files are in the current directory?"

Output:

I'll list the files in the current directory.

[Tool: shell]
Input: ls -la
Output:
total 32
drwxr-xr-x   8 user  staff   256 Apr  9 10:30 .
drwxr-xr-x   5 user  staff   160 Apr  9 10:30 ..
-rw-r--r--   1 user  staff  1234 Apr  9 10:30 Cargo.toml
-rw-r--r--   1 user  staff   567 Apr  9 10:30 README.md
drwxr-xr-x  10 user  staff   320 Apr  9 10:30 src

Found 5 entries: Cargo.toml, README.md, src directory, and 2 others.

Usage: 245 input tokens, 89 output tokens
Cost: $0.004 USD

docs.title: Example 2: Interactive Session (Multi-Turn)
docs.text:
Start an interactive session to work on a multi-step task:

hone --session my-project

Terminal demo:

Hone Session: my-project
Type prompts and press Enter. Type /help for commands.

You: Show me the main.rs file
Assistant: I'll read the main.rs file for you.

[Tool: read_file]
Input: {"path": "src/main.rs"}
Output: (file contents shown)

You: Add error handling to the parse function
Assistant: I'll add error handling to the parse function.

[Tool: edit_file]
Input: {"path": "src/main.rs", "old_text": "fn parse(s: &str) {", "new_text": "fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<()> {"}
Output: Edit successful

Usage: 1523 input tokens, 412 output tokens
Cost: $0.028 USD
Session total: $0.032 USD
Budget remaining: $9.97 / $10.00

You: /quit
Session my-project saved.

docs.title: What Happens Behind the Scenes
docs.text:
1. Token Count: Every turn shows input and output tokens
  2. Cost Tracking: Real USD cost based on your provider's pricing
  3. Tool Calls: File reads, edits, shell execution, git operations
  4. Context Optimization: Hone automatically keeps relevant code in context
  5. Session Memory: Previous turns are remembered and compressed when context gets large

docs.title: 7. Session Management
docs.text: Sessions are named conversations that persist across runs. Start a named session once, resume it later—context is preserved.

docs.title: Create and List Sessions
docs.text:
# Start a new named session
hone --session debug-auth

# List all saved sessions
hone session list

Output of session list:

ID                              Created              Updated              Name              Messages
──────────────────────────────  ──────────────────  ──────────────────  ──────────────    ────────
550e8400-e29b-41d4-a716-4467   2026-04-09 15:22   2026-04-09 15:45    debug-auth        42
550e8400-e29b-41d4-a716-4468   2026-04-09 14:10   2026-04-09 14:10    my-project        5
550e8400-e29b-41d4-a716-4469   2026-04-08 18:30   2026-04-08 18:30    refactor-api      18

docs.title: Resume a Session
docs.text:
Pick up where you left off:

hone session resume debug-auth

All prior messages and context are restored. New turns are added to the session.

docs.title: Rename and Delete
docs.text:
# Rename a session
hone session rename debug-auth debug-authentication

# Delete a session (permanent)
hone session delete old-session

docs.title: Ephemeral Mode (No Persistence)
docs.text:
For sensitive work or testing, skip auto-save:

hone --ephemeral

The session runs but isn't saved after it exits. Useful for:

  • Sensitive code review
  • One-off debugging
  • Cost-limited testing

docs.title: Session Workflow Example
docs.text:
# Day 1: Start a feature branch
hone --session feature/user-auth
# Conversation happens, auto-saved after each turn

# Day 2: Resume work
hone session list
# Find feature/user-auth in the list

hone session resume feature/user-auth
# Pick up right where you left off, full context restored

# Done, rename it
hone session rename feature/user-auth feature/user-auth-complete

docs.title: 8. Modes of Operation
docs.text: Hone supports multiple modes. Choose the right one for your task.

docs.title: Shell Commands
docs.text:
Run native shell commands directly from Hone without exiting the TUI.

!ls                 # List files, output shown inline
!git status         # Check git status
!cargo test         # Run tests
!cd src             # Change directory (confined to project)
!nvim file.rs       # Open editor, suspend TUI, restore on exit

Full Example:

> !cargo test
  running 12 tests
  test test_add ... ok
  test test_subtract ... ok
  12 passed, 0 failed

  claude-sonnet │ $0.00 │ ▓▓▓░░░░░░░ 28% ctx │ !shell

Features:

  • All standard shell commands supported
  • Output captured and displayed inline
  • Directory changes persist for the session
  • !cd confined to project root (security)
  • !nvim, !vim, !vi, or any $EDITOR suspend TUI and restore after exit

docs.title: Vim Keybindings
docs.text:
Enable vim-style keybindings for navigating and editing within Hone.

Start vim mode:

hone --vim

Or toggle in interactive mode:

:set vim      # Enable vim mode
:set novim    # Disable vim mode

Normal Mode:

j         Move down
k         Move up
h         Move left
l         Move right
gg        Jump to top
G         Jump to bottom
w         Jump to next word
b         Jump to previous word
i         Enter insert mode (before cursor)
a         Enter insert mode (after cursor)
o         Insert new line below
O         Insert new line above
d         Delete (dd = delete line)
y         Yank/copy (yy = copy line)
p         Paste
u         Undo
Ctrl-r    Redo
:q        Quit to previous view
:wq       Save and quit

Insert Mode:

Type normally to edit text
Esc       Return to normal mode

Full Example:

> :set vim
Vim mode enabled.

> gg              # Jump to top of input
> i               # Enter insert mode
> (type new prompt)
> Esc             # Return to normal mode
> :q              # Submit

docs.title: TDD Workflow
docs.text:
Watch source files and automatically run tests on change. Perfect for test-driven development.

Start TDD mode:

:tdd cargo test

Hone will now: 1. Watch all source files (300ms debounce) 2. Run cargo test when files change 3. Display PASS/FAIL inline 4. Repeat until you stop

Stop TDD mode:

:tdd off

Full Example:

> :tdd cargo test
  [TDD] watching for changes, running: cargo test

  ... (waiting for edits) ...

  [TDD] change detected: src/lib.rs — running tests...
  [TDD] tests PASSED
    12 passed in 0.4s

  [TDD] change detected: src/main.rs — running tests...
  [TDD] tests FAILED
    test test_parse ... FAILED (expected Ok, got Err)

  [TDD] change detected: src/main.rs — running tests...
  [TDD] tests PASSED
    12 passed in 0.5s

Use Cases:

  • Red-Green-Refactor workflow
  • Continuous verification while implementing
  • Early detection of regressions
  • Works with any test command: cargo test, pytest, npm test, etc.

docs.title: One-Shot Mode (Fast)
docs.text:
Run a single prompt and exit. No interactive TUI.

hone "List all Python files in src/"

Use when:

  • Quick questions
  • Scripting (output to stdout)
  • Quick file exploration

Output goes to stdout, suitable for piping:

hone "Analyze error in this log" < error.log > analysis.txt

docs.title: Interactive Mode (Default)
docs.text:
Start a conversational session with the TUI.

hone

or

hone --session my-project

Use when:

  • Multi-step tasks (exploration → implementation → testing)
  • Iterative development
  • Real-time feedback

TUI features:

  • Type prompts freely
  • Press ? for help
  • Type /cmd for commands
  • Streaming tokens in real-time
  • Cost tracking on each turn

Commands in interactive mode:

/model <provider:model>   — Switch models mid-session
/budget <usd>             — Set spending limit
/clear                    — Clear conversation history
/export <path>            — Save session to JSON
/help                     — Show all commands
/quit                     — Exit

docs.title: Orchestrate Mode (Complex Tasks)
docs.text:
Decompose complex tasks into parallel subtasks, executed by worker agents, then merged.

Recommended for: Features with multiple concerns (API + CLI + tests), complex refactors.

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
hone --orchestrate "Add comprehensive email validation: write tests, implement validation logic, build CLI interface, document API"

What happens:

1. Orchestrator decomposes: test_suite, validation_impl, cli_build, api_docs
2. 4 workers execute in parallel
3. Results merged into coherent output
4. Final response shows all changes

Output example:

[Orchestrator] Decomposing task...

[PlanCreated]
Subtask 1: write_test_suite (worker 0)
Subtask 2: implement_validation (worker 1)
Subtask 3: build_cli_interface (worker 2)
Subtask 4: document_api (worker 3)

[WorkerStarted] Worker 0: write_test_suite
[WorkerStarted] Worker 1: implement_validation
[WorkerStarted] Worker 2: build_cli_interface
[WorkerStarted] Worker 3: document_api

[WorkerCompleted] Worker 0: test_suite.rs (450 tokens)
[WorkerCompleted] Worker 1: validation.rs (1200 tokens)
[WorkerCompleted] Worker 2: cli.rs (890 tokens)
[WorkerCompleted] Worker 3: docs.md (340 tokens)

[MergingResults]
Combining all outputs...

[Final Output]
Complete email validation system with tests, logic, CLI, and docs.

Total tokens: 4521 input, 892 output
Total cost: $0.084 USD

docs.title: Ensemble Mode (Ranking Best Response)
docs.text:
Run N parallel candidates with varied temperatures and automatically rank the best.

hone --ensemble 3 "Implement a binary search function"

What happens:

1. Run 3 workers with T=0.1, T=0.5, T=0.8
2. Each produces a different response
3. Ranker evaluates all 3
4. Returns the best one

Use when:

  • You want the best result, not just any result
  • Task quality matters more than speed
  • Budget allows 3x API calls

docs.title: Recipe Mode (Structured Workflows)
docs.text:
Run a pre-defined workflow (TDD, bug-fix, code-review, refactor).

hone --recipe tdd-feature

Built-in recipes:

  • tdd-feature — Write tests first, then implementation
  • bug-fix — Root cause analysis, fix, test
  • code-review — Systematic code review with checklist
  • refactor — Analyze, plan, implement, verify

Each recipe is a YAML workflow defining the steps, prompts, and validation rules.

docs.title: Agent Persona Mode
docs.text:
Switch to a specialized agent persona.

hone --agent debugger "There's a segfault in main"
hone --agent security-auditor "Review this authentication module"
hone --agent code-reviewer "Review the PR changes"

Available personas:

  • code-reviewer — Code quality, style, testing
  • debugger — Debugging, root cause analysis
  • security-auditor — Security issues, vulnerabilities
  • test-architect — Test design and coverage
  • ml-recommendations-expert — ML/AI algorithm design
  • ai-researcher — Research, papers, novel ideas
  • python-expert — Python-specific improvements
  • rust-expert — Rust idioms and performance

docs.title: Decision Guide: Which Mode for Which Task?
docs.text: Task Mode Command Quick Q&A One-shot hone "What is..." Multi-turn debugging Interactive hone --session debug Complex feature (API + tests + CLI) Orchestrate hone --orchestrate "..." Choose best of 3 solutions Ensemble hone --ensemble 3 "..." TDD workflow Recipe hone --recipe tdd-feature Code review focus Agent hone --agent code-reviewer Complex reasoning problem Agent hone --agent ai-researcher

docs.title: 9. MCP Extensions
docs.text: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers extend Hone with external tools: GitHub, Slack, databases, custom integrations.

docs.title: What is MCP?
docs.text:
MCP is a protocol for AI agents to call external services. Instead of hardcoding GitHub, Slack, and database tools into Hone, we use MCP servers as plugins.

Example: With the GitHub MCP server, Hone can:

  • List open PRs
  • Create issues
  • Add comments
  • Merge PRs
  • Query workflows

docs.title: Quick Setup
docs.text:
Create .hone/mcp.json in your project:

{
  "mcp_servers": [
    {
      "name": "github",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"],
      "env": {
        "GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "slack",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["@modelcontextprotocol/server-slack"],
      "env": {
        "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN": "${SLACK_BOT_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Set environment variables:

export GITHUB_TOKEN="ghp_..."
export SLACK_BOT_TOKEN="xoxb-..."
hone

Hone now has GitHub and Slack available as tools.

docs.title: Available MCP Servers
docs.text: See the MCP Extensions Guide for a complete list and setup instructions.

docs.title: 10. Remote Access (honed)
docs.text: Run Hone as a persistent daemon server accessible over the network.

docs.title: Start the Daemon
docs.text:
honed 7070  # Listen on port 7070

With auth token:

export HONE_AUTH_TOKEN="sk-hone-abc123def456..."
honed 7070

With custom session database path:

export HONE_SESSION_DB="$HOME/.local/share/hone/sessions.db"
honed 7070

Daemon output:

honed 0.1.0

Listening on http://0.0.0.0:7070
Auth enabled: true
Session storage: SQLite at /Users/user/.local/share/hone/sessions.db

docs.title: Connect from Another Machine
docs.text:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-hone-abc123..." \
  https://remote-hone-server.example.com:7070/health

docs.text:

docs.title: API Key Not Found
docs.text:
Error:

error: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY not set

Solution:

Set the environment variable:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
hone

Or add to ~/.config/hone/config.toml:

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "sk-ant-..."

Verify:

echo $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

docs.title: Model Not Found
docs.text:
Error:

error: model 'anthropic:claude-unknown' not supported

Solution:

List available models:

hone --list-models

Use a valid model name:

hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5 "hello"

docs.title: Network Error or Timeout
docs.text:
Error:

error: failed to connect to Anthropic API (timeout after 30s)

Solutions:

  1. Check internet connection: 

    curl https://api.anthropic.com

  2. Check firewall/proxy: 

    [http]
proxy = "http://proxy.example.com:8080"

  3. Increase timeout: 

    hone --timeout 60

  4. Check API status: https://status.anthropic.com

docs.title: Sandbox Policy Violation
docs.text:
Error:

error: sandbox policy denied access to /secret/data

Explanation:

Hone's sandbox prevents unauthorized file access for security. The file path isn't in the allowlist.

Solution:

Add the path to ~/.config/hone/config.toml:

[sandbox.defaults]
allow_read = ["{project_root}", "/secret/data"]

docs.title: Out of Memory / Context Exceeded
docs.text:
Error:

error: context window exceeded (64k > 200k limit)

Solution:

Clear the session history:

/clear

Or reduce context limit:

hone --context-limit 32000

docs.title: Configuration File Not Found
docs.text:
Error:

error: config file not found at ~/.config/hone/config.toml

Solution:

Create the directory and file:

mkdir -p ~/.config/hone
hone configure

docs.title: Ollama Connection Failed
docs.text:
Error:

error: failed to connect to Ollama at http://localhost:11434

Solutions:

  1. Start Ollama server: 

    ollama serve

  2. Check it's running: 

    curl http://localhost:11434/api/tags

  3. Verify models are installed: 

    ollama list

  4. If using custom host: 

    export OLLAMA_HOST="http://192.168.1.10:11434"
hone --model ollama:llama3.2

docs.title: Sessions Database Issues
docs.text:
Error:

error: failed to open sessions database

Solutions:

  1. Ensure directory exists: 

    mkdir -p ~/.local/share/hone

  2. Check permissions: 

    ls -la ~/.local/share/hone/

  3. Repair database: 

    rm ~/.local/share/hone/sessions.db
hone session list  # Creates fresh database

docs.title: Goose Pass-Through Provider Research
docs.text: Date: 2026-04-05 Context: Research into Goose's (block/goose) CLI provider pattern to inform Hone's ClaudeCliProvider and GeminiCliProvider implementation strategy.

docs.title: 1. How the Pattern Works
docs.text: Goose's CLI provider pattern is a two-generation design. Understanding both generations is essential because the first generation (which Hone currently mirrors) has been deprecated.

docs.title: Generation 1: Raw stdin/stdout subprocess (deprecated)
docs.text:
The original claude-code, gemini-cli, and codex providers in Goose work exactly as Hone's current implementation does:

  • Spawn the CLI binary as a child process with piped stdin/stdout.
  • A CliProcess struct owns the child process lifecycle.
  • Messages are serialised into a flat text prompt with role prefixes (Human: / Assistant: for Claude Code, plain text for Gemini CLI).
  • Streaming responses are read line-by-line from stdout:
  • Claude Code — parses newline-delimited JSON events (--output-format stream-json).
  • Codex — parses newline-delimited JSON events.
  • Gemini CLI — reads plain text; no structured envelope.
  • Cursor Agent — parses a JSON response envelope.
  • Communication is one-shot per turn: one prompt in, streamed text out. There is no bidirectional channel.

Critical limitation: Goose's own extension system (MCP tool servers) is silently stripped from the system prompt before sending to the subprocess, because the CLI tool has its own internal tool ecosystem. No tool calls issued by the model are relayed back to the Goose orchestrator. The subprocess either handles them internally (Claude CLI's built-in tools) or they are lost.

sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Hone / Goose Orchestrator
    participant C as CLI Binary (claude/gemini)
    H->>C: spawn(binary, args=[--output-format stream-json, -p, prompt])
    C-->>H: stdout: newline-delimited JSON or plain text tokens
    note over H,C: Tool calls inside the CLI are handled internally<br/>by the CLI binary. Goose/Hone never sees them.
    C-->>H: EOF (process exits)
    H->>H: reconstruct full text response

docs.title: Generation 2: Agent Client Protocol / ACP (current)
docs.text:
Goose replaced the raw subprocess approach with the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), which is now the default via providers named claude-acp, codex-acp, and gemini-acp.

ACP is a JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol over stdio (with WebSocket and HTTP planned). The agent binary runs as a local subprocess that stays alive across turns, and the orchestrator communicates with it via structured JSON-RPC messages:

Method Direction Purpose session/initialize orchestrator → agent declare capabilities, pass MCP server list session/new orchestrator → agent start a new conversation session session/prompt orchestrator → agent send a user turn session/update agent → orchestrator stream response tokens / tool call events session/cancel orchestrator → agent abort in-flight request 
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Goose Orchestrator
    participant A as ACP Agent Process (claude-acp)
    H->>A: {jsonrpc, method: session/initialize, params: {mcpServers: [...]}}
    A-->>H: {result: {capabilities: [...]}}
    H->>A: {method: session/new}
    loop each turn
        H->>A: {method: session/prompt, params: {message: "..."}}
        A-->>H: {method: session/update, params: {type: token, text: "..."}}
        A-->>H: {method: session/update, params: {type: toolCall, name: "...", args: {...}}}
        A-->>H: {method: session/update, params: {type: toolCallResult, ...}}
        A-->>H: {method: session/update, params: {type: done}}
    end

Because ACP is bidirectional and the subprocess is long-lived, the orchestrator can now pass its own MCP tool servers to the agent at initialization. Tool calls that the agent model makes can be surfaced back through session/update notifications and routed to the correct tool executor.

docs.title: 2. Key Architectural Decisions in Goose
docs.text:
1. Per-CLI adapters, not a generic wrapper. Each CLI binary gets its own adapter struct because the output format varies significantly (JSON-RPC vs. newline-delimited JSON vs. plain text). There is no single generic "CLI provider" abstraction.

  2. System prompt filtering is mandatory. The CLI tools run their own agent loop internally. Injecting Goose's MCP tool definitions into the system prompt causes conflicts. Goose filters them out entirely for Generation 1 providers.

  3. ACP is the answer to tool passthrough. The only way Goose solved the tool-call problem is by moving to a protocol (ACP) where the subprocess declares its capabilities and the orchestrator can inspect or relay tool events. Raw stdio line-reading cannot carry structured bidirectional tool-call/result pairs reliably.

  4. Generation 1 is a convenience shim, not a production integration. Goose's own documentation describes the deprecated CLI providers as included "purely as a convenience" and explicitly states they do not give access to the extension ecosystem. The GitHub maintainers noted that using them means you "don't get most of the features."

docs.title: 3. What Hone Should Adopt or Change
Where Hone currently stands
docs.text:
Hone's ClaudeCliProvider and GeminiCliProvider in crates/hone-providers/src/adapters/ implement Generation 1 faithfully:

  • /adapters/cli_common.rs — spawn_cli_stream reads stdout line-by-line and emits ProviderEvent::Token for every non-empty line.
  • /adapters/claude_cli.rs — passes --output-format stream-json and a flat text prompt; supports_tools: false is correctly set.
  • /adapters/gemini_cli.rs — similar pattern.

The supports_tools: false flag is accurate: the current design cannot relay tool calls back to Hone's tool dispatcher.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
Option A — Accept Generation 1 as a subscription-cost shortcut only (low effort)

Keep the current implementation as-is, make the limitation explicit in documentation, and do not wire these providers into Hone's tool-call dispatch path. Use them solely for conversational turns where the model's built-in tools (file read/write inside claude) are sufficient and Hone's own tools are not needed. This matches Goose's own positioning of these providers before deprecation.

Option B — Implement ACP for Claude Code and Gemini CLI (high value)

Implement the session/initialize → session/prompt → session/update JSON-RPC-over-stdio protocol in a new AcpCliProvider (or per-CLI variants). This would:

  • Keep the subprocess alive across turns (no re-spawn overhead).
  • Allow passing Hone's MCP tool server list to the agent at initialization.
  • Surface toolCall and toolCallResult events so Hone's Dispatcher can handle them.
  • Mirror exactly what Goose does with claude-acp / gemini-acp.

The ACP spec is public at agentclientprotocol.com and Goose's source is open for reference.

Option C — Use Claude's --output-format json with print mode for richer tool events (medium effort)

Rather than flat text prompts, drive claude --print --output-format stream-json in a loop, parsing the structured JSONL envelope that includes tool_use and tool_result content blocks. This does not require ACP but does require Hone to manage conversation state externally and re-invoke the binary each turn with the full history. It gives tool-call visibility without the persistent-process complexity of ACP. This is likely sufficient for Hone's near-term needs if full ACP implementation is too costly.

docs.title: 4. Limitations of the Pass-Through Approach (Any Generation)
docs.text:
Limitation Generation 1 Generation 2 (ACP) Tool calls visible to orchestrator No Yes (via notifications) Hone's own MCP tools usable No Yes (declared at init) Long-lived session / no re-spawn No Yes Structured token cost reporting Partial (JSON parsing) Yes Cancellation mid-stream Process kill only session/cancel message Platform support macOS/Linux only macOS/Linux (Windows untested) CLI binary authentication state Inherited from user shell Inherited from user shell Model selection flexibility Binary flag Declared capability Rate limits / billing Via user's subscription Via user's subscription Debuggability Low (opaque subprocess) Medium (structured logs)

The fundamental constraint that neither generation fully resolves: the CLI binary is an opaque agent. It has its own planning loop, its own context window management, and its own tool set. When Hone delegates to it, Hone surrenders control of the agent loop. For simple "use your subscription credits" use cases this is acceptable. For workflows where Hone needs precise control over tool dispatch, context injection, or multi-step orchestration, the direct API providers (anthropic, openai) remain the correct choice.

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
Hone is an open-source, privacy-first, terminal-native AI coding agent designed to unify the best capabilities from every existing tool in the category — while filling the critical gaps none of them address.

The terminal AI coding agent market has exploded to 15+ serious contenders serving millions of developers daily. Yet no single tool combines provider-agnostic model support, kernel-level sandboxing, LSP code intelligence, a layered tool architecture that uses native CLI for speed and MCP for extensibility, adaptive pattern learning, and secure remote access. Developers are forced to juggle 2–3 tools, fragmenting context and compounding costs.

Hone eliminates this fragmentation. It is built on three foundational principles:

  1. Your models, your machine, your rules. Run any model — local or cloud, any provider — with data that never leaves your control unless you explicitly choose otherwise.
  2. Intelligence compounds. Hone learns your patterns, preferences, and project conventions through a local-first adaptive memory system that gets smarter with every session.
  3. Work from anywhere. A secure client-server architecture lets you start a task in the terminal and seamlessly continue from your phone, tablet, or browser — all through an encrypted tunnel with zero cloud dependency.

docs.title: 2.1 The Fragmentation Tax
docs.text:
Developers in 2026 use an average of 2.3 terminal AI coding agents. Each tool excels in one dimension but forces painful trade-offs in others:

Pain Point Cause Impact Vendor lock-in Claude Code (Anthropic only), Codex (OpenAI only), Gemini CLI (Google only) Developers can't use the best model for each task No real security OpenCode admits its permissions are "not designed to provide security isolation" Autonomous mode is a liability No pattern memory Most tools start fresh each session; config files are manual Repeated explanations, inconsistent output No remote access Only OpenCode has client-server; no tool has a mobile-optimized UI Can't monitor or intervene from a phone Context amnesia Auto-compaction loses early instructions; no persistent semantic index Agents forget what matters mid-session Cost opacity No tool shows real-time token consumption before executing $50+ surprise sessions are common No test-driven loop Agents guess at correctness instead of iterating against a test contract Bugs shipped to production

docs.title: 3.1 Product Vision
docs.text: Hone is the last terminal coding agent you'll ever need — an open-source, self-hosted, privacy-respecting AI development partner that learns your style, runs any model, works from any device, and gets smarter every day.

docs.title: 3.2 Positioning Statement
docs.text: For professional developers who demand privacy, model freedom, and mobility, Hone is the terminal AI coding agent that unifies kernel-enforced security, LSP code intelligence, a layered tool architecture (native CLI + MCP + Code Mode), and adaptive pattern learning into a single open-source tool. Unlike Claude Code, Codex CLI, or OpenCode, Hone never locks you to a vendor, never sends data without consent, and never forgets what it learned about your codebase.

docs.title: 3.3 Design Principles
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[Privacy by Default] --> B[Intelligence Compounds]
    B --> C[Extensibility over Features]
    C --> D[Speed is a Feature]
    D --> E[Terminal First, Multi-Surface]
    E --> F[Open Source, Open Governance]

    style A fill:#E94560,color:#fff
    style B fill:#0F3460,color:#fff
    style C fill:#16213E,color:#fff
    style D fill:#1A1A2E,color:#fff
    style E fill:#533483,color:#fff
    style F fill:#2B2D42,color:#fff
  1. Privacy by Default — Local-first. No telemetry. No data leaves the machine unless the user opts in. Encrypted at rest and in transit.
  2. Intelligence Compounds — Every session makes the next one better. Memory, conventions, and learnings persist locally and improve over time.
  3. Extensibility over Features — Build the platform, not every feature. A layered tool architecture — native CLI for hot-path operations, MCP for external integrations, Code Mode for complex orchestration, Skills for guidance — means each layer does what it does best without taxing the others.
  4. Speed is a Feature — Sub-100ms startup. Streaming responses. Rust core for hot paths. Never make the developer wait for the tool.
  5. Terminal First, Multi-Surface — The CLI is the primary interface. Web, mobile, and IDE are secondary surfaces consuming the same backend.
  6. Open Source, Open Governance — Apache 2.0 license. Community-driven roadmap. Aiming for Linux Foundation / AAIF membership alongside Goose and MCP.

docs.title: 4.1 Primary Personas
docs.text:
The Privacy-Conscious Professional — Senior engineer at a regulated company (finance, healthcare, government). Needs local model support, audit trails, and zero data leakage. Currently uses Aider + Ollama but lacks intelligence and remote access.

The Multi-Stack Polyglot — Full-stack developer working across 3–5 languages and repositories. Needs the best model for each task (Claude for architecture, GPT for speed, local for sensitive code). Currently switches between Claude Code and OpenCode depending on task.

The Mobile-First Operator — DevOps/SRE or indie developer who monitors and manages deployments from a phone. Needs to kick off tasks, review diffs, and approve changes remotely. Currently SSH-es into a tmux session as a workaround.

The Team Lead — Manages 5–15 developers and needs governance: spend caps, model policies, approved extensions, audit logs. Currently has no visibility into team AI usage.

docs.title: 4.2 Secondary Personas
docs.text:
The Open-Source Contributor — Wants to extend Hone with MCP servers, custom agents, and recipes. Values documentation, plugin APIs, and community.

The Student/Hobbyist — Budget-constrained. Needs the free tier (local models) to be genuinely capable, not a teaser for paid features.

docs.title: 6.3 Client-Server Split
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Phone as Mobile / Web
    participant Tunnel as WireGuard Tunnel
    participant Server as honed (dev machine)
    participant Sandbox as Kernel Sandbox
    participant Model as LLM (local/cloud)
    participant LSP as LSP Server
    participant FS as File System

    Phone->>Tunnel: Encrypted request
    Tunnel->>Server: Forward to honed
    Server->>Server: Authenticate (token/mTLS)
    Server->>Model: Send prompt + context
    Model-->>Server: Stream tokens
    Server->>Sandbox: Execute tool call
    Sandbox->>FS: Read/write within sandbox
    Sandbox->>LSP: Validate edit
    LSP-->>Sandbox: Diagnostics
    Sandbox-->>Server: Result + diagnostics
    Server-->>Tunnel: Stream response
    Tunnel-->>Phone: Encrypted response
    Server->>Server: Update memory + cost tracker

The honed daemon runs on the developer's machine (or a self-hosted server). All clients — CLI, web, mobile, IDE — connect to the same instance. Sessions persist across disconnects. The server holds all state; clients are stateless renderers.

docs.title: 8.1 Universal Model Support
docs.text:
Hone must treat LLM providers as interchangeable backends. No model provider receives special treatment or tighter integration than any other.

Provider abstraction layer:

graph TB
    subgraph "Model Router"
        ROUTER[Smart Router<br/>Selects model per task]
        FALLBACK[Fallback Chain<br/>Auto-retry on failure]
        COST_R[Cost Optimizer<br/>Route cheap tasks to cheap models]
    end

    subgraph "Provider Adapters"
        A1[Anthropic Adapter]
        A2[OpenAI Adapter]
        A3[Google Adapter]
        A4[Ollama Adapter]
        A5[llama.cpp Adapter]
        A6[vLLM Adapter]
        A7[OpenRouter Adapter]
        A8[AWS Bedrock Adapter]
        A9[Azure OpenAI Adapter]
        A10[CLI Pass-through<br/>Claude Code / Codex / Gemini CLI]
        A11[Custom OpenAI-Compatible]
    end

    ROUTER --> FALLBACK
    FALLBACK --> COST_R
    COST_R --> A1
    COST_R --> A2
    COST_R --> A3
    COST_R --> A4
    COST_R --> A5
    COST_R --> A6
    COST_R --> A7
    COST_R --> A8
    COST_R --> A9
    COST_R --> A10
    COST_R --> A11

Key capabilities:

  • Hot-swap models mid-session without losing context (conversation history is model-agnostic)
  • Per-agent model configuration: define a "fast-local" agent using Qwen 3 via Ollama and a "deep-cloud" agent using Claude Opus 4.6
  • Model routing rules: "Use local model for file reads; use cloud model for multi-file refactors"
  • Fallback chains: if primary model is rate-limited, auto-switch to secondary
  • CLI pass-through providers: piggyback on existing Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI subscriptions
  • Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint support for self-hosted or enterprise deployments

Configuration example (hone.toml):

[models.default]
provider = "ollama"
model = "qwen3:32b"
context_length = 131072

[models.deep]
provider = "anthropic"
model = "claude-opus-4-6"
context_length = 1000000
api_key_env = "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"

[models.fast]
provider = "openai"
model = "gpt-5.3-codex-spark"
context_length = 256000

[routing]
file_read = "default"          # cheap local model
multi_file_edit = "deep"       # powerful cloud model
test_generation = "fast"       # speed-optimized
planning = "deep"
code_review = "deep"

docs.title: 8.2 Kernel-Enforced Sandboxing
docs.text:
The sandbox is not a permission prompt. It is a kernel-level enforcement boundary that the agent cannot bypass.

graph TB
    subgraph "Autonomy Modes"
        M1[Manual<br/>Approve every action]
        M2[Supervised<br/>Auto-approve reads,<br/>prompt for writes]
        M3[Autonomous<br/>Full auto within sandbox]
    end

    subgraph "Sandbox Layers"
        L1[Filesystem<br/>Landlock / Seatbelt<br/>Project dir only]
        L2[Network<br/>Disabled by default<br/>Allowlist domains]
        L3[Process<br/>seccomp-BPF<br/>Blocked syscalls]
        L4[Resource<br/>cgroups v2<br/>CPU/memory limits]
    end

    subgraph "Escape Hatches"
        E1[User approval<br/>Explicit per-action]
        E2[Allowlisted commands<br/>Per-project config]
        E3[Protected paths<br/>.git, .hone, ~, /etc]
    end

    M3 --> L1
    M3 --> L2
    M3 --> L3
    M3 --> L4

    M2 --> E1
    M2 --> E2

    M1 --> E1
    M1 --> E3

Implementation details:

  • macOS: Dynamic Apple Seatbelt profiles generated at runtime based on project directory and configured permissions. Profiles are compiled and enforced by the kernel.
  • Linux: Three-layer defense — Bubblewrap (user namespace isolation) + Landlock (filesystem access control) + seccomp-BPF (syscall filtering). A dedicated hone-sandbox helper binary with minimal privileges.
  • Container mode: For environments without kernel sandbox support, spawn tool execution inside an OCI container (Podman/Docker) with volume-mounted project directory. Zero runtime dependencies beyond the container engine.
  • Network policy: Network is OFF by default in Autonomous mode. Users define domain allowlists in hone.toml. DNS resolution is filtered through the sandbox.
  • Protected paths: .git/, .hone/, home directory, system directories are NEVER writable in any autonomous mode. Modifications require explicit user approval regardless of mode.
  • Fail-closed design: If the sandbox cannot be initialized (missing kernel support, permission denied), Hone refuses to enter Autonomous mode and falls back to Manual.

docs.title: 8.3 LSP-Powered Code Intelligence
docs.text:
Every file edit is validated by the actual language toolchain, not by pattern matching or the LLM's judgment.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent as Hone Agent
    participant LSP as LSP Server
    participant FS as File System
    participant Index as Semantic Index

    Agent->>FS: Read file (pre-edit)
    Agent->>LSP: textDocument/didOpen
    Agent->>FS: Apply edit
    Agent->>LSP: textDocument/didChange
    LSP-->>Agent: publishDiagnostics

    alt Diagnostics clean
        Agent->>Index: Update semantic index
        Agent->>Agent: Continue to next step
    else Errors found
        Agent->>Agent: Auto-fix attempt (max 3)
        Agent->>LSP: textDocument/didChange (retry)
        LSP-->>Agent: publishDiagnostics
    end

    Note over Agent,LSP: Also available to agent
    Agent->>LSP: textDocument/hover
    Agent->>LSP: textDocument/definition
    Agent->>LSP: textDocument/references
    Agent->>LSP: workspace/symbol

Supported language servers (P0 launch):

TypeScript (tsserver), Go (gopls), Python (Pyright), Rust (rust-analyzer), Java (Eclipse JDT), C/C++ (clangd), PHP (Intelephense), Ruby (Solargraph), Elixir (ElixirLS), Zig (zls)

Additional servers (P1):

Kotlin, Swift, C#, Haskell, OCaml, Lua, Terraform, SQL, YAML, Dockerfile

Auto-detection: Hone scans the project for language markers (package.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml, etc.) and automatically starts the appropriate LSP servers. No configuration required for standard setups.

docs.title: 8.4 Layered Tool Architecture
docs.text:
Hone's most critical architectural decision: core tools are native, external tools use MCP, complex flows use Code Mode, and guidance uses Skills. This is a deliberate rejection of the "MCP everything" approach (used by Goose) based on hard production data showing that MCP schema overhead can consume 55,000–143,000 tokens before a conversation even starts, degrading both cost and LLM response quality.

graph TB
    subgraph "Layer 3: Skills — HONE.md"
        S1[Markdown instructions<br/>Conventions, workflows, patterns]
        S_NOTE["Zero tokens at runtime<br/>Loaded on demand when relevant"]
    end

    subgraph "Layer 2: Native Tools — Rust hot path"
        N1[hone-fs: read/write/search]
        N2[hone-shell: sandboxed exec]
        N3[hone-git: commit/branch/diff]
        N4[hone-lsp: diagnostics/hover/refs]
        N5[hone-index: semantic search]
        N6[hone-cost: token/budget tracking]
        N_NOTE["Direct Rust function calls<br/>Zero protocol overhead, sub-ms"]
    end

    subgraph "Layer 1: MCP — External integrations"
        M1[GitHub / GitLab]
        M2[Jira / Linear / Slack]
        M3[Databases / Cloud / K8s]
        M4[Custom enterprise APIs]
        M_NOTE["JSON-RPC protocol<br/>Auth, state, audit trails<br/>Schemas loaded lazily"]
    end

    subgraph "Layer 0: Code Mode — Orchestration"
        C1[Agent writes TS or Python]
        C2[Calls native + MCP via SDK]
        C_NOTE["1 LLM pass replaces N tool calls<br/>50%+ token reduction"]
    end

    style N1 fill:#E94560,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#E94560,color:#fff
    style N3 fill:#E94560,color:#fff
    style N4 fill:#E94560,color:#fff
    style M1 fill:#0F3460,color:#fff
    style M2 fill:#0F3460,color:#fff
    style C1 fill:#533483,color:#fff
    style S1 fill:#059669,color:#fff

Why not MCP for everything? Production evidence is clear:

  • A five-MCP-server setup with 58 tools consumes ~55,000 tokens of context before the user types anything (StackOne production data)
  • Some deployments report 70,000–90,000 tokens consumed by tool schemas alone — up to 72% of the context window
  • LLM instruction-following quality degrades as tool definitions fill the context window
  • Perplexity, Cloudflare, and multiple Y Combinator companies have independently moved core operations away from MCP to direct CLI approaches in 2026
  • Anthropic's own engineering blog recommends Code Mode — having the agent write code to call tools rather than invoking them directly via MCP

Why not CLI for everything? CLI tools assume shell access, which mobile clients, browser extensions, and non-technical integrations cannot provide. CLI has no standardized discovery, authentication, or audit trail. External services with OAuth flows, connection pooling, and state management genuinely benefit from MCP infrastructure.

The layered approach — which layer handles what:

Task Layer Why This Layer Read/write project files Native (L2) Direct Rust fs calls, zero overhead, sub-ms Run tests, build, lint Native (L2) Shell execution, structured output, already exists Git operations Native (L2) git CLI is battle-tested, agents parse it well LSP diagnostics after edit Native (L2) Direct IPC to language server, latency-critical Search codebase (grep/ripgrep) Native (L2) Text search + tree-sitter AST, fast and precise Coding conventions and style Skills (L3) Loaded contextually from HONE.md, zero tokens when unused Connect to GitHub API MCP (L1) OAuth, pagination, webhooks — needs infrastructure Post to Slack / update Jira MCP (L1) External service with auth and audit requirements Query a database MCP (L1) Connection pooling, credentials, type-safe results Multi-tool orchestration (5+ steps) Code Mode (L0) Agent writes a script calling both native + MCP tools; 1 LLM pass

Practical result: A task like "read the auth module, find the bug, fix it, run tests, commit" hits zero MCP overhead — all native Layer 2. A task like "find the Jira ticket, update it, post to Slack, create a PR on GitHub" uses MCP for external integrations but orchestrates them via Code Mode in a single inference pass.

MCP extension management (Layer 1):

  • hone ext list — show installed and available MCP servers
  • hone ext add <name> — install from registry or URL
  • hone ext remove <name> — uninstall
  • Lazy schema loading: MCP tool schemas are NOT loaded into context at session start. They load only when the agent determines a task requires an external integration, and only the relevant server's tools are loaded.
  • Per-project extensions in hone.toml; global extensions in ~/.config/hone/extensions.toml
  • Extension permissions are sandboxed: an MCP server for Slack cannot access the filesystem unless explicitly granted

Code Mode implementation (Layer 0):

When the agent detects a task requiring 3+ tool calls across multiple services, it switches to Code Mode:

  1. Agent receives the task description
  2. Agent generates a TypeScript/Python script importing a Hone SDK
  3. Script calls both native tools (hone.fs.read(), hone.git.commit()) and MCP tools (hone.mcp.github.createPR()) programmatically
  4. Script executes inside the kernel sandbox
  5. Only the final result returns to LLM context — intermediate data stays in script memory

This avoids the anti-pattern where intermediate results (e.g., a full document body from Google Drive) pass through the LLM context multiple times, compounding token costs.

docs.title: 8.5 File Editing System
docs.text:
Hone uses a hybrid editing approach that combines the best of each competitor:

Technique Used When Derived From Exact string replacement Small, targeted edits OpenCode Patch/diff application Multi-line changes Codex CLI Full file write New files or complete rewrites Claude Code AST-aware transforms Rename symbol, extract function Novel

Every edit passes through:

  1. Pre-edit snapshot — Git stash or internal checkpoint
  2. Edit application — Using the most token-efficient method
  3. LSP validation — Diagnostics check for errors
  4. Auto-fix loop — Up to 3 retry attempts if errors found
  5. Post-edit index update — Semantic index refreshed incrementally
  6. Git commit — Automatic commit with descriptive message (configurable)

Undo/redo: Full git-backed undo (/undo) and redo (/redo) at any point. Branching for exploratory edits (/branch experiment-name).

docs.title: 8.6 Cost Estimation Engine
docs.text:
Before every action that consumes tokens, Hone displays an estimated cost:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Estimated cost for this operation:              │
│                                                  │
│  Input tokens:  ~45,000  ($0.34)                │
│  Output tokens: ~12,000  ($0.18)                │
│  Total:                   $0.52                  │
│                                                  │
│  Session total so far:    $3.27                  │
│  Daily budget remaining:  $16.73                 │
│                                                  │
│  [Enter] Proceed  [c] Cheaper model  [s] Skip   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Implementation:

  • Token estimation based on context window state + planned tool calls
  • Per-provider pricing tables updated weekly via a lightweight config fetch
  • Configurable daily/weekly/monthly budget caps with hard enforcement
  • Budget alerts at 50%, 80%, and 95% thresholds
  • Cost breakdown per session, per day, per project in hone stats

docs.text: Threat Mitigation Malicious model output (prompt injection via code) Kernel sandbox prevents execution outside project dir; network deny-by-default Supply chain attack via MCP server MCP servers (Layer 1 only) run in isolated processes with declared permissions; sandboxed filesystem access; core tools are native Rust and not exposed to MCP attack surface Credential leakage API keys stored in OS keychain, never in config files; environment variables cleared from sandbox Remote access interception WireGuard/Tailscale encrypted tunnel; mTLS for API authentication; no plaintext HTTP Runaway cost Hard budget caps enforced at the server level; auto-pause at threshold Data exfiltration Network deny-by-default in Autonomous mode; DNS filtering; audit log for all network requests

docs.title: 10.2 Privacy Guarantees
docs.text:
1. Zero telemetry by default. No usage data, crash reports, or analytics are sent unless the user explicitly enables them in settings.
  2. Memory is local-only. The adaptive learning system stores all data in an encrypted SQLite database on the user's machine. No cloud sync. No Sourcegraph-style server storage.
  3. Model choice = privacy choice. Using Ollama/llama.cpp means literally zero data leaves the machine. Using a cloud API means data goes to that provider under their terms. Hone makes this trade-off explicit and visible.
  4. Encrypted at rest. The memory database, session history, and semantic index are encrypted with a user-provided passphrase or OS keychain integration.
  5. Ephemeral mode. hone --ephemeral starts a session that retains nothing — no memory updates, no session history, no index changes. For sensitive one-off tasks.
  6. Audit trail. Every piece of data sent to any external service is logged locally. Users can review exactly what was transmitted.

docs.title: 11.3 Learning Loop
docs.text:
1. Observe: Track which edits the user accepts, modifies, or rejects
  2. Extract: Identify patterns (naming conventions, import ordering, error handling style)
  3. Hypothesize: Formulate a convention ("this user prefers early returns over nested if/else")
  4. Verify: On the next relevant edit, apply the convention and check if accepted
  5. Solidify: After 3+ consistent confirmations, promote to active memory
  6. Surface: Periodically suggest adding solidified patterns to HONE.md for explicitness

Memory decay: Patterns not confirmed in 30+ days gradually decay in priority. This prevents stale conventions from persisting after code style evolves.

User control: hone memory list, hone memory show <id>, hone memory forget <id>, hone memory export, hone memory import. Full transparency and control over what Hone has learned.

docs.title: 12.2 Mobile Experience
docs.text:
The mobile PWA is not a dumbed-down view. It is a touch-optimized surface for the full Hone experience:

  • Session list: See all active and recent sessions with status (running, waiting for input, completed)
  • Live streaming: Watch the agent work in real-time with syntax-highlighted diffs
  • Approve/reject: Swipe to approve or reject pending actions
  • Voice input: Dictate instructions via phone microphone with local Whisper transcription
  • Push notifications: "Task completed," "Approval needed," "Budget threshold reached"
  • Cost dashboard: Real-time spend tracking per session and per day
  • Quick actions: Start new session, resume last session, run a saved recipe

docs.title: 12.3 Session Persistence
docs.text:
Sessions survive disconnects, sleep, and reconnects. The honed daemon maintains all state server-side. Clients are ephemeral renderers.

  • hone attach — reconnect to the most recent active session
  • hone attach <session-id> — reconnect to a specific session
  • hone sessions — list all sessions with status and last activity
  • hone sessions gc — garbage-collect completed sessions older than N days

docs.title: 14.1 Recipe System
docs.text:
Recipes are declarative YAML workflows that encode repeatable multi-step tasks. They are Goose's best idea, refined with type-safe parameters and composability.

Example recipe — Feature Implementation with TDD:

name: tdd-feature
description: Implement a feature using test-driven development
parameters:
  - name: feature_description
    type: string
    required: true
  - name: test_framework
    type: enum
    values: [jest, pytest, go-test, cargo-test]
    default: auto-detect
  - name: review_model
    type: model
    default: deep

steps:
  - name: plan
    agent: planner
    model: deep
    prompt: |
      Analyze the following feature request and create an implementation plan.
      Feature: {{ feature_description }}
      Output: list of files to create/modify, test cases to write

  - name: write-tests
    agent: coder
    model: default
    prompt: |
      Write failing tests for the planned feature using {{ test_framework }}.
      Plan: {{ steps.plan.output }}

  - name: run-tests
    tool: hone-shell
    command: "{{ test_command }}"
    expect: failure  # Tests should fail (TDD red phase)

  - name: implement
    agent: coder
    model: default
    prompt: |
      Implement the minimum code to make all tests pass.
      Tests: {{ steps.write-tests.output }}
    validate:
      - tool: hone-shell
        command: "{{ test_command }}"
        expect: success

  - name: refactor
    agent: coder
    model: deep
    prompt: |
      Refactor the implementation for clarity and performance.
      Ensure all tests still pass.
    validate:
      - tool: hone-shell
        command: "{{ test_command }}"
        expect: success

  - name: review
    agent: reviewer
    model: "{{ parameters.review_model }}"
    prompt: |
      Review all changes for correctness, style, and potential issues.
      Output: review comments and approval/rejection

docs.title: 14.2 Custom Agents
docs.text:
Agents are defined as Markdown files in .hone/agents/:

# .hone/agents/security-reviewer.md

## Role
You are a security-focused code reviewer. You specialize in identifying
vulnerabilities, injection risks, authentication flaws, and data leakage.

## Model
deep

docs.title: 1. TDD Workflow Overview
docs.text:
Every task in this plan follows the same Red → Green → Refactor cycle. The flow below applies at every level: unit, integration, and property-based tests.

flowchart TD
    START([New task]) --> RED
    RED["RED\nWrite a failing test\nthat describes the behavior\nyou want"] --> COMPILE
    COMPILE{Does it compile?}
    COMPILE -- No --> FIXTYPE["Fix type errors\n(don't make the test pass yet)"]
    FIXTYPE --> COMPILE
    COMPILE -- Yes --> RUNFAIL{Does it fail\nfor the right reason?}
    RUNFAIL -- No --> REVISIT["Revise test —\nit may be testing the wrong thing"]
    REVISIT --> RED
    RUNFAIL -- Yes --> GREEN
    GREEN["GREEN\nWrite the minimum code\nto make the test pass\n(no premature abstraction)"] --> RUNPASS
    RUNPASS{All tests pass?}
    RUNPASS -- No --> GREEN
    RUNPASS -- Yes --> REFACTOR
    REFACTOR["REFACTOR\nImprove code quality:\n- extract duplication\n- clarify names\n- tighten types\n- add error variants"] --> RUNPASS2
    RUNPASS2{All tests still pass?}
    RUNPASS2 -- No --> REFACTOR
    RUNPASS2 -- Yes --> COMMIT["Commit: tests + impl together"]
    COMMIT --> NEXT([Next task])

docs.title: 9. Property-Based Testing Plan
docs.text:
Use proptest for all parsing, encoding, and index operations where the input space is large.

Component Property Generator hone-proto Message serialize/deserialize roundtrip any::<Message>() hone-config Valid TOML always parses without panic r"[a-z_]+ = .*" hone-providers estimate_tokens never exceeds actual Random message sequences hone-tools EditTool with valid diff never corrupts other lines File content + diff params hone-index Indexed file always searchable by symbol name Random valid Rust source hone-memory Decay never increases weight Random weight + decay factor 
// Example: proto roundtrip property test
proptest! {
    #[test]
    fn message_roundtrip(role in any::<Role>(), content in ".*") {
        let msg = Message { role, content: Content::Text(content.clone()), tool_calls: vec![] };
        let json = serde_json::to_string(&msg).unwrap();
        let decoded: Message = serde_json::from_str(&json).unwrap();
        prop_assert_eq!(msg, decoded);
    }
}

docs.title: 10. Benchmark Plan
docs.text:
All benchmarks use criterion with BenchmarkGroup for organized output. They run in CI with --no-run (compile check only) and weekly in a dedicated performance job with regression detection.

Benchmark Target Method cli_startup <100ms Time from main() entry to first rendered frame first_token_local <500ms Agent::run_turn → first AgentEvent::Token with Ollama first_token_cloud <1.5s Same with real Anthropic (weekly job, env gated) memory_idle <50MB RSS Measure RSS after startup, before any turn memory_active <200MB RSS Measure RSS during a turn with all tools active index_build_50k <30s Index the hone repo itself (~50K LOC) lsp_diagnostic_roundtrip <500ms Request diagnostics → receive response context_build_messages <1ms ContextManager::build_messages for 1000 turns tool_registry_lookup <100µs ToolRegistry::get for 50 registered tools 
// Example benchmark
fn bench_context_build(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let messages = generate_messages(1000);
    let mgr = ContextManager::new(200_000);
    c.bench_function("context_build_1000_turns", |b| {
        b.iter(|| mgr.build_messages(black_box(&messages), 100_000))
    });
}

    BENCH_RUN["cargo bench --workspace\ncriterion + regression check"] --> PERF_REPORT["post performance\nreport to PR"]

docs.text:
• main — always green, release-ready

// hone-core/src/audit.rs

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct AuditEntry {
    pub id: String,
    pub session_id: String,
    pub timestamp: u64,
    pub kind: AuditKind,
    pub actor: String,        // user ID or "system"
    pub detail: Value,        // tool name+args, model ID, etc.
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum AuditKind {
    ToolCall,
    ModelRequest,
    SessionStart,
    SessionEnd,
    PolicyViolation,
}

#[async_trait]
pub trait AuditLog: Send + Sync {
    async fn record(&self, entry: AuditEntry) -> Result<(), AuditError>;
    async fn query(&self, filter: &AuditFilter) -> Result<Vec<AuditEntry>, AuditError>;
    async fn export(&self, path: &Path) -> Result<(), AuditError>;
}
