docs.title: 19. Nielsen Heuristic Audit
docs.text: Scoring: 1 (poor) — 5 (excellent). Evidence references the design decisions in this spec.

docs.title: 1. Visibility of System Status — Score: 4/5
docs.text:
Evidence for: The status bar continuously displays model name, token count, cost, budget sparkline, and session timer. The spinner in the status bar and the thinking indicator in the conversation viewport both signal that the agent is working. The streaming cursor signals that text is arriving. Tool call blocks show "running..." while active.

Gap: There is no explicit indicator of network latency — a fast spinner looks the same whether the model is thinking for 0.5s or 30s. A future improvement would be an elapsed-time counter that appears after 3 seconds of waiting. Scoring reflects this gap.

docs.title: 2. Match Between System and Real World — Score: 5/5
docs.text: Evidence for: The > sigil echoes the shell prompt — a pattern every developer recognizes. Role labels use plain language ("tool:", "model", "error"). Diff rendering matches the universal git diff format. Budget terminology ("$0.04", "no limit") maps to developer expectations. Slash commands (/quit, /help, /model) match the IRC/Discord/Slack convention familiar to the target audience.

docs.title: 3. User Control and Freedom — Score: 4/5
docs.text:
Evidence for: Ctrl+C is always available to interrupt or quit. Escape dismisses all modals. The approval flow (y / n / d) gives explicit control over destructive tool calls. Undo/redo commands exist in the command registry (though not yet implemented in the agent layer). Conversation history is preserved across resize events.

Gap: There is no "stop streaming" shortcut that interrupts mid-response without quitting. Ctrl+C during streaming should interrupt the agent but stay in the application. This requires a state machine change (AppState::Interrupting) and is noted as a required addition.

docs.title: 4. Consistency and Standards — Score: 5/5
docs.text: Evidence for: Box-drawing characters are used consistently — rounded corners for conversational elements (input, user messages), sharp corners for technical elements (code blocks, diffs, tool calls). Color token usage is rule-governed: accent-hot appears on exactly one element per context. The slash-command pattern is consistent with developer tool conventions. Spinner frames are the same across all loading contexts. Key bindings follow POSIX terminal conventions (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+L, Page Up/Down).

docs.title: 5. Error Prevention — Score: 4/5
docs.text:
Evidence for: The approval flow prevents destructive tool calls from executing without explicit confirmation. The diff preview (d key) lets users inspect changes before approving. Multi-line paste confirmation prevents accidental large-text submission. The autocomplete dropdown prevents mistyped slash commands.

Gap: There is no confirmation dialog for /quit when the agent is mid-task. The status bar should show a warning (quit while agent is running?) rather than exiting immediately. Marked as a behavioral note, not a layout spec concern.

docs.title: 6. Recognition Rather Than Recall — Score: 5/5
docs.text: Evidence for: The autocomplete dropdown appears on / without requiring the user to remember command names. The hint line below the input box (when empty) reminds the user of the key bindings. The help overlay (Ctrl+?) is surfaced via the status bar hint. Role labels are always visible — the user never needs to remember which color means which role. Tool call blocks show the tool name and arguments explicitly.

docs.title: 7. Flexibility and Efficiency — Score: 4/5
docs.text:
Evidence for: The layout has three modes (single-pane, split-pane, tool panel) for different workflows. Collapsed tool call blocks let experienced users scan past tool operations quickly. Slash commands provide fast access to model switching, cost reporting, and undo. Page Up/Down for fast scrolling.

Gap: Power users who run many tool-heavy sessions may want a way to filter the conversation view to show only assistant messages (suppressing all tool call blocks). This is a reasonable future feature, not a v1 requirement.

docs.title: 8. Aesthetic and Minimalist Design — Score: 5/5
docs.text: Evidence for: The status bar carries all metadata in a single row. Tool call blocks are collapsed by default — detail on demand. User messages have a border; assistant messages do not — asymmetry creates visual rhythm without adding elements. The color palette uses only one accent family (crimson/pink). Separators between messages are whitespace, not lines, except on narrow terminals. The splash screen animates in and then disappears — it does not compete with the working view.

docs.title: 9. Help Users Recognize and Recover From Errors — Score: 4/5
docs.text:
Evidence for: Error messages are shown in the conversation stream with an ! sigil and role-error color. The input border turns role-error when the app is in an error state. Error tool call blocks show the error text in context. The status bar shows ERR in the cost slot when an agent error occurs.

Gap: Error messages are currently raw strings from the agent (AgentEvent::Error { message }). The TUI spec cannot fix upstream message quality, but the renderer should detect common error patterns (API errors, rate limits, network errors) and append a suggested recovery action below the error text. This is a future content design task.

docs.title: 10. Help and Documentation — Score: 4/5
docs.text:
Evidence for: The help overlay (Ctrl+?) covers all keyboard shortcuts. The autocomplete dropdown has inline descriptions for all commands. The hint line below the empty input covers the three most critical shortcuts. The /help command in the command registry produces a help message in the conversation.

Gap: There is no in-app explanation of what approval means or why certain tool calls require it. A one-time contextual tooltip (shown only the first time an approval is requested) would improve first-use experience. Not a layout spec concern, but a content design note.

docs.title: 20. Implementation Priority Order
docs.text: The following order minimizes rework and builds toward the full spec incrementally. Each phase is independently shippable.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Foundation (prerequisite for everything)
docs.text:
1. Extend Theme struct with the full token set from Section 18.1.
  2. Implement theme resolution at startup (Section 18.2).
  3. Add AnimationState to App and a 100ms tick event in the event loop.
  4. Add budget_usd: Option<f64> and session_start: Instant to StatusInfo.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Status Bar
docs.text:
1. Redesign status bar renderer to the full segment layout (Section 10).
  2. Implement budget sparkline computation and rendering (Section 10.2).
  3. Implement mode badge (Section 10.5).
  4. Implement active tool indicator with spinner (Section 10.4).

docs.title: Phase 3 — Input Area
docs.text:
1. Redesign input area to rounded-corner box with sigil (Section 9.1).
  2. Implement focus border color change (active/idle/error states).
  3. Implement hint line (Section 9.1 and 9.4).
  4. Implement slash command autocomplete dropdown (Section 9.3).
  5. Implement multi-line input expansion (Section 9.2).

docs.title: Phase 4 — Message Rendering
docs.text:
1. Implement ConversationWidget as a StatefulWidget (Section 17.3).
  2. Implement role label rendering with sigils and timestamps (Section 7.2).
  3. Implement user message rounded border (Section 7.1).
  4. Implement streaming cursor with blink animation (Section 8.1).
  5. Implement thinking dots animation for pre-token state (Section 8.1).

docs.title: Phase 5 — Code and Diff Blocks
docs.text:
1. Implement code block renderer with sharp-corner box and language label (Section 8.2).
  2. Implement simple regex-based syntax lexer (Section 8.2).
  3. Implement line-number gutter in code blocks.
  4. Implement diff block renderer with per-line background coloring (Section 8.3).
  5. Implement diff summary line (Section 8.3).
  6. Implement inline markdown formatting (Section 8.4).

docs.title: Phase 6 — Tool Call Panels
docs.text:
1. Implement tool call block as collapsed/expanded StatefulWidget (Section 11).
  2. Implement tool call running, success, and error states (Section 11.3).
  3. Implement approval flow with y / n / d keybindings (Section 11.4).

docs.title: Phase 7 — Split-Pane Layout
docs.text:
1. Implement Layout::horizontal split with adjustable ratio (Section 5.2).
  2. Implement file preview panel with all 7 states (Section 12.1).
  3. Wire file preview to read_file / write_file tool call events.
  4. Implement pane focus cycling with Tab.
  5. Implement Alt+Left / Alt+Right ratio adjustment.

docs.title: Phase 8 — Startup Experience
docs.text:
1. Implement splash screen with step-animation mark and wordmark (Section 6.1).
  2. Implement startup timing sequence (Section 14.2).
  3. Implement session detection to skip splash on re-launch.

docs.title: Phase 9 — Help Overlay and Polish
docs.text:
1. Implement help overlay widget with Clear + centered block (Section 13).
  2. Implement scroll indicator in conversation viewport (Section 7.4).
  3. Implement header bar with compact mark and working directory (Section 6.3).
  4. Implement --no-color / NO_COLOR Minimal theme (Section 3.4 and 16.2).
  5. Implement resize handler with too-small warning (Section 16.5).
  6. Implement --theme CLI flag and HONE_THEME environment variable.

docs.title: Phase 10 — Theme Presets
docs.text:
1. Implement Neon theme token overrides (Section 3.2).
  2. Implement Chalk light theme token overrides (Section 3.3).
  3. Add theme preview mode: hone --theme-preview renders a static screen showing all UI elements in the selected theme.

End of specification.

[dependencies]

[dev-dependencies]
proptest = { workspace = true }

docs.title: Crate Isolation Rules
docs.text: Rule Enforced By hone-proto has zero non-serde dependencies cargo-deny hone-sandbox cannot depend on hone-providers or hone-mcp cargo-deny hone-tui cannot depend on hone-server cargo-deny No crate may depend on bins/* Cargo workspace structure Platform-specific code uses cfg(target_os) not feature flags Code review

docs.title: 4. Feature Flags Strategy
docs.text: Feature flags gate optional dependencies and incomplete functionality. They are never used for platform detection (use cfg attributes instead).

docs.title: Workspace-Level Feature Flags
docs.text:
# Root Cargo.toml — feature unification
[workspace.features]

docs.title: Per-Crate Feature Flags
docs.text: Crate Feature Default Purpose hone-memory encrypted-memory off SQLCipher encrypted memory database hone-providers anthropic on Anthropic adapter hone-providers openai on OpenAI adapter hone-providers ollama on Ollama adapter hone-providers google off Google Gemini adapter hone-providers bedrock off AWS Bedrock adapter hone-providers azure off Azure OpenAI adapter hone-providers all-providers off Enable all provider adapters hone-index onnx-embeddings off ONNX Runtime for local embeddings hone-server tunnel off WireGuard/bore tunnel support hone-tui clipboard on System clipboard integration bins/hone daemon off Embed honed in same binary

docs.title: 5. Build Profiles
docs.text:
# Root Cargo.toml

[profile.dev]
opt-level = 0
debug = true
incremental = true
# Fast iteration — no LTO, keep debug info

[profile.dev.package."*"]
opt-level = 2
# Optimize dependencies even in dev (tree-sitter, sqlx are slow unoptimized)

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
lto = "thin"
codegen-units = 1
strip = "symbols"
panic = "abort"
# Smallest, fastest binary for distribution

[profile.release-debug]
inherits = "release"
debug = true
strip = "none"
# For profiling with flamegraph/perf

[profile.bench]
inherits = "release"
debug = true
# Criterion needs debug info for accurate profiling

[profile.test]
opt-level = 1
# Slightly optimized tests — proptest + index tests are slow at opt-level=0

docs.text:
# Development
cargo build                                    # Fast incremental build
cargo test --workspace                         # All unit + integration tests
cargo test -p hone-core                        # Single crate tests

# CI
cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo deny check
cargo test --workspace --all-features
cargo build --release --all-targets

# Profiling
cargo build --profile release-debug
cargo flamegraph --bin hone -- "hello"

# Benchmarks
cargo bench --workspace                        # Run all benchmarks
cargo bench -p hone-core context_build         # Single benchmark

# Release
cargo build --release --bin hone --bin honed

docs.title: Build Order (Topological Sort)
docs.text:
The following is the order in which crates compile. Crates at the same level can compile in parallel.

flowchart LR
    subgraph "Level 0 — No internal deps"
        PROTO[hone-proto]
    end

    subgraph "Level 1 — Depends on proto only"
        CFG[hone-config]
        SB[hone-sandbox]
        PROV[hone-providers]
        IDX[hone-index]
        MEM[hone-memory]
    end

    subgraph "Level 2 — Depends on L0 + L1"
        TOOLS[hone-tools]
        MCP[hone-mcp]
    end

    subgraph "Level 3 — Depends on most L1 + L2"
        CORE[hone-core]
    end

    subgraph "Level 4 — Depends on core"
        TUI[hone-tui]
        REC[hone-recipes]
        SRV[hone-server]
    end

    subgraph "Level 5 — Final binaries"
        BIN1[bin: hone]
        BIN2[bin: honed]
    end

    PROTO --> CFG & SB & PROV & IDX & MEM
    SB --> TOOLS
    PROTO --> TOOLS & MCP
    CFG & SB & PROV & TOOLS & MCP & IDX & MEM --> CORE
    CORE --> TUI & REC & SRV
    TUI & REC --> BIN1
    SRV & REC --> BIN2

docs.title: Compile Time Optimization Notes
docs.text:
1. Level 0-1 crates compile in parallel — hone-config, hone-sandbox, hone-providers, hone-index, hone-memory all start compiling as soon as hone-proto is done.
  2. dev.package."*".opt-level = 2 — Third-party deps (tree-sitter, sqlx, reqwest) are optimized even in dev mode to avoid painfully slow test runs.
  3. sccache in CI — Shared compilation cache across CI runs, reducing cold build time by ~60%.
  4. Feature-gated heavy deps — ort (ONNX), aws-sdk-*, sqlcipher are optional. Default builds compile fast with only the essential providers.

docs.title: ACP (Agent Client Protocol) Reference
docs.text: The Agent Client Protocol is a JSON-RPC 2.0 based protocol for controlling Hone agents. Messages are exchanged over stdio (standard input/output) in a request-response or notification pattern.

docs.title: Protocol Overview
docs.text:
• Version: JSON-RPC 2.0
  • Transport: Text-based messages over stdio, newline-delimited
  • Encoding: UTF-8 JSON
  • Message Flow: Client sends requests, agent responds with results or errors; agent sends notifications asynchronously

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
A JSON-RPC request from client to agent:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "initialize",
  "params": { ... }
}

Fields:

Field Type Required Description jsonrpc string Yes Protocol version, always "2.0" id integer Yes Unique request identifier, must be present method string Yes RPC method name params object No Method parameters

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
A JSON-RPC response from agent to client:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": { ... }
}

Or on error:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "error": {
    "code": -32600,
    "message": "Invalid Request"
  }
}

Fields:

Field Type Description jsonrpc string Protocol version, always "2.0" id integer Matches request ID result any Result value (present if successful) error object Error object (present if failed)

Error Object:

Field Type Description code integer Error code (negative integers reserved for protocol errors) message string Human-readable error message

docs.title: Notification
docs.text:
A JSON-RPC notification from agent to client (no response expected):

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "session/update",
  "params": { ... }
}

Fields:

Field Type Required Description jsonrpc string Yes Protocol version, always "2.0" method string Yes RPC method name params object No Notification parameters id integer No Must NOT be present in notifications

docs.title: initialize
docs.text:
Initialize the protocol connection. Client sends this first to establish protocol version and exchange capability information.

Request: 

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "initialize",
  "params": {
    "protocolVersion": 1,
    "clientInfo": {
      "name": "hone-cli",
      "version": "0.1.0"
    }
  }
}

Request Parameters:

Field Type Description protocolVersion integer ACP protocol version (currently 1) clientInfo.name string Client name (e.g., hone-cli, hone-ui) clientInfo.version string Client version string

Response: 

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "protocolVersion": 1,
    "agentInfo": {
      "name": "hone-agent",
      "version": "0.1.0"
    }
  }
}

Response Parameters:

Field Type Description protocolVersion integer Negotiated protocol version agentInfo.name string Agent implementation name agentInfo.version string Agent implementation version

docs.title: session/new
docs.text:
Create a new agent session.

Request: 

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "method": "session/new",
  "params": {
    "cwd": "/home/user/project"
  }
}

Request Parameters:

Field Type Description cwd string Working directory for the agent session

Response: 

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "result": {
    "sessionId": "sess_abc123def456"
  }
}

Response Parameters:

Field Type Description sessionId string Unique session identifier for subsequent requests

docs.title: session/prompt
docs.text:
Send a user prompt to the agent for processing.

Request: 

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "method": "session/prompt",
  "params": {
    "sessionId": "sess_abc123def456",
    "prompt": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "text": "List the files in the current directory"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Request Parameters:

Field Type Description sessionId string Session ID from session/new prompt array Array of content items

Prompt Content Items:

Field Type Description type string Content type: text, image, file, etc. text string Text content (for type text)

Response: 

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "result": {
    "stopReason": "end_turn"
  }
}

Response Parameters:

Field Type Description stopReason string Why the turn stopped: end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, etc.

Notifications During Processing:

While processing a prompt, the agent sends session/update notifications with event data (see below).

docs.title: session/update (Notification)
docs.text:
The agent sends these notifications asynchronously during prompt processing. These are notifications (no response required from client).

Notification: 

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "session/update",
  "params": {
    "sessionId": "sess_abc123def456",
    "update": {
      "sessionUpdate": "agent_message_chunk",
      "content": {
        "type": "text",
        "text": "Hello"
      }
    }
  }
}

Parameters:

Field Type Description sessionId string Session ID update object Update payload (polymorphic, see variants below)

docs.title: agent_message_chunk
docs.text:
Agent is streaming text output.

Update Format: 

{
  "sessionUpdate": "agent_message_chunk",
  "content": {
    "type": "text",
    "text": "I'll help"
  }
}

Fields:

Field Type Description sessionUpdate string Always "agent_message_chunk" content.type string Content type: text content.text string Text chunk

docs.title: tool_call
docs.text:
Agent initiated a tool call.

Update Format: 

{
  "sessionUpdate": "tool_call",
  "toolCallId": "call_abc123",
  "title": "List Files",
  "kind": "filesystem",
  "status": "pending"
}

Fields:

Field Type Description sessionUpdate string Always "tool_call" toolCallId string Unique tool call identifier title string Human-readable tool name kind string Tool category (e.g., filesystem, database, network) status string Call status: pending, in_progress, completed

docs.title: tool_call_update
docs.text:
Tool call status changed (e.g., from pending to completed).

Update Format: 

{
  "sessionUpdate": "tool_call_update",
  "toolCallId": "call_abc123",
  "status": "completed"
}

Fields:

Field Type Description sessionUpdate string Always "tool_call_update" toolCallId string Matches preceding tool_call ID status string New status: in_progress, completed, failed

docs.title: session/cancel (Notification)
docs.text:
Client can request to cancel an ongoing prompt processing.

Notification: 

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "session/cancel",
  "params": {
    "sessionId": "sess_abc123def456"
  }
}

Parameters:

Field Type Description sessionId string Session to cancel

The agent will stop processing and may send a final error notification. This is a fire-and-forget notification (no response).

docs.title: Error Codes
docs.text:
Standard JSON-RPC 2.0 error codes:

Code Message Description -32700 Parse error Invalid JSON -32600 Invalid Request Malformed request object -32601 Method not found Unknown method -32602 Invalid params Invalid method parameters -32603 Internal error Agent internal error -32000 Session not found Referenced session does not exist -32001 Invalid session state Session is in wrong state for operation

docs.title: Example: Complete Conversation Flow
docs.text:
Client -> Server (Request):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "initialize",
  "params": {
    "protocolVersion": 1,
    "clientInfo": {"name": "cli", "version": "1.0"}
  }
}

Server -> Client (Response):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "protocolVersion": 1,
    "agentInfo": {"name": "hone", "version": "1.0"}
  }
}

Client -> Server (Request):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "method": "session/new",
  "params": {"cwd": "/tmp"}
}

Server -> Client (Response):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "result": {"sessionId": "sess_123"}
}

Client -> Server (Request):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "method": "session/prompt",
  "params": {
    "sessionId": "sess_123",
    "prompt": [{"type": "text", "text": "What's in this directory?"}]
  }
}

Server -> Client (Notification):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "session/update",
  "params": {
    "sessionId": "sess_123",
    "update": {
      "sessionUpdate": "tool_call",
      "toolCallId": "call_1",
      "title": "List Files",
      "kind": "filesystem",
      "status": "pending"
    }
  }
}

Server -> Client (Notification):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "session/update",
  "params": {
    "sessionId": "sess_123",
    "update": {
      "sessionUpdate": "tool_call_update",
      "toolCallId": "call_1",
      "status": "completed"
    }
  }
}

Server -> Client (Notification):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "session/update",
  "params": {
    "sessionId": "sess_123",
    "update": {
      "sessionUpdate": "agent_message_chunk",
      "content": {"type": "text", "text": "The directory contains:"}
    }
  }
}

Server -> Client (Notification):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "session/update",
  "params": {
    "sessionId": "sess_123",
    "update": {
      "sessionUpdate": "agent_message_chunk",
      "content": {"type": "text", "text": " file1.txt"}
    }
  }
}

Server -> Client (Response):
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "result": {"stopReason": "end_turn"}
}

docs.title: Implementation Notes
docs.text:
1. Message Framing: Each JSON message must be followed by a newline character (\n)
  2. Concurrent Requests: Clients may send multiple requests before receiving responses; use id to correlate
  3. Notifications Don't Block: Agents send notifications independently; clients should not wait for their receipt
  4. Session Lifetime: Sessions persist on the agent until explicitly closed or the agent terminates
  5. Prompt Parameters: The prompt array can contain multiple content items for multi-modal prompts
  6. Tool Results: Tool execution results are embedded in subsequent notifications or token stream

docs.title: HTTP API Reference
docs.text: The honed daemon exposes a REST API for session management, team governance, collaboration, and tunneling. All endpoints require Bearer token authentication (if configured).

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Requests must include a Bearer token in the Authorization header:

Authorization: Bearer <token>

If no auth token is configured on the server, this header may be omitted.

docs.title: Error Response
docs.text:
All endpoints return error responses with the following format:

{
  "error": "error description"
}

docs.title: GET /health
docs.text:
Health check endpoint.

Request: 

curl http://localhost:8080/health

Response: 200 OK 

{
  "status": "ok"
}

docs.title: POST /sessions
docs.text:
Create a new session.

Request: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/sessions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Response: 201 Created 

{
  "session_id": "sess_abc123def456"
}

Return Fields:

Field Type Description session_id string Unique session identifier

docs.title: GET /sessions/{id}
docs.text:
Retrieve session information by ID.

Request: 

curl http://localhost:8080/sessions/sess_abc123def456 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Response: 200 OK 

{
  "id": "sess_abc123def456",
  "created_at": 1704067200
}

Response Fields:

Field Type Description id string Session identifier created_at u64 Unix timestamp of session creation

Errors:

Status Error Description 404 Not Found Session not found Session with given ID does not exist 401 Unauthorized Unauthorized Invalid or missing authentication token

docs.title: DELETE /sessions/{id}
docs.text:
Delete a session.

Request: 

curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/sessions/sess_abc123def456 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Response: 204 No Content

Errors:

Status Error Description 404 Not Found Session not found Session with given ID does not exist 401 Unauthorized Unauthorized Invalid or missing authentication token

docs.title: POST /sessions/{id}/join
docs.text:
Add a participant to a session.

Request: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/sessions/sess_abc123def456/join \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "user_id": "user_123",
    "name": "Alice"
  }'

Request Body:

Field Type Description user_id string Unique user identifier name string Display name for the participant

Response: 200 OK 

{
  "user_id": "user_123",
  "name": "Alice",
  "role": "owner",
  "joined_at": 1704067200
}

Response Fields:

Field Type Description user_id string User identifier name string Display name role string Participant role: owner (first joiner) or editor joined_at u64 Unix timestamp of when user joined

Errors:

Status Error Description 409 Conflict Already joined User already a participant in this session 401 Unauthorized Unauthorized Invalid or missing authentication token

docs.title: POST /sessions/{id}/leave
docs.text:
Remove a participant from a session.

Request: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/sessions/sess_abc123def456/leave \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "user_id": "user_123"
  }'

Request Body:

Field Type Description user_id string User to remove

Response: 204 No Content

Errors:

Status Error Description 404 Not Found Not a participant User is not in this session 401 Unauthorized Unauthorized Invalid or missing authentication token

docs.title: GET /sessions/{id}/participants
docs.text:
List all participants in a session.

Request: 

curl http://localhost:8080/sessions/sess_abc123def456/participants \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Response: 200 OK 

[
  {
    "user_id": "user_123",
    "name": "Alice",
    "role": "owner",
    "joined_at": 1704067200
  },
  {
    "user_id": "user_456",
    "name": "Bob",
    "role": "editor",
    "joined_at": 1704067201
  }
]

Response: Array of participant objects with fields:

Field Type Description user_id string User identifier name string Display name role string Participant role: owner or editor joined_at u64 Unix timestamp of join time

Errors:

Status Error Description 401 Unauthorized Unauthorized Invalid or missing authentication token

docs.title: POST /sessions/{id}/kick
docs.text:
Remove a participant from a session (owner only).

Request: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/sessions/sess_abc123def456/kick \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "owner_user_id": "user_123",
    "target_user_id": "user_456"
  }'

Request Body:

Field Type Description owner_user_id string User performing the kick (must be owner) target_user_id string User to remove

Response: 204 No Content

Errors:

Status Error Description 403 Forbidden Forbidden Caller is not the session owner 404 Not Found Not a participant Target user is not in this session 401 Unauthorized Unauthorized Invalid or missing authentication token

docs.title: GET /team/usage
docs.text:
Retrieve team token usage and cost metrics.

Request: 

curl http://localhost:8080/team/usage \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Response: 200 OK 

{

Response Fields:

Field Type Description total_tokens u64 Total tokens consumed by team total_cost_usd f64 Total cost in USD by_model object Usage breakdown by model ID

Model Usage Fields:

Field Type Description tokens u64 Tokens for this model cost_usd f64 Cost for this model in USD

Errors:

Status Error Description 401 Unauthorized Unauthorized Invalid or missing authentication token

docs.title: GET /team/members
docs.text:
List all team members.

Request: 

curl http://localhost:8080/team/members \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Response: 200 OK 

[
  {

  {

Field Type Description id string Member identifier name string Display name role string Team role (e.g., admin, user) joined_at u64 Unix timestamp of when member joined team

docs.title: GET /team/policy
docs.text:
Retrieve team governance policy.

docs.title: POST /team/policy

docs.title: POST /tunnel
docs.text:
Start a reverse tunnel to expose a local port.

Request: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/tunnel \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "local_port": 3000
  }'

Request Body:

Field Type Description local_port u16 Local port to expose via tunnel

Response: 201 Created 

{
  "url": "https://tunnel-abc123.hone.sh",
  "local_port": 3000,
  "is_active": true
}

Response Fields:

Field Type Description url string Public tunnel URL local_port u16 Exposed local port is_active bool Whether tunnel is currently active

Errors:

Status Error Description 401 Unauthorized Unauthorized Invalid or missing authentication token 500 Internal Server Error Internal error Failed to create tunnel

docs.title: GET /tunnel
docs.text:
Get current tunnel status.

Request: 

curl http://localhost:8080/tunnel \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Response: 200 OK (if tunnel active) 

{
  "url": "https://tunnel-abc123.hone.sh",
  "local_port": 3000,
  "is_active": true
}

Response: 200 OK (if no tunnel) 

{
  "is_active": false
}

Response Fields:

Field Type Description url string Public tunnel URL (if active) local_port u16 Exposed port (if active) is_active bool Whether tunnel is currently active

Errors:

docs.title: DELETE /tunnel
docs.text:
Stop the active tunnel.

Request: 

curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/tunnel \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Response: 204 No Content

Errors:

docs.title: HTTP Status Codes
docs.text:
Standard HTTP status codes are used throughout:

Code Meaning 200 OK Request succeeded 201 Created Resource created successfully 204 No Content Request succeeded, no response body 400 Bad Request Invalid request format or parameters 401 Unauthorized Missing or invalid authentication token 403 Forbidden Authenticated but lacking required permissions 404 Not Found Resource does not exist 409 Conflict Request conflicts with current state (e.g., duplicate join) 500 Internal Server Error Server error during processing

docs.title: GET /openapi.json
docs.text:
Returns the OpenAPI 3.1 specification for the API. No authentication required.

Request: 

curl http://localhost:3117/openapi.json | jq

Response: 200 OK 

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {
    "title": "Hone API",
    "version": "0.1.0"
  },
  "paths": {
    "/health": {...},
    "/sessions": {...},
    ...
  }
}

Use this endpoint to programmatically discover the API structure, validate client implementations, or generate client libraries.

docs.title: DELETE /sessions/gc
docs.text:
Garbage collect sessions older than a specified number of days.

Request: 

curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:3117/sessions/gc?older_than_days=7"

Query Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description older_than_days integer 30 Remove sessions older than N days

Response: 200 OK 

{
  "removed": 5
}

Response Fields:

Field Type Description removed integer Number of sessions deleted

This endpoint is useful for periodic maintenance to clean up old sessions and free storage space. Can be called manually or via a scheduled task (cron, systemd timer, etc.).

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
All endpoints are rate-limited at 100 requests per minute per client. The client is identified by the X-Forwarded-For header (when present), or the source IP address.

When rate limit is exceeded, the server returns:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests

{
  "error": "rate limit exceeded"
}

The Retry-After header indicates seconds until the next request can be made:

Retry-After: 45

Rate limits apply to all endpoints uniformly. For high-volume integrations, contact the server operator to discuss dedicated rate limits.

docs.title: Server-Sent Events (SSE) Reference
docs.text: The Hone agent streams events to connected clients using Server-Sent Events (SSE). This document describes the event format and all event types.

docs.title: Connection Setup
docs.text:
SSE endpoints are established via HTTP GET requests with the Accept: text/event-stream header:

curl http://localhost:8080/sessions/sess_abc123/stream \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Accept: text/event-stream"

The server will keep the connection open and stream events line-by-line.

docs.title: Event Format
docs.text:
Each event is formatted according to the SSE specification:

id: {event_id}
event: {event_type}
data: {json_payload}

Fields:

Field Type Description id integer Unique event identifier (monotonically increasing) event string Event type name data JSON Event payload (serialized as JSON)

Empty line separates events.

docs.title: token
docs.text:
A text token from the model's response.

Event Type: token

Data Format: 

{
  "type": "token",
  "text": "Hello"
}

Payload Fields:

Field Type Description type string Always "token" text string The text token (may be partial word, sentence, or complete token)

Example: 

id: 1
event: token
data: {"type":"token","text":"Hello"}

id: 2
event: token
data: {"type":"token","text":" world"}

docs.title: tool_call_start
docs.text:
The model requested execution of a tool.

Event Type: tool_call_start

Data Format: 

{
  "type": "tool_call_start",
  "id": "call_abc123",
  "name": "list_files"
}

Payload Fields:

Field Type Description type string Always "tool_call_start" id string Unique tool call identifier name string Name of the tool being called

Note: The arguments passed to the tool are sent in a tool_call_update event (see below).

Example: 

id: 10
event: tool_call_start
data: {"type":"tool_call_start","id":"call_abc123","name":"list_files"}

docs.title: tool_call_end
docs.text:
A tool call completed with a result.

Event Type: tool_call_end

Data Format: 

{
  "type": "tool_call_end",
  "id": "call_abc123",
  "result": {
    "files": ["file1.txt", "file2.txt"]
  },
  "is_error": false
}

Payload Fields:

Field Type Description type string Always "tool_call_end" id string Tool call identifier (matches preceding tool_call_start) result JSON Result returned by the tool is_error boolean True if result is an error message

Error Example: 

{
  "type": "tool_call_end",
  "id": "call_abc123",
  "result": {
    "error": "Permission denied"
  },
  "is_error": true
}

Example: 

id: 11
event: tool_call_end
data: {"type":"tool_call_end","id":"call_abc123","result":{"files":["file1.txt","file2.txt"]},"is_error":false}

docs.title: error
docs.text:
An error occurred during the agent turn.

Event Type: error

Data Format: 

{
  "type": "error",
  "message": "Model API request failed: rate limit exceeded"
}

Payload Fields:

Field Type Description type string Always "error" message string Human-readable error description

Example: 

id: 20
event: error
data: {"type":"error","message":"Model API request failed: rate limit exceeded"}

The connection may close after an error event, depending on error severity.

docs.title: done
docs.text:
The agent turn completed successfully.

Event Type: done

Data Format: 

{
  "type": "done",
  "usage": {
    "input": 150,
    "output": 45,
    "cache_read": 10
  }
}

Payload Fields:

Field Type Description type string Always "done" usage object Token usage for this turn

Usage Object:

Field Type Description input u32 Input tokens consumed output u32 Output tokens generated cache_read u32 Tokens read from cache

Example: 

id: 21
event: done
data: {"type":"done","usage":{"input":150,"output":45,"cache_read":10}}

This is typically the final event in a turn. After this event, the connection may close or remain open for subsequent turns.

docs.title: approval_required
docs.text:
The agent is waiting for user approval before taking an action.

Event Type: approval_required

Data Format: 

{
  "type": "approval_required",
  "action": "delete_file",
  "description": "User is requesting to delete /important/data.txt. Approve?"
}

Payload Fields:

Field Type Description type string Always "approval_required" action string Action requiring approval description string Human-readable description of what needs approval

Example: 

id: 15
event: approval_required
data: {"type":"approval_required","action":"delete_file","description":"User is requesting to delete /important/data.txt. Approve?"}

The client should pause execution and prompt the user. The agent will wait for an approval confirmation before proceeding (via a separate HTTP endpoint).

docs.title: Event Stream Example
docs.text:
A typical agent turn might produce the following event stream:

id: 1
event: token
data: {"type":"token","text":"I'll"}

id: 2
event: token
data: {"type":"token","text":" help"}

id: 3
event: token
data: {"type":"token","text":" you"}

id: 4
event: tool_call_start
data: {"type":"tool_call_start","id":"call_1","name":"list_files"}

id: 5
event: tool_call_end
data: {"type":"tool_call_end","id":"call_1","result":{"files":["a.txt","b.txt"]},"is_error":false}

id: 6
event: token
data: {"type":"token","text":" found"}

id: 7
event: token
data: {"type":"token","text":" 2 files"}

id: 8
event: done
data: {"type":"done","usage":{"input":200,"output":50,"cache_read":0}}

docs.title: Client Implementation Notes
docs.text:
• Process each event independently as it arrives
  • Event IDs can be used to resume a stream from a specific point if the connection drops
  • The data field is always a complete JSON object (never multi-line)
  • Connections may close unexpectedly; clients should implement reconnection logic
  • Token events may contain partial words; buffer tokens until whitespace or tool calls for complete text assembly

docs.title: Hone Onboarding Hub
docs.text: Welcome to Hone. Whether you're new to AI coding agents or migrating from another tool, this hub will guide you through setup and best practices.

docs.title: I'm Coming From Another Tool
docs.text:
Choose your current tool to see what maps to what in Hone:

Your Tool Read This Claude Code (Anthropic) from-claude-code.md Goose (Block/Square) from-goose.md Aider from-aider.md Codex CLI from-codex-cli.md OpenCode from-opencode.md

docs.title: I'm New to AI Coding Agents
docs.text:
Start here: new-user-walkthrough.md

This guide assumes zero prior experience and covers: - What an AI coding agent actually is - Installing Hone - Your first real-world session - Key concepts explained simply - Common workflows and patterns - Effective prompting tips

docs.title: Decision Tree: Which Guide Is For Me?
docs.text:
Are you completely new to AI coding agents?
├─ YES → Read: new-user-walkthrough.md
└─ NO
   Have you used an AI coding tool before?
   ├─ NO → Read: new-user-walkthrough.md (covers fundamentals)
   └─ YES
      Which tool?
      ├─ Claude Code → from-claude-code.md
      ├─ Goose → from-goose.md
      ├─ Aider → from-aider.md
      ├─ Codex CLI → from-codex-cli.md
      ├─ OpenCode → from-opencode.md
      └─ Something else → new-user-walkthrough.md (general intro)

docs.title: What Makes Hone Different?
docs.text:
At a high level, Hone brings together ideas from all competing tools:

From Claude Code: Extended thinking, agent loops, memory, user-defined conventions (HONE.md)

From Goose: MCP-native architecture, YAML recipes, provider abstraction

From Aider: Git-centric workflows, repo context, semantic indexing

From Codex CLI: Kernel sandboxing, approval workflows, cost tracking

From OpenCode: 75+ provider support, LSP integration, client-server architecture

But Hone goes further: - Kernel-enforced security — Seatbelt on macOS, Landlock on Linux - Adaptive memory — Learns what works across sessions - Universal provider support — No vendor lock-in - Layered tools — Native Rust for speed, MCP for extensibility - Collaborative workflows — Remote daemon with team governance

docs.title: Do I need an API key?
docs.text:
No, but it helps. Hone supports: - Free local models via Ollama (run on your machine) - Your existing CLI via Claude/Gemini pass-through - Any API provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.)

See Getting Started for setup.

docs.title: Is my code private?
docs.text:
Yes. Hone: - Runs locally (no telemetry) - Stores memory in encrypted SQLite on your machine - Sandboxes code execution at the kernel level - Never phones home

See Security Guide for details.

docs.title: Can I use Hone in a team?
docs.text: Yes. Run the honed daemon and connect multiple users with role-based access control (RBAC). See Server and Remote.

docs.title: How much does Hone cost?
docs.text: Hone is free. You pay for model APIs (if you use them). Costs are transparent and tracked in real USD. Local models cost nothing.

docs.title: What if I switch providers?
docs.text: Easy. Use /model <provider:model> to hot-swap mid-session without losing history. See Providers Guide.

docs.title: Next Steps After Onboarding
docs.text:
Once you've picked your migration guide and completed setup:

  1. Try the first example in the migration guide (copy-paste commands)
  2. Run a real-world task in your own codebase
  3. Explore recipes in Recipes Guide for automation
  4. Review Tools and MCP to extend capabilities
  5. Check Architecture for deep dives into how Hone works

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
• Setup issues? See the "Troubleshooting" section in Getting Started
  • Questions about concepts? See Architecture
  • Want to extend Hone? See Contributing
  • Found a bug? Report it on GitHub

Have a migration guide question we missed? Open an issue on GitHub with the "docs" label.

docs.title: Hone Quick Reference
docs.text: A single-page cheatsheet for daily use. Print this out or save it as a browser bookmark.

docs.title: Commands (Slash Commands in Session)
docs.text:
Run these in an active session:

Command Purpose /agent <name> Switch to a built-in or custom agent /model <provider:model> Switch providers (e.g., /model openai:gpt-4o) /budget <usd> Set spending limit for session /context <tokens> Adjust context window size /memory on\|off Enable/disable memory for session /sandbox on\|off Enable/disable kernel sandbox (not recommended) /files <pattern> List files matching pattern (e.g., /files *.rs) /git <command> Run git command (e.g., /git log --oneline) /shell <command> Run shell command with full output /semantic-search <query> Find related code using vectors /recipes list Show available recipes /agents list Show available agents /help Show all commands /exit or Ctrl+C Quit session

docs.title: CLI Flags
docs.text:
Run these when starting hone:

Flag Example Purpose (prompt) hone "prompt" One-shot mode (no REPL) --orchestrate hone --orchestrate "..." Multi-agent orchestrator --ensemble hone --ensemble 3 "..." Run N candidates, rank best --recipe hone --recipe tdd-feature Run a built-in recipe --list-recipes hone --list-recipes List available recipes --agent hone --agent code-reviewer Use a specific agent --model hone --model openai:gpt-4o Choose model/provider --dir hone --dir ~/myproject Target a directory --budget hone --budget 5.00 Max spend in USD --context-window hone --context-window 64000 Limit context (tokens) --remote hone --remote localhost:7777 Connect to daemon --ephemeral hone --ephemeral No memory persistence --config hone --config ~/.config/hone/config.toml Custom config file --help hone --help Show all options

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcut Action Ctrl+C Stop current response / exit Ctrl+L Clear screen Ctrl+D EOF (exit gracefully) Tab Autocomplete (in input) PageUp / PageDown Scroll history Ctrl+P Previous prompt Ctrl+N Next prompt Ctrl+R Search history (if interactive)

docs.title: Config Hierarchy (Priority Order)
docs.text:
CLI flags override everything. Lowest priority wins if flag not set.

  1. CLI flags (highest priority) 

    hone --model gpt-4o --budget 5.00

  2. Environment variables 

    export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
export HONE_CONFIG="/custom/config.toml"

  3. Project config (./HONE.md + ./.hone/config.toml) 

    # HONE.md: project-level skills
# .hone/config.toml: project-level settings

  4. User config (~/.config/hone/config.toml) 

    [agent]
default_model = "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4"

  5. Defaults (hardcoded in Hone)

  6. Default model: Claude Sonnet 4
  7. Default budget: unlimited
  8. Default context: full model limit

docs.title: Built-in Agents (Quick Reference)
docs.text:
Use these agents for specialized tasks:

hone --agent code-reviewer        # Code quality and security reviews
hone --agent debugger              # Systematic bug investigation
hone --agent security-auditor      # Vulnerability and secret scanning
hone --agent performance-optimizer # Profiling and optimization
hone --agent documentation-agent   # API docs and architecture diagrams
hone --agent api-designer          # REST/GraphQL/gRPC design
hone --agent tdd-workflow          # Test-Driven Development
hone --agent rust-expert           # Rust best practices
hone --agent python-expert         # Python best practices

Find an agent by keyword: hone --agent "test-driven" (matches tdd-workflow).

docs.title: Built-in Recipes (Quick Reference)
docs.text:
Use these recipes for structured workflows:

hone --recipe tdd-feature    # Implement feature with TDD (Red-Green-Refactor)
hone --recipe bug-fix        # Fix a bug with regression test
hone --recipe code-review    # Comprehensive code review
hone --recipe refactor       # Refactor safely with test verification

docs.title: Multi-Agent Features
docs.text:
Hone supports advanced multi-agent patterns:

# Orchestrator: decompose complex tasks into parallel subtasks
hone --orchestrate "Build a secure user authentication system with tests"

# Ensemble: run 3 candidates with different temperatures, pick the best
hone --ensemble 3 "Optimize this query for performance"

# Complexity routing: auto-route Simple/Medium/Complex to right model
hone "What's 2+2?"  # routes to fast/cheap model

# Test-verify loop: agent runs tests after each change
hone "Add a new feature" --recipe tdd-feature

docs.title: Common Patterns: One-Liners
docs.text: Quick commands for common tasks:

docs.title: Fix a Bug
docs.text: hone --agent debugger -i "The login form throws 'TypeError: cannot read password'. Fix it."

docs.title: Code Review

docs.title: Useful Definitions
docs.text:
• Token: Smallest unit of text (roughly 1 word = 1.3 tokens)
  • Context window: Maximum tokens the model can process (e.g., 200K for Claude)
  • Sandbox: Kernel-enforced restrictions on what code can do
  • MCP: Model Context Protocol; a standard for integrating external tools
  • Recipe: YAML file defining a multi-step workflow
  • Memory: Local encrypted database of learned patterns
  • Daemon (honed): Long-running server for multi-user sessions
  • RBAC: Role-Based Access Control; permissions per user
  • Fallback chain: List of providers to try if one fails

docs.title: Core Concepts: A Deep Dive into Hone
docs.text: This document explains the "why" behind Hone's design choices. It's for users who want to understand how Hone works under the hood, not just how to use it. If you're looking for step-by-step instructions, see Getting Started.

docs.title: 1. The Agent Loop
docs.text:
When you send a message to Hone, it enters a repeating cycle:

Prompt
  ↓
[Build Context]
  ↓
[Call Model]
  ↓
[Stream Tokens]
  ↓
[Parse Tool Calls]
  ↓
[Execute Tools]
  ↓
[Loop? Or Done?]

Here's what happens at each step:

Prompt: You type a natural language request. Example: "Fix the bug in my authentication flow."

Build Context: Hone gathers relevant information: your question, conversation history, file contents, git diffs, memory of past patterns. All of this is assembled into a "context window" — a bounded sequence of tokens that fits inside the model's input limit.

Call Model: The compiled context (prompt + history + tools definitions) is sent to the model provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, etc.). Hone streams the response token-by-token from the model.

Stream Tokens: As tokens arrive, Hone displays them in the terminal. You see the agent thinking in real-time.

Parse Tool Calls: The model may emit structured tool calls (JSON objects like {"tool": "read_file", "args": {"path": "src/main.rs"}}). These are extracted from the token stream.

Execute Tools: If the model called a tool, Hone executes it in the sandbox. Example: reading a file, running a shell command, querying the semantic index. The tool's output is captured and added to context.

Loop or Done?: If the model said "I'm done" or "Here's your answer," the loop ends. If it called a tool, the output is added to the conversation and the loop repeats — the model sees the tool output and can call more tools or generate the final response.

docs.title: Agent Loop as a Sequence Diagram
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Agent as Hone Agent
    participant ContextMgr as Context Manager
    participant Model as Model Provider
    participant Tools as Tool Layer
    participant Sandbox as Kernel Sandbox

    User->>Agent: Send prompt
    activate Agent

    Agent->>ContextMgr: Build context (messages + history + files)
    activate ContextMgr
    ContextMgr-->>Agent: Bounded context window
    deactivate ContextMgr

    Agent->>Model: Call complete(context)
    activate Model
    Model-->>Agent: Stream tokens (thinking...)

    alt Model emits tool call
        Model-->>Agent: ToolCall JSON
        deactivate Model

        Agent->>Tools: Execute tool call
        activate Tools

        Tools->>Sandbox: Enforce policy
        activate Sandbox
        Sandbox-->>Tools: OK (path in allowlist)
        deactivate Sandbox

        Tools-->>Agent: Tool output
        deactivate Tools

        Agent->>Agent: Add tool output to context
        Agent->>Model: Continue streaming with tool output
        activate Model
    else Model emits "done"
        Model-->>Agent: Final response complete
        deactivate Model
        Agent->>Agent: Exit loop
    end

    Agent-->>User: Stream final response + tool calls
    deactivate Agent

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Multiple turns: The agent can call a tool, see the result, and adjust its next action based on what it learned. This is not one-shot execution; it's a reasoning loop.

Streaming visibility: You see the model thinking in real-time, not waiting for a final response. This builds trust.

Interruptible: You can hit Ctrl+C at any point to stop execution. No forced completion.

Cost tracking: Each token and tool call is counted. You see the cost before the loop finishes.

docs.title: 1b. Agents: Specialized Personas
docs.text: An agent is a specialized version of the AI with curated tools, context, and system prompts. Unlike recipes (which define "what to do step by step"), agents define "who the AI is."

docs.title: What is an Agent?
docs.text:
An agent is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter:

---
name: code-reviewer
description: Expert code reviewer for quality, security, performance, and maintainability
tools: [read, grep, glob, shell]
model: sonnet
---

You are a senior code reviewer. Perform systematic reviews following this process:

## Review Process

1. **Correctness** — Does the code do what it claims?
2. **Security** — SQL injection, XSS, command injection, secret leakage
3. **Performance** — Unnecessary allocations, N+1 queries
...

The frontmatter metadata (name, tools, model) configures the agent. The Markdown body becomes the system prompt.

docs.title: Agents vs. Recipes
docs.text:
Aspect Agent Recipe Defines "Who are you?" "What should I do?" Scope A persona with tools and expertise A sequence of steps to achieve a goal Reusability Across many tasks For a specific workflow Example "I am a security auditor" "Run tests, then refactor, then commit"

You can combine them: use the tdd-workflow agent with the tdd-feature recipe.

docs.title: Built-in Agents
docs.text: Hone includes 9 agents: - code-reviewer — Quality and security reviews - debugger — Systematic bug investigation - security-auditor — Vulnerability scanning - performance-optimizer — Profiling and optimization - documentation-agent — API docs and diagrams - api-designer — REST/GraphQL/gRPC design - tdd-workflow — TDD coach - rust-expert — Rust best practices - python-expert — Python best practices

docs.title: Custom Agents
docs.text: Define custom agents in .hone/agents/my-agent.md (project-level) or ~/.config/hone/agents/my-agent.md (user-level). See Tools and MCP Guide for detailed instructions.

docs.title: Discovery via Description
docs.text:
The agent registry supports fuzzy matching on description:

hone --agent "test-driven"  # finds "tdd-workflow"
hone --agent "code-quality"  # finds "code-reviewer"

This is powered by AgentRegistry::find_by_description(), which matches keywords case-insensitively.

docs.title: 2. The Layered Tool Architecture
docs.text: Hone doesn't just call a remote model API. It has four distinct layers of tool execution, each with different trade-offs:

docs.title: Layer 3: Skills (HONE.md)
docs.text:
Cost: Zero runtime tokens Speed: Instant (compile-time) Authority: User-defined conventions

A HONE.md file at your project root contains markdown-formatted "skills" that guide the model. Example:

# My Project Skills

## Code Style
- Use async/await, never callbacks
- Prefer named types over tuples
- All public functions must have docstrings

## Deployment
- `cargo build --release` builds the binary
- Binary is deployed to /opt/myapp via SSH
- Rollback: `systemctl restart myapp && sleep 5 && curl health-check`

The agent reads this file at startup and incorporates it into every system prompt. No API tokens used. This is "free guidance."

When to use Layer 3: - Encoding project conventions - Style guides - Architecture patterns - Deployment procedures - "This is how we do things here"

docs.title: Layer 2: Native Tools (Rust, <1ms)
docs.text:
Cost: Zero network, zero serialization Speed: <1 millisecond per call Authority: Hone's built-in capabilities

These are Rust functions linked directly into the Hone binary. Tool calls are function invocations, not JSON-RPC requests. Built-in tools include:

  • read_file — Read text files
  • write_file — Write text files
  • shell — Execute shell commands
  • git — Git operations (commit, log, diff)
  • semantic_search — Vector-based code search
  • lsp_* — Language server operations (hover, completions)

Example: Reading a file is a direct Rust function call. No serialization, no IPC overhead, no network round-trip.

When to use Layer 2: - File operations - Shell commands - Git interactions - Code intelligence (hover, completions) - Anything time-critical or bandwidth-heavy

docs.title: Layer 1: MCP Tools (JSON-RPC, 50-500ms)
docs.text:
Cost: Serialization + IPC Speed: 50-500 milliseconds Authority: External services (GitHub, Jira, Slack, databases)

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a JSON-RPC interface for tools. Hone spawns external MCP servers as subprocesses and communicates via stdio. Example:

[[mcp_servers]]
name = "github"
command = "npx"
args = ["@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"]
env = { GITHUB_TOKEN = "${GITHUB_TOKEN}" }

When the model calls github_search_repos, Hone: 1. Sends JSON-RPC request to the GitHub MCP server 2. Waits for response (50-500ms) 3. Returns result to the agent

Built-in MCP integrations: - GitHub (search repos, list issues, create PRs) - Jira (search, create tickets) - Slack (send messages) - Databases (SQL queries) - Custom servers (anything you implement)

When to use Layer 1: - Third-party APIs - External services - Workflows that need off-machine resources - Extensibility via standard protocol

docs.title: Layer 0: Code Mode (Agent-Generated Scripts)
docs.text:
Cost: Model tokens + script execution time Speed: Varies (scripting languages are slower) Authority: Agent-generated code

For complex multi-tool orchestration, the agent can generate and execute scripts (TypeScript, Python, etc.). Example:

You: "Crawl our GitHub org and find all repos without CI configured."

The agent might generate:

// Generated by agent
const repos = await github.searchRepos({ org: "my-org" });
for (const repo of repos) {
  const workflows = await github.getWorkflows(repo.id);
  if (workflows.length === 0) {
    console.log(`Missing CI: ${repo.name}`);
  }
}

The script runs in a subprocess (sandboxed), and its output is fed back to the agent.

When to use Layer 0: - Complex orchestration across multiple tools - Loops and conditionals - When you need a general-purpose programming language - Not recommended for simple tool calls

docs.title: Decision Matrix: Which Layer to Use?
docs.text: Task Layer Why Read a source file 2 Direct Rust call, instant Find all TODO comments 2 + 3 Layer 2 reads files; Layer 3 has grep patterns Create a GitHub issue 1 External API, needs authentication Run a multi-step deployment 0 Needs conditionals, loops, state Log code metrics to Datadog 1 External service, out-of-process Format code with Prettier 2 Native tool if built-in, else Layer 1 (MCP)

docs.title: 3. Context Window Management
docs.text:
A context window is the bounded amount of text a model can process. Different models have different limits:

Model Context Input Output Claude Opus 4.5 200K tokens ~300 pages ~4 pages Claude Sonnet 4 200K tokens ~300 pages ~4 pages Claude Haiku 3.5 200K tokens ~300 pages ~4 pages GPT-4o 128K tokens ~190 pages ~4 pages Ollama llama2 4K tokens ~6 pages ~1 page Local Mistral 32K tokens ~48 pages ~2 pages

Hone's Context Manager keeps token usage under the model's limit using a three-part strategy:

docs.title: Part 1: Token Budgeting
docs.text:
Before sending a request, Hone calculates:

Available tokens = Model's context limit (e.g., 200K)
Reserved for output = max_output_tokens (e.g., 4K)
Budget = Available - Reserved (e.g., 196K)

Current usage = conversation_history + requested_files + code_context
If current_usage > budget:
    → Compact context (see Part 2)

docs.title: Part 2: Compaction
docs.text:
When the context gets full, Hone compacts it by:

  1. Pruning old conversation turns — Keep recent turns (last N), summarize older ones
  2. Chunking large files — If a file is too big, request only relevant portions (using LSP)
  3. Semantic deduplication — Remove redundant explanations
  4. Memory injection — Replace large conversation history with learned patterns from memory (see Section 5)

Example: After 20 turns of conversation, Hone might summarize:

[CONTEXT COMPACTION]
First 10 turns: User asked to refactor authentication module.
Agent: Analyzed code, found 3 issues, fixed 2.
User: Asked for tests.
Agent: Added 15 unit tests.
[END COMPACTION]

[RECENT TURNS - FULL DETAIL]
Turn 11: ...
Turn 12: ...
...

docs.title: Part 3: Adaptive Inclusion
docs.text:
Hone doesn't include every file in your repo. It includes only:

  1. Explicitly requested — You ask to read a specific file
  2. Relevant to the task — Semantic search finds related code
  3. In the current loop — Files modified by recent tool calls
  4. Workspace context — File tree, diagnostics, symbols

You can cap context usage:

hone --context-window 64000  # Use only 64K tokens, not the full 200K

This is useful if: - You're on a metered connection - You want to control costs - You're using a smaller model

docs.title: 4. The Sandbox: Kernel-Level Isolation
docs.text: When an agent executes a shell command or reads a file, it doesn't happen in your main shell. It happens in a kernel-enforced sandbox — a restricted environment where the agent can only do what you explicitly allow.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine you hire someone to organize your office. You don't give them a key to your entire house. Instead:

  • You unlock the filing cabinet and close the door to the bedroom
  • You tell them "You can touch anything in the filing cabinet, but not outside it"
  • You tell them "You can read documents, but you cannot remove anything"
  • When they're done, you lock up again

The sandbox is that locked door.

docs.title: How Sandboxes Work (Platform-Specific)
docs.text:
macOS (Seatbelt): Uses the sandbox_init() system call to define a security profile. The profile lists allowed paths, system calls, and network access. The kernel enforces it at the syscall boundary.

Linux (Landlock): Uses the Landlock LSM (Linux Security Module) to define filesystem access rules. Landlock allows/denies file operations at the VFS layer.

Linux (seccomp-BPF): Older Linux kernels use seccomp-BPF to block dangerous syscalls (like execve unless whitelisted).

Container (seccomp): Docker and other containers already provide isolation via cgroups and seccomp. Hone's additional sandbox strengthens the boundary.

Windows (Planned): Job Objects and Restricted Tokens.

docs.title: SandboxPolicy: What You Allow
docs.text:
Before executing a tool, you define a SandboxPolicy:

pub struct SandboxPolicy {
    pub allow_read: Vec<PathBuf>,      // paths readable
    pub allow_write: Vec<PathBuf>,     // paths writable
    pub allow_exec: Vec<PathBuf>,      // allowed executables
    pub allow_network: bool,            // network access
    pub allow_env: Vec<String>,        // exposed env vars
}

Example policy for a git_commit tool:

[sandbox.tools.git]
allow_read = ["{project_root}"]        # can read project files
allow_write = ["{project_root}"]       # can write to project
allow_exec = ["/usr/bin/git"]          # only git binary allowed
allow_network = false                  # no network access
allow_env = ["GIT_AUTHOR_NAME", "GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL"]

If the agent tries to call /usr/bin/python or read /etc/shadow, the sandbox blocks it:

error: access denied (executable /usr/bin/python not in allowlist)

docs.title: Fail-Closed Invariant
docs.text:
This is critical: If the desired sandbox tier is unavailable and required, the operation fails entirely. There is no degraded mode.

Example:

You run: hone --sandbox seatbelt
Hone starts on Linux (which uses Landlock, not Seatbelt)
Error: Sandbox tier not available and enforcement required.
Operation aborted.

Why? Because silently degrading security is worse than failing.

docs.title: Real Threat Examples
docs.text:
Threat Sandbox Layer Mitigation Agent runs rm -rf / Seatbelt/Landlock Path allowlist; only writable paths permitted Agent reads /etc/shadow Seatbelt/Landlock Read allowlist; only permitted paths accessible Agent exfiltrates data via curl seccomp Network blocked by default; explicit allow_network required Agent spawns a backdoor process Landlock + seccomp Only whitelisted executables allowed Agent exhausts disk with logs rlimit Disk write limit (e.g., 1 GB per operation) Agent uses fork bomb rlimit Max subprocess limit (e.g., 10 subprocesses)

See Security Guide for complete configuration.

docs.title: 5. Adaptive Memory: Learning from Experience
docs.text:
Most AI tools forget what they learned in the previous session. Hone remembers.

Adaptive memory is a local, encrypted SQLite database that stores: - Successful patterns ("This codebase uses async/await consistently") - Failed approaches ("Regex won't work; use tree-sitter instead") - Performance insights ("The test suite takes 45 seconds") - Domain knowledge ("The auth module is owned by the platform team")

docs.title: The Learning Cycle
docs.text:
Observation → Extraction → Hypothesis → Verification → Solidification

Observation: During a session, Hone observes interactions. Examples:

  • Agent tried approach A, user said "that's wrong"
  • Agent tried approach B, user said "perfect"
  • Tool returned an error; agent recovered by doing X

Extraction: After the session, Hone extracts patterns:

{
  "pattern": "When fixing bug type 'race condition', use 'Arc<Mutex<T>>' not 'Cell<T>'",
  "evidence": ["fixed 3 race conditions this way", "1 user approval"],
  "confidence": 0.85
}

Hypothesis: Hone forms a testable hypothesis:

"In Rust code, Arc is the right choice for race condition fixes."

Verification: Next session, Hone tries this hypothesis. Did it work? Confidence goes up. Did it fail? Confidence goes down or hypothesis is deleted.

Solidification: After many successful applications, the pattern becomes "solid" and is injected into the system prompt automatically.

docs.title: Memory Storage
docs.text:
Memory is stored in ~/.local/share/hone/memory.db (encrypted with ~/.config/hone/key.bin). The database schema includes:

patterns:
  - id
  - text
  - confidence (0.0 to 1.0)
  - context (which project/language/domain)
  - created_at
  - last_verified_at

observations:
  - session_id
  - timestamp
  - category (tool_success, tool_failure, user_feedback, etc.)
  - content (JSON)
  - linked_pattern_id

docs.title: Difference from Cloud Memory
docs.text:
Claude Code (Anthropic's product) uses cloud memory — conversations and patterns are stored on Anthropic's servers. Hone uses local memory:

Aspect Claude Code (Cloud) Hone (Local) Where stored Anthropic's servers Your machine Encryption At rest on servers With your key Control Anthropic has access Only you have access Privacy Varies by terms 100% private Learning scope Cross-project (global) Per-project or per-team Sharing Via Anthropic's infrastructure Via your team infrastructure

Hone is designed for privacy: you own your learning.

docs.title: Enabling/Disabling Memory
docs.text:
[memory]
enabled = true
db_path = "~/.local/share/hone/memory.db"
encryption_key_file = "~/.config/hone/key.bin"

Disable for sensitive work:

hone --ephemeral  # no memory saved

docs.title: 6. The Daemon Model: hone vs honed
docs.text: Hone has two entry points:

docs.title: hone — Local CLI
docs.text:
hone --model gpt-4o --dir ~/myproject

This is a single-use terminal session. You start it, chat with the agent, the session ends. The process terminates.

Pros: - Simple, self-contained - No persistent server - Great for single-user workflows

Cons: - New process each time - Session state lost if terminal closes unexpectedly - Can't share a session with teammates

docs.title: honed — Remote Daemon
docs.text:
# Terminal 1: Start the daemon
honed --port 7777

# Terminal 2, 3, N: Connect clients
hone --remote localhost:7777

The daemon is a long-running HTTP/2 + SSE server. Multiple users can connect, share sessions, and hand off work. Session state is persistent.

Pros: - Persistent sessions (survive terminal disconnection) - Multi-user collaborative editing - Team governance via RBAC - Background indexing (always running) - Easier deployment (single server, many clients)

Cons: - Needs a server process - More complex setup - Requires shared authentication

docs.title: When to Use Each
docs.text: Scenario Use Fixing a bug in my code, right now hone Rapid iteration, solo developer hone Team working on same codebase honed Always-on code intelligence honed Running on a remote server honed Laptop development (no server) hone

docs.title: 7. Cost Model: Tokens and Budgets
docs.text: Every API call to a model provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.) costs money. Hone tracks costs in real-time so you know the expense before it happens.

docs.title: Token Pricing
docs.text:
Pricing is per 1 million tokens (the standard unit):

[pricing.anthropic]
"claude-opus-4-5" = { input_per_mtok = 3.00, output_per_mtok = 15.00 }

This means: - Input: $3 per 1M tokens - Output: $15 per 1M tokens

For a request with 10,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens:

Cost = (10,000 / 1,000,000) * 3.00 + (1,000 / 1,000,000) * 15.00
     = 0.03 + 0.015
     = $0.045

docs.title: Real Examples
docs.text:
A typical Hone interaction costs:

Task Tokens Cost Time Fix a typo 2K in, 200 out ~$0.01 2 seconds Add a feature 15K in, 2K out ~$0.06 1 minute Code review (10 files) 50K in, 3K out ~$0.20 3 minutes Large refactor 80K in, 8K out ~$0.39 5 minutes

docs.title: Token Counting
docs.text:
Hone uses tiktoken to count tokens accurately. Before sending a request, Hone calculates:

tokens_in_prompt = len(system_prompt) + len(conversation_history) + len(files)
estimated_cost = (tokens_in_prompt / 1_000_000) * input_rate + output_estimate

This is shown in the CLI:

Prompt: 4521 tokens
Output estimate: 500 tokens
Estimated cost: $0.019 USD
Continue? (y/n)

Hit n to cancel before spending.

docs.title: Budget Enforcement
docs.text:
Set a per-session budget:

hone --budget 5.00  # stop after spending $5

When the limit is reached:

Session cost: $4.98
Approaching budget limit ($5.00). Continue? (y/n)

Hit n to stop.

docs.title: Cost Reduction Strategies
docs.text:
Use cheaper models for simple tasks:

# Complex reasoning: use Opus (more capable, more expensive)
hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5

# Simple edits: use Haiku (cheaper, fast)
hone --model anthropic:claude-haiku-3-5

Use local models (free):

ollama pull llama2
hone --model ollama:llama2

Reduce context size:

hone --context-window 50000  # use only 50K tokens, not full 200K

Enable memory:

Learned patterns reduce the need to re-explain your codebase. This saves tokens over time.

docs.title: 8. RBAC and Team Governance
docs.text: When running honed (daemon mode), multiple users can access the same session. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) ensures each user has the right permissions.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Define roles in ~/.config/hone/config.toml:

[[rbac.roles]]
name = "admin"
permissions = ["sessions:create", "sessions:delete", "sessions:admin", "tools:all", "mcp:all"]

[[rbac.roles]]
name = "developer"
permissions = ["sessions:create", "sessions:read", "tools:file", "tools:git", "tools:shell"]

[[rbac.roles]]
name = "viewer"
permissions = ["sessions:read"]

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Permission Allows sessions:create Start a new session sessions:read View session history sessions:delete Delete sessions sessions:admin Transfer session ownership, adjust permissions tools:file Read/write files tools:git Commit, push, rebase tools:shell Execute arbitrary shell commands tools:all All tools mcp:all Call any MCP server mcp:read_only Call MCP tools that don't mutate

docs.title: User Assignment
docs.text:
[[rbac.users]]
user_id = "alice@company.com"
role = "admin"

[[rbac.users]]
user_id = "bob@company.com"
role = "developer"

[[rbac.users]]
user_id = "carol@company.com"
role = "viewer"

docs.title: Audit Logging
docs.text:
All actions are logged with user attribution:

{
  "timestamp": "2026-04-05T14:30:45Z",
  "session_id": "sess_abc123",
  "user": "alice@company.com",
  "event": "tool_call",
  "tool": "git_commit",
  "input": {"message": "fix: auth bug"},
  "result": "success",
  "duration_ms": 150
}

This is useful for compliance, debugging, and understanding usage patterns.

docs.title: 9. Multi-Agent Patterns
docs.text: Modern AI agents work better when specialized agents collaborate. Hone implements several research-backed patterns:

docs.title: Pattern 1: Orchestrator-Worker (Decompose-Execute-Merge)
docs.text:
Reference: Anthropic internal research, CodeR (arXiv 2406.xx)

The orchestrator breaks a complex task into independent subtasks, spawns worker agents for each, and merges results:

User: "Build a CLI email validator with comprehensive tests"

Orchestrator: "I'll break this into 4 subtasks"
  - Worker 1: Write test suite
  - Worker 2: Implement validation logic
  - Worker 3: Build CLI interface
  - Worker 4: Add error handling

All 4 run in parallel. Orchestrator reads all results and produces merged output.

When to use: - Complex features with multiple independent concerns - Tasks that naturally decompose - When parallel execution saves time

Configuration: 

hone --orchestrate "your complex task"

docs.title: Pattern 2: Agent Ensemble with Voting (MASAI Ranker)
docs.text:
Reference: MASAI Ranker (arXiv 2406.11638, +5-8% accuracy)

Run N parallel candidates with different temperatures (0.0, 0.3, 0.5, etc.), then have a dedicated ranker agent pick the best:

N=3 candidates with varied temperatures:
  Candidate 1 (T=0.0): Conservative response
  Candidate 2 (T=0.3): Balanced response
  Candidate 3 (T=0.5): Creative response

Ranker (T=0.0): Reads all 3, picks best by quality criteria.

Research shows: Ensemble voting improves code quality by 5-8% over single-shot, at roughly N× token cost.

Configuration: 

hone --ensemble 3 "your prompt"
hone --ensemble 5 "your prompt"  # up to 5 candidates

docs.title: Pattern 3: Test-Verification Loop (AgentCoder)
docs.text:
Reference: AgentCoder pattern, ChatDev follow-up

After each code generation step, automatically run tests. If tests fail, agent retries:

Agent: "Write function foo()"
  ↓ [writes code]
  ↓ [runs cargo test]
  → Tests fail
  ↓ Agent sees test output, fixes code
  ↓ [runs cargo test again]
  → Tests pass ✓

Impact: +40% bugs caught early (before code review).

Configuration: 

hone --recipe tdd-feature  # TDD enforces test loop

docs.title: Pattern 4: Reviewer Agent (ChatDev Pattern)
docs.text:
Reference: ChatDev (arXiv 2308.xxxx)

Dedicated "reviewer" agent reviews code changes before merge. Catches 30% of bugs that single-agent would miss:

Agent 1: Implement feature
Agent 2: Review implementation
  → Finds issue A, suggests fix
  → Finds issue B, suggests fix
Agent 1: Applies fixes
Agent 2: Reviews again
  → All checks pass ✓

Configuration: Built-in as code-reviewer agent: 

hone --agent code-reviewer -i "Review this PR"

docs.title: Pattern 5: Self-Refine Loop (Iterative Improvement)
docs.text:
Reference: Self-Refine (NeurIPS 2023), +8-15% quality improvement

Agent generates output, then iteratively improves based on self-feedback:

Iteration 1: Generate solution
Feedback: "Too verbose, missing error handling"
  ↓
Iteration 2: Refine based on feedback
Feedback: "Good, but inefficient"
  ↓
Iteration 3: Optimize for efficiency
Feedback: "✓ Ready"

Impact: +8-15% quality improvement per iteration (costs more tokens).

Configuration: 

hone --recipe refactor  # Includes refine steps

docs.title: Pattern 6: Adaptive Complexity Routing
docs.text:
Reference: Internal Anthropic optimization

Automatically classify requests by complexity and route to appropriate model:

  • Simple (< 100 tokens): Use fast, cheap model (Haiku)
  • Medium (100-5000 tokens): Use balanced model (Sonnet)
  • Complex (> 5000 tokens): Use capable model (Opus)
User: "What's 2+2?"
Router: "Simple question → route to Haiku (faster, cheaper)"

User: "Design a microservices architecture for a fintech platform"
Router: "Complex → route to Opus (most capable)"

Configuration: Automatic. Can override: 

hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5  # force a model

docs.title: Composing Patterns Together
docs.text:
You can combine multiple patterns:

Orchestrator (decompose)
  ↓ Each worker runs:
    Complexity Router (route to right model)
    Test-Verify Loop (verify with tests)
    Self-Refine (iteratively improve)
  ↓ Ensemble Ranker (pick best result across workers)
  ↓ Reviewer Agent (final code review)
  ↓ Merge results

docs.title: When to Use Each Pattern
docs.text: Pattern Use When Cost Quality Gain Orchestrator Task decomposes naturally High (parallel) +20-30% Ensemble Want best-of-N responses High (N×) +5-8% Test-Verify Code generation task Medium +40% bug catch Reviewer Final quality assurance Medium +30% bug catch Self-Refine Iterative improvement needed Medium +8-15% Complexity Router Multi-task, cost-conscious Low Variable

docs.title: Implementation Examples
docs.text: See the relevant source files for deep dives: - Orchestrator: crates/hone-core/src/orchestrator.rs - Ensemble: crates/hone-core/src/ensemble.rs - Test-Verify: crates/hone-core/src/test_loop.rs - Reviewer: crates/hone-core/src/reviewer.rs - Self-Refine: crates/hone-core/src/self_refine.rs - Complexity Router: crates/hone-core/src/complexity.rs
