docs.title: Migrating from Aider to Hone
docs.text: You know Aider. You're comfortable with git-centric workflows, repo maps, voice input, and multi-file editing. Here's how Hone extends those ideas—and what's new.

docs.title: Concept Mapping
docs.text: Aider Hone Equivalent Notes Repo map (code context) Semantic index (AST + embeddings) More powerful, adaptive /add / /drop (context management) Context window management + agent control Automatic in Hone Auto-commit AutoCommitter + git tools Implemented + git undo/redo Voice input Voice input (planned) Not yet, but CLI is stable /architect (plan mode) Model routing (use opus for planning) Implemented Multi-file editing Multi-file edits via agent loop Native support Edit request format Edit tool + natural language More flexible, agent chooses strategy Chat history Memory + encrypted SQLite More powerful adaptive learning Model switching /model <provider:model> hot-swap Same command, broader provider support

docs.title: Aider Workflow
docs.text:
# Start with a project
cd my-project
aider

# In session:
# /add src/main.py tests/test_main.py  (add files to context)
# Implement user login with password hashing
# /drop tests/  (remove from context)
# Now add two-factor auth
# /architect  (switch to planning mode)
# Design the database schema

Strengths: Git-aware, can modify multiple files in one turn, voice input.

docs.title: Hone Workflow
docs.text:
# Start with a project
cd my-project
hone

# In session:
# Implement user login with password hashing
# (Hone automatically finds relevant files via semantic search)
# Now add two-factor auth
# (Hone adjusts context window as needed)
# /model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5  (switch to most capable for planning)
# Design the database schema

Differences: - No /add /drop — Hone manages context automatically - No explicit "architect mode" — Use /model to route to a capable model - Voice coming (planned, not yet implemented)

docs.title: 1. Semantic Indexing (Better Than Repo Map)
docs.text:
Aider uses basic lexical search. Hone uses semantic indexing:

Aider repo map: 

src/
  auth/
    - login.py (100 lines)
    - verify.py (50 lines)
  db/
    - schema.py (200 lines)
    - models.py (300 lines)
tests/
  - test_auth.py (100 lines)
  - test_db.py (80 lines)

When you ask to "add two-factor auth," Aider searches by keywords ("factor", "auth").

Hone semantic index: 

# Understand structure + meaning
hone -i "Find functions that handle authentication"
# Result: Returns auth.login(), auth.verify_token(), auth.setup_2fa()
# (by meaning, not keywords)

hone -i "Where is the user table defined?"
# Result: models.py, schema.py, migrations/ (related files)

Hone uses: - Tree-sitter for AST parsing (language-aware) - SQLite vector embeddings (semantic similarity) - Persistent index (learned, cached across sessions)

docs.title: 2. Automatic Context Management
docs.text:
Aider requires you to /add files manually. Hone does it automatically:

Aider: 

aider
# /add src/auth/login.py src/db/models.py tests/
# Now it's in context. When context is full:
# /drop tests/  (drop something to make room)

Hone: 

hone
# Agent automatically:
# 1. Finds relevant files via semantic search
# 2. Estimates tokens needed
# 3. Adds to context
# 4. If context overflows, removes least-relevant files
# All automatic, visible in debug logs

You can still control it: 

/context show      # See what's loaded
/context add path  # Manually add a file
/context drop path # Manually remove

docs.title: 3. Git UndoStack (Beyond Auto-Commit)
docs.text:
Aider auto-commits. Hone goes further with a full undo/redo system:

Aider: 

# Agent makes changes, auto-commits
# If you don't like it, undo with git
git revert HEAD

Hone: 

# Agent makes changes, auto-commits (if enabled)
# You can:
git_undo          # Revert last change
git_redo          # Reapply
git_diff          # Review before accepting
/undo             # Undo last agent turn (not just last commit)
/redo             # Redo undone turn

Hone tracks agent turns, not just commits.

docs.title: 4. Kernel Sandboxing
docs.text:
Aider relies on process isolation. Hone uses kernel-level containment:

  • macOS: Seatbelt (same as Safari)
  • Linux: Landlock (same as systemd)

When agent edits files or runs commands, the OS enforces restrictions at kernel level. No privilege escalation possible.

docs.title: 5. LSP Integration
docs.text:
Aider has no built-in LSP. Hone bridges language servers:

hone -i "What's the return type of this function?"
# Agent calls: lsp_hover(file="main.rs", line=42, col=10)
# Returns: type information from Rust analyzer

hone -i "Fix the type errors in this file"
# Agent calls: lsp_diagnostics(file="main.rs")
# Sees all errors, fixes them systematically

docs.title: 6. Provider Freedom
docs.text:
Aider locks you to OpenAI. Hone supports 75+ providers:

hone --model openai:gpt-4o              # OpenAI (Aider's default)
hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5  # Anthropic (more capable for planning)
hone --model ollama:llama2              # Local (free, private)

Hot-swap mid-session without losing history.

docs.title: 1. No Voice (Yet)
docs.text:
Aider supports voice input. Hone doesn't (planned). For now, type or pipe input:

# Voice workaround (until Hone adds native support)
hone << 'EOF'
Refactor the authentication module to support JWT tokens
EOF

# Or use a voice-to-text tool
say "Refactor the authentication module" | \
  speech-to-text | \
  hone

docs.title: 2. No Explicit /architect Mode
docs.text:
Aider has /architect for planning. Hone routes to capable models instead:

Aider: 

/architect
Design a caching layer for the API

Hone: 

/model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5  (switch to most capable model)
Design a caching layer for the API

Or let Hone route automatically (planned feature): 

# Hone detects "design" keywords and routes to opus automatically
Design a caching layer for the API

docs.title: 3. Multi-File Edits Work Differently
docs.text:
Aider: You specify files, agent edits all of them in one turn: 

/add src/auth.py src/db.py src/tests/test_auth.py
Now add two-factor authentication (modify both auth.py and db.py)
# Agent makes edits to both files

Hone: Agent loops and makes multiple edits: 

Add two-factor authentication to the auth module
# Agent turn 1: reads auth.py, designs changes
# Agent turn 2: edits auth.py
# Agent turn 3: reads db.py, designs schema changes
# Agent turn 4: edits db.py
# Agent turn 5: runs tests, verifies

Why? Hone's layered tool architecture allows granular, auditable changes.

docs.title: 4. Config Format
docs.text:
Aider: Command-line flags or .aider.conf.json

Hone: TOML config + HONE.md conventions

# ~/.config/hone/config.toml
[agent]
default_model = "openai:gpt-4o"  # match your Aider default
max_iterations = 20
auto_commit = true               # same as Aider

[git]
commit_on_change = true
require_approval = false

[memory]
enabled = true

[sandbox]
strategy = "seatbelt"  # macOS: seatbelt, Linux: landlock

# HONE.md (in your project)
## Skill: Multi-File Edits

When making related changes across multiple files:
1. Read all affected files first
2. Design changes in natural language
3. Execute edits one file at a time
4. Test changes with unit tests
5. Commit with clear messages

docs.title: 1. Install Hone
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/anthropics/hone.git
cd hone
cargo build --release
sudo cp target/release/hone /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: 2. Configure Your Default Model
docs.text:
If you've been using OpenAI with Aider:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

# Create config
mkdir -p ~/.config/hone
cat > ~/.config/hone/config.toml << 'EOF'
[providers.openai]
api_key = "${OPENAI_API_KEY}"

[agent]
default_model = "openai:gpt-4o"
auto_commit = true
EOF

docs.title: 3. Create HONE.md for Your Project
docs.text:
Copy any Aider system prompts or project guidelines:

# Project Skills

## Skill: Multi-File Edits

When making changes across files:
1. Read all affected files
2. Plan changes clearly
3. Edit files one at a time
4. Run tests after each edit
5. Commit with a clear message

## Skill: Testing

Always run pytest after making changes:
  pytest -v tests/

## Skill: Code Review

Before committing:
1. Review changes with `git diff`
2. Check for error handling
3. Verify all unwrap() calls are justified
4. Run clippy/pylint as appropriate

docs.title: 4. Test Your First Session
docs.text:
cd /your/aider/project
hone

Try a familiar workflow: 

Refactor the login module to use JWT tokens

Hone will: 1. Search for related files (no /add needed) 2. Read them automatically 3. Make changes 4. Test (if it finds test files) 5. Commit (if auto_commit is true)

docs.title: 5. Set Up Auto-Commit (Optional)
docs.text:
If you liked Aider's auto-commit:

[git]
auto_commit = true
require_approval = false  # false = commit automatically, true = ask first

Or in session: 

/auto-commit on

docs.title: Do I need to /add files like in Aider?
docs.text: No. Hone manages context automatically via semantic search. You can still /context add if you want to force something.

docs.title: Will Hone support voice input?
docs.text: Yes, it's planned. For now, type or pipe input from a speech-to-text tool.

docs.title: How does Hone handle multi-file edits compared to Aider?
docs.text: Differently. Hone edits one file at a time (more auditable). For large refactors, it may take more turns, but each change is reviewable.

docs.title: Can I use my Aider system prompt in Hone?
docs.text: Yes, move it to HONE.md. Same format, same semantics.

docs.title: How do I switch models mid-session like I did with Aider?
docs.text:
Use /model: 

/model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5  # switch to Claude
/model openai:gpt-4o              # switch back to OpenAI

Context is preserved across switches.

docs.title: What about Aider's chat history?
docs.text:
Hone stores chat history in memory (encrypted SQLite). Sessions are replayable. You can also export: 

/export session.json

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Install: Follow step 1 above
  2. Config: Create ~/.config/hone/config.toml with your model preference
  3. HONE.md: Create HONE.md in your project with project guidelines
  4. Test: Run hone and try a simple task
  5. Explore: Read Semantic Index for how context works
  6. Recipes: Read Recipes Guide for automation

Migrating from Aider? Questions? Open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Migrating from Claude Code to Hone
docs.text: You know Claude Code. You're comfortable with CLAUDE.md, slash commands, the agent loop, and extended thinking. Here's how those concepts map to Hone—and what you gain.

docs.title: Concept Mapping
docs.text: Claude Code Hone Equivalent Status CLAUDE.md (project conventions) HONE.md Implemented /compact (reduce verbosity) /compact Implemented /model <name> (switch models) /model <provider:model> Implemented Agent tools (Read, Edit, Bash) Layer 2 tools (read_file, edit_file, shell) Implemented Memory (remember context) hone-memory (encrypted SQLite, adaptive learning) Implemented Extended thinking Model routing (use opus for complex, sonnet for speed) Implemented TodoWrite tool Recipes (YAML workflows) Implemented Agent orchestration Multi-agent mode (plan + execute) Planned Hooks (pre/post commit) config.toml hooks Planned MCP servers MCP Layer 1 (same protocol, better integration) Implemented

docs.title: Claude Code Session
docs.text:
# Set up CLAUDE.md with conventions
cat > CLAUDE.md << 'EOF'
# Python Testing

Always use pytest. After writing code, run `pytest -v` to verify.
EOF

# Start interactive session
claude

# In session: agent reads CLAUDE.md, learns conventions (token cost: ~500 tokens)
# Type: Fix the failing test in test_utils.py
# Agent loops: reads file → finds bug → fixes → runs pytest → commits

Cost: Every session re-reads CLAUDE.md (token overhead).

docs.title: Hone Session
docs.text:
# Set up HONE.md (same format, same content)
cat > HONE.md << 'EOF'
# Python Testing

Always use pytest. After writing code, run `pytest -v` to verify.
EOF

# Start interactive session
hone

# HONE.md parsed once at startup (no token cost, compiled into system prompt)
# Type: Fix the failing test in test_utils.py
# Agent loops: reads file → finds bug → fixes → runs pytest → commits

Benefit: HONE.md is zero-cost. It's parsed once and baked into the system prompt (no token streaming overhead).

docs.title: 1. Provider Freedom
docs.text:
Claude Code locks you to Anthropic. Hone supports 75+ providers:

# Same session, different models
hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5   # Most capable
hone --model openai:gpt-4o                # Alternative
hone --model ollama:llama2                # Free, local
hone --model claude-cli:claude-opus       # Your existing CLI

Hot-swap mid-session without losing history: 

You: /model openai:gpt-4o
Hone: Switched to gpt-4o. Conversation preserved.

docs.title: 2. Kernel Sandboxing
docs.text:
Claude Code relies on process isolation. Hone uses kernel-level sandboxing:

  • macOS: Seatbelt (same as Safari)
  • Linux: Landlock (same as systemd)
  • Other: seccomp (same as Docker)

Tool calls are auditable and confined:

# See the sandbox policy in effect
hone --show-sandbox-policy
# Output: Using Seatbelt on macOS
#   Deny network (except: api.anthropic.com, api.openai.com)
#   Deny /etc, /var, /tmp (except: /tmp/.hone-*)
#   Allow read: project root, ~/.local/share/hone
#   Allow execute: /bin, /usr/bin, cargo, python3

docs.title: 3. Adaptive Memory
docs.text:
Claude Code has basic memory. Hone's memory learns patterns:

# After a few sessions where you run pytest, then clippy, then commit...
# Hone learns this workflow and suggests it automatically

You: Fix the bug in main.rs
Hone: Based on your recent pattern, should I also run `cargo clippy` and commit?

Memory is encrypted, stored locally in SQLite:

[memory]
db_path = "~/.local/share/hone/memory.db"
encryption_key_file = "~/.config/hone/key.bin"

docs.title: 4. Local Models (Free)
docs.text:
Run private, zero-cost inference:

ollama pull llama2
ollama serve  # in another terminal

hone --model ollama:llama2
# No API key needed, no privacy concerns

docs.title: 5. Remote Daemon with Team Governance
docs.text:
Claude Code is single-user, single-machine. Hone can run as a server:

# On a shared machine
honed --port 7070

# From your laptop (another terminal or network)
hone --remote myserver:7070

Team governance with roles: - admin — manage settings, users, budgets - operator — run sessions, read all code - viewer — read-only access

See Server and Remote.

docs.title: 1. CLI Model Spec
docs.text:
Claude Code: 

claude --model claude-opus-4-5

Hone: 

hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5
# Format: <provider>:<model>
# Providers: anthropic, openai, ollama, claude-cli, gemini-cli, acp, ...

docs.title: 2. Built with Rust (Not Node.js)
docs.text:
Claude Code is a Node.js CLI. Hone is a Rust binary.

Benefits: - Single, self-contained binary (no Node.js dependency) - Faster startup (~100ms vs ~500ms) - Smaller memory footprint - Native support for Seatbelt/Landlock sandboxing

For you: No behavioral difference. Just works.

docs.title: 3. Recipes Replace Inline Prompts
docs.text:
Claude Code approach: 

# Use TodoWrite to track inline TODOs
claude << 'EOF'
Read src/main.rs, find all TODO comments, create issues on GitHub
EOF

Hone approach: 

# Create a recipe: scripts/process-todos.yaml
name: process-todos
description: Find TODOs and create GitHub issues
steps:
  - tool: file_search
    query: "TODO|FIXME"
  - agent:
      prompt: "For each TODO, create a GitHub issue"
      model: anthropic:claude-opus-4-5

# Run it anytime
hone --recipe scripts/process-todos.yaml

Benefits of recipes: - Reusable across projects - Shareable with teammates - Versioned with git - No token overhead (syntax is simple YAML, not natural language)

See Recipes Guide.

docs.title: 4. Daemon-First Architecture
docs.text:
Claude Code is CLI-only. Hone defaults to daemon:

# Start the daemon (persists across sessions)
honed

# In another terminal, connect
hone --remote localhost:7070

# Sessions are stored, replayable, auditable

For local use, the CLI still works: 

hone  # Works as before, no daemon needed

docs.title: 1. Install Hone
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/anthropics/hone.git
cd hone
cargo build --release
sudo cp target/release/hone /usr/local/bin/

See Getting Started for details.

docs.title: 2. Copy Your CLAUDE.md to HONE.md
docs.text:
cd /your/project
cp CLAUDE.md HONE.md  # Exact same format, Hone understands it

Hone parses HONE.md at startup (zero token cost).

docs.title: 3. Configure Providers
docs.text:
Copy your API keys from Claude Code config to Hone config:

Claude Code location: ~/.claude/config.json or env vars

Hone location: ~/.config/hone/config.toml

Example migration:

# If you had Claude Code using Anthropic API
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."

# Hone will read the same env var automatically
hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5

Or create ~/.config/hone/config.toml:

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "sk-ant-..."

[agent]
default_model = "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5"
context_window_tokens = 16000
max_iterations = 20

[memory]
enabled = true
db_path = "~/.local/share/hone/memory.db"

docs.title: 4. Run Your First Session
docs.text:
cd /your/project
hone

You'll see: - HONE.md loaded (0 tokens spent) - Agent ready with all conventions - Familiar tool calls (read, edit, shell) - Slash commands (same as Claude Code)

docs.title: 5. Migrate Inline Workflows to Recipes (Optional)
docs.text:
If you had TodoWrite tasks:

Before (Claude Code): 

claude << 'EOF'
1. Read tests/
2. Run pytest
3. For each failure, fix the code
4. Commit changes
EOF

After (Hone recipes):

Create scripts/fix-tests.yaml:

name: fix-failing-tests
description: Find and fix test failures
steps:
  - tool: file_search
    pattern: "tests/**/*.py"

  - agent:
      prompt: "Run pytest and identify failures"
      model: anthropic:claude-opus-4-5

  - agent:
      prompt: "For each failure, fix the underlying code"
      model: anthropic:claude-opus-4-5

  - tool: git_commit
    message: "fix: resolve failing tests"

Run it: 

hone --recipe scripts/fix-tests.yaml

docs.title: Do I need to rewrite my CLAUDE.md?
docs.text: No. Copy it to HONE.md as-is. Same format, same content. Hone understands it.

docs.title: Will my memory transfer?
docs.text: No. Claude Code and Hone have separate memory systems. But Hone's memory is more powerful—it learns patterns automatically. You'll build up new memories quickly.

docs.title: Can I use both Claude Code and Hone?
docs.text: Yes. They run independently. Keep both if you want to compare, then switch fully when ready.

docs.title: How do I set a budget like Claude Code's /budget?
docs.text:
Same command: 

/budget 10.00  # max $10 per session

Or in config.toml: 

[agent]
max_spend_usd = 10.00

docs.title: What about extended thinking?
docs.text:
Hone supports model-specific features via /model: 

# Use a model that supports extended thinking
hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5  # supports extended thinking
hone --model openai:gpt-4o              # does not (yet)

Hone also routes complex tasks automatically (planned feature).

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Install: Follow step 1 above
  2. Configure: Create ~/.config/hone/config.toml or set env vars
  3. Test: Run hone in a small project and try a familiar task
  4. Explore: Read Providers Guide for hot-swapping
  5. Recipes: Read Recipes Guide for automation
  6. Tools: Read Tools and MCP to extend capabilities

Migrating from Claude Code? Have questions? Open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Migrating from Codex CLI to Hone
docs.text: You know Codex CLI. You're comfortable with kernel sandboxing, approval workflows, and running code safely. Here's how Hone takes those ideas further—and what's new.

docs.title: Concept Mapping
docs.text: Codex CLI Hone Equivalent Notes seccomp sandbox Seatbelt/Landlock/seccomp Same approach, kernel-level Approval workflow Approval workflow + diffs Implemented, more granular OpenAI models 75+ providers (including OpenAI) Not locked to OpenAI suggest mode Agent loop with streaming Same paradigm auto-edit mode AutoCommitter tool Implemented full-auto mode Recipes with multi-step automation More structured, auditable Cost tracking Real-time cost tracking per turn Better visibility Diff review git_diff tool + approval Natural git integration

docs.title: Codex CLI Workflow
docs.text:
# Start session (suggest mode)
codex suggest

# In session:
# Prompt: Fix the null pointer exception in main.rs
# Codex suggests changes, you review diffs
# Accept or reject

# For automation, switch to auto-edit mode
codex auto-edit

# Prompt: Add logging to all database queries
# Codex makes changes automatically, asks for approval

Strengths: Safe by default (approvals required), OpenAI integration, cost tracking.

docs.title: Hone Workflow
docs.text:
# Start session
hone

# In session:
# Prompt: Fix the null pointer exception in main.rs
# Hone loops: reads file, identifies issue, suggests fix
# Shows diff (same as Codex)
# You accept or reject

# For automation, use a recipe
hone --recipe scripts/add-logging.yaml

# Executes multi-step workflow:
#   1. Find database queries
#   2. Add structured logging
#   3. Run tests
#   4. Commit (if approved)

Key differences: - Approvals are more flexible (per-turn, per-tool, per-file) - Recipes replace mode switching (more composable) - Sandbox is kernel-enforced (more secure)

docs.title: 1. Kernel Sandboxing (Better Than seccomp)
docs.text:
Codex CLI uses seccomp. Hone uses OS-native sandboxing:

Platform Codex CLI Hone Benefit macOS seccomp (emulated) Seatbelt (native) Same API as Safari, more reliable Linux seccomp Landlock (newer) Supports deny-on-access, more flexible Other seccomp seccomp Same

Real example:

hone --show-sandbox-policy

# Output:
# Sandbox: Seatbelt on macOS
#   Deny: /etc/* (except whitelisted)
#   Deny: /var/* (except ~/.local/share/hone)
#   Deny: Network (except api.openai.com, api.anthropic.com)
#   Allow: read /Users/you/project, execute /bin/bash, /usr/bin/python3

Policies are auditable and configurable.

docs.title: 2. Provider Freedom (No OpenAI Lock-In)
docs.text:
Codex CLI only works with OpenAI. Hone supports 75+ providers:

hone --model openai:gpt-4o              # OpenAI (match Codex CLI)
hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5  # Anthropic (more capable)
hone --model ollama:llama2              # Local (free, private)

Hot-swap mid-session: 

You: /model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5
Hone: Switched to claude-opus-4-5. Conversation preserved.

Why this matters: - Vendor negotiating power (shop around for pricing) - Avoid API outages (fallback chains) - Use local models for sensitive code - Experiment with different models

docs.title: 3. Recipes (Better Than Mode Switching)
docs.text:
Codex CLI has 3 modes: suggest, auto-edit, full-auto. Hone has recipes:

Codex CLI: 

# Mode switching
codex suggest   # interactive, show diffs
codex auto-edit # auto-apply, ask for approval
codex full-auto # fully automatic (risky)

Hone: 

# recipes/add-logging.yaml
name: add-structured-logging
description: Add structured logging to database queries

approvals:
  require_approval: true
  on: ["edit_file", "git_commit"]  # approve edits and commits

steps:
  - tool: file_search
    pattern: "src/**/*.rs"

  - agent:
      prompt: "Find database query calls"
      model: openai:gpt-4o

  - agent:
      prompt: "Add structured logging to each query"
      model: openai:gpt-4o
      approval_before: true  # ask before agent edits

  - tool: shell
    cmd: "cargo test"
    approval_before: true

  - tool: git_commit
    message: "feat: add structured logging to database queries"
    approval_before: true

Run it: 

hone --recipe scripts/add-logging.yaml
# Executes step by step, asks for approval at each approval point

Benefits: - Fully composable (tools + agents + conditions) - Auditable (each step is logged) - Reusable (version with git) - Safer than "full-auto" (explicit approval points)

docs.title: 4. Real-Time Cost Tracking (Transparent Billing)
docs.text:
Both Codex CLI and Hone track costs. Hone is more granular:

Codex CLI: 

# Session total at end
Total cost: $0.42 (OpenAI API usage)

Hone: 

# Per-turn cost tracking (streaming)
Usage: 4521 input tokens, 312 output tokens
Cost: $0.019 USD (openai:gpt-4o)
Session total: $0.24 USD
Budget remaining: $9.76 / $10.00

# Turn 2
Usage: 1200 input tokens, 89 output tokens
Cost: $0.004 USD
Session total: $0.28 USD

Plus built-in budget limits: 

hone --budget 5.00
# Session stops when $5.00 is spent

Or in config: 

[agent]
max_spend_usd = 5.00

docs.title: 5. LSP Integration (No Language Gaps)
docs.text:
Codex CLI has basic language support. Hone bridges all language servers:

hone -i "Fix type errors in this Rust file"
# Agent calls: lsp_diagnostics(file="main.rs")
# Sees all type errors from rust-analyzer
# Fixes them systematically

hone -i "What does this Python function do?"
# Agent calls: lsp_hover(file="utils.py", line=42, col=10)
# Returns docstring + type info from Pylance

Supports Python, Rust, TypeScript, Go, Java, C++, etc.

docs.title: 6. Multi-User & Audit Logging
docs.text:
Codex CLI is single-user. Hone can be multi-user with full audit logging:

# Start daemon
honed --port 7070 --audit-log /var/log/hone/audit.log

# From your laptop
hone --remote myserver:7070

# Audit log shows:
# 2026-04-05 12:34:56 [user=alice, session=abc123]
#   Tool: read_file, path=/home/alice/project/src/main.rs
#   Result: OK
# 2026-04-05 12:34:57 [user=alice, session=abc123]
#   Tool: shell, cmd=cargo test
#   Result: OK (0 failures)
# 2026-04-05 12:35:00 [user=alice, session=abc123]
#   Tool: git_commit, message=fix: null pointer exception
#   Result: OK

Useful for: - Compliance (HIPAA, SOC 2, etc.) - Team accountability - Security investigations - Cost tracking per user

docs.title: 1. Approval Workflow Is More Granular
docs.text:
Codex CLI: Approve or reject entire turn

Hone: Approve specific actions:

# In session, Hone shows each tool call
[Tool: read_file] src/main.rs
[Tool: edit_file] src/main.rs (line 42)
  - Old: if ptr != null { ... }
  - New: if let Some(ptr) = ptr { ... }
  [Approve? y/n] y

[Tool: shell] cargo test
[Output: 15 tests passed]
  [Approve? y/n] y

[Tool: git_commit] fix: null pointer exception
  [Approve? y/n] y

More fine-grained control.

docs.title: 2. Recipes Are YAML, Not Modes
docs.text:
Codex CLI modes are implicit. Hone recipes are explicit YAML files.

Benefit: Reusable, versionable, shareable.

docs.title: 3. Sandbox Policy Is Configurable
docs.text:
Codex CLI sandbox is hardcoded. Hone sandbox is policy-based:

# ~/.config/hone/config.toml

[sandbox]
strategy = "seatbelt"  # macOS

[sandbox.policies.file_system]
allow_read = ["/Users/you/project", "/usr/lib", "/usr/local/bin"]
deny_read = ["/etc", "/var", "/private/var"]
allow_write = ["/Users/you/project", "/tmp"]
deny_write = ["/etc", "/var", "/private/var"]

[sandbox.policies.network]
deny_all = true
allow_exceptions = ["api.openai.com", "github.com"]

[sandbox.policies.process]
deny_all = true
allow_execute = ["/bin/bash", "/usr/bin/python3", "/usr/local/bin/cargo"]

You can tighten or loosen policies per project.

docs.title: 4. Distributed Execution
docs.text:
Codex CLI is single-machine. Hone can run on a server:

# Codex CLI: always local
codex suggest

# Hone: local or remote
hone                        # local
hone --remote myserver:7070 # remote (daemon)

Remote daemon handles authentication, audit logging, cost tracking per user.

docs.title: 1. Install Hone
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/anthropics/hone.git
cd hone
cargo build --release
sudo cp target/release/hone /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: 2. Configure OpenAI (Your Existing Provider)
docs.text:
If you've been using Codex CLI with OpenAI:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."  # same as Codex CLI

# Create config
mkdir -p ~/.config/hone
cat > ~/.config/hone/config.toml << 'EOF'
[providers.openai]
api_key = "${OPENAI_API_KEY}"

[agent]
default_model = "openai:gpt-4o"
max_spend_usd = 10.00  # your budget

[sandbox]
strategy = "seatbelt"  # macOS
EOF

docs.title: 3. Test Your First Session
docs.text:
cd /your/codex/project
hone

Try a familiar task: 

Fix the null pointer exception in main.rs

Hone will: 1. Find the file 2. Read it 3. Identify the issue 4. Suggest a fix 5. Show the diff 6. Ask for approval 7. Apply the fix 8. Commit (if you approve)

docs.title: 4. Create Your First Recipe
docs.text:
If you had workflows you ran repeatedly with Codex CLI, turn them into recipes.

Example: "Refactor legacy Python to use type hints"

Create scripts/add-type-hints.yaml:

name: add-type-hints
description: Add type hints to legacy Python code

approvals:
  require_approval: true
  on: ["edit_file", "git_commit"]

steps:
  - tool: file_search
    pattern: "src/**/*.py"

  - agent:
      prompt: "Add comprehensive type hints to these Python files"
      model: openai:gpt-4o
      approval_before: true

  - tool: shell
    cmd: "python -m mypy src/"
    approval_before: false  # no approval for read-only check

  - tool: git_commit
    message: "refactor: add type hints to Python modules"
    approval_before: true

Run it: 

hone --recipe scripts/add-type-hints.yaml

docs.title: 5. Explore Approval Workflows
docs.text:
Unlike Codex CLI's rigid modes, Hone lets you customize approval points:

steps:
  - agent:
      prompt: "Refactor the main function"
      approval_before: true   # approve before agent runs
      approval_after: false   # auto-apply changes (still review via git_diff)

  - tool: git_diff
    # Show changes (read-only)

  - tool: git_commit
    message: "refactor: improve main function"
    approval_before: true    # approve before committing

docs.title: Can I use the same OpenAI API key with Hone?
docs.text: Yes. Set OPENAI_API_KEY env var or config file. Hone reads the same keys.

docs.title: Is Hone's sandbox as safe as Codex CLI's?
docs.text: Yes, and arguably better. Hone uses OS-native sandboxing (Seatbelt on macOS, Landlock on Linux) instead of seccomp emulation. Policies are auditable.

docs.title: Do recipes replace approval workflows?
docs.text: No. Recipes define multi-step workflows; approvals control which steps require manual review. Use together: - Recipes for orchestration - Approvals for safety

docs.title: How do I migrate my Codex CLI workflows?
docs.text: Turn them into recipes. Example: - Codex CLI "full-auto mode" → Hone recipe with approval_before: false on most steps - Codex CLI "suggest mode" → Hone session with /model and manual approval per turn

docs.title: Can I set per-step budgets?
docs.text:
Not yet, but you can set global budget: 

[agent]
max_spend_usd = 10.00

When recipe hits the budget, it stops.

docs.title: What about rate limiting?
docs.text: Hone respects provider rate limits. If OpenAI rate-limits you: 1. Hone waits (configurable timeout) 2. Falls back to next provider (if configured) 3. Logs the event for debugging

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Install: Follow step 1 above
  2. Config: Create ~/.config/hone/config.toml with OpenAI settings
  3. Test: Run hone and try a familiar task
  4. Recipes: Read Recipes Guide to automate workflows
  5. Security: Read Security Guide for sandbox policies
  6. Team: Read Server and Remote for multi-user setup

Migrating from Codex CLI? Questions? Open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Migrating from Goose to Hone
docs.text: You know Goose. You're comfortable with MCP-native architecture, recipes, extensions, and provider flexibility. Here's how Hone builds on those ideas—and what's new.

docs.title: Concept Mapping
docs.text: Goose Hone Equivalent Notes Extensions (custom tools) Layer 2 native tools + Layer 1 MCP Hone has faster native layer + MCP Recipes (YAML workflows) Recipes (same YAML format) 100% compatible with Goose recipes Providers Providers (same abstraction) 75+ providers, same flexibility CLI providers (custom agents) ACP providers (Agent Client Protocol) More formalized, better integration MCP servers MCP Layer 1 (JSON-RPC) Same protocol, same servers work Goose config HONE.md + config.toml Config is TOML, conventions are HONE.md

docs.title: Goose Workflow
docs.text:
# Create a recipe with custom tool
cat > recipes/analyze.yaml << 'EOF'
name: code-analysis
steps:
  - provider: gpt-4
  - extension: my-custom-linter  # custom Python extension
    input: "Analyze src/main.rs"
  - mcp: github
    call: create_issue
    with:
      title: "Linting issues found"
      body: "{output}"
EOF

goose --recipe recipes/analyze.yaml

docs.title: Hone Workflow
docs.text:
# Same recipe, simpler tooling
cat > recipes/analyze.yaml << 'EOF'
name: code-analysis
steps:
  - tool: file_search
    pattern: "src/**"
  - agent:
      prompt: "Analyze code for issues"
      model: openai:gpt-4
  - tool: github_create_issue
    title: "Linting issues found"
    body: "{output}"
EOF

hone --recipe recipes/analyze.yaml

Key difference: Hone splits tools into layers: - Layer 2 (native) — file_search, shell, git, LSP (fast, no IPC) - Layer 1 (MCP) — github, jira, slack, databases (flexible, pluggable)

docs.title: 1. Kernel Sandboxing
docs.text:
Goose relies on process isolation. Hone adds kernel-level containment:

# See what Hone's sandbox allows
hone --show-sandbox-policy

# Example output:
# Sandbox: Seatbelt (macOS)
#   Allow read: /Users/you/project (allow-list)
#   Allow execute: /usr/bin/python3, /usr/local/bin/cargo
#   Deny network: (except whitelisted: api.openai.com, github.com)
#   Deny environment: (except whitelisted: PATH, PYTHONPATH)

Tool calls are confined at kernel level. No privilege escalation possible.

docs.title: 2. Native Layer (Zero-Cost Tools)
docs.text:
Goose routes everything through MCP (or extensions). Hone has a native layer for speed:

Goose approach: 

# Every file read goes through extension IPC
extension: file_reader
  call: read_file
  with: path="main.rs"
# Latency: 10-100ms (IPC overhead)

Hone approach: 

# Direct Rust function call, <1ms latency
hone -i "Read main.rs"
# Agent calls: read_file(path="main.rs")
# Latency: <1ms (no IPC)

# For MCP tools (if needed):
hone -i "Open a GitHub issue"
# Agent calls: github_create_issue(...)
# Latency: 10-100ms (JSON-RPC)

Layer 2 (native) is ~100x faster than Layer 1 (MCP). You get both.

docs.title: 3. Semantic Indexing
docs.text:
Goose has basic repo context. Hone has adaptive semantic indexing:

hone -i "Find functions that handle authentication"
# Hone searches by meaning (not keywords)
# Result: Returns auth() in auth.rs, verify_token() in middleware.rs, etc.

Powered by: - Tree-sitter AST parsing (language-aware) - SQLite vector embeddings (semantic search) - Persistent index (cached, reused across sessions)

docs.title: 4. LSP Integration
docs.text:
Goose has no built-in LSP. Hone bridges to language servers:

hone -i "What's the type of this variable?"
# Agent calls: lsp_hover(file="main.rs", line=10, col=5)
# Returns: type information from language server

hone -i "Show me all errors in this file"
# Agent calls: lsp_diagnostics(file="main.rs")

Supports Python, Rust, TypeScript, Go, Java, etc.

docs.title: 5. Remote Access & Team Governance
docs.text:
Goose is single-user. Hone can be multi-user:

# Start daemon on a shared machine
honed --port 7070

# From your laptop
hone --remote myserver:7070

# In HONE.md or config, define roles
[team.roles]
alice = "admin"      # manage settings, users
bob = "operator"     # run sessions, read code
charlie = "viewer"   # read-only access

Audit logging tracks who did what: 

honed --audit-log /var/log/hone/audit.log
# Logs: user, session_id, timestamp, tools_called, files_accessed

docs.title: 1. Extensions vs. Layers
docs.text:
Goose: All custom code is an "extension" (plugin).

Hone: Layers formalize tool categories: - Layer 2 — Native tools (implement in Rust, add to hone-tools crate) - Layer 1 — MCP servers (implement in any language, subprocess) - Layer 0 — Code Mode (agent generates TypeScript/Python, sandboxed execution) - Layer 3 — Skills (markdown conventions, zero cost)

For most use cases, use Layer 1 (MCP). It's the same as Goose extensions.

docs.title: 2. Recipes Are Identical (Mostly)
docs.text:
Goose recipes work in Hone with minimal changes:

Goose recipe: 

name: lint-project
steps:
  - provider: anthropic:claude-opus
  - extension: eslint
    call: lint_files
    with:
      path: "src/"
  - extension: github_client
    call: comment_on_pr
    with:
      issue: "{pr_number}"
      body: "Linting issues: {output}"

Hone recipe: 

name: lint-project
steps:
  - tool: file_search
    pattern: "src/**/*.js"
  - agent:
      prompt: "Lint these files using eslint"
      model: anthropic:claude-opus-4-5
  - tool: github_create_comment
    issue: "{pr_number}"
    body: "Linting issues: {output}"

The structure is the same; tool names may differ (Layer 1 MCP tools have different naming).

docs.title: 3. ACP (Formalized Custom Agents)
docs.text:
Goose has CLI providers (spawn a subprocess). Hone formalizes this as ACP:

Goose CLI provider: 

goose --provider cli:/path/to/my-agent --model custom

Hone ACP provider: 

# config.toml
[providers.acp]
server_path = "/path/to/my-agent"
server_args = ["--port", "9000"]

# CLI
hone --model acp:my-custom-agent

ACP is the Agent Client Protocol (same idea, standardized).

docs.title: 4. Config Format
docs.text:
Goose: YAML or JSON config files

Hone: TOML config + HONE.md conventions

# ~/.config/hone/config.toml
[agent]
default_model = "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5"
max_iterations = 20

[memory]
enabled = true

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}"

[[mcp_servers]]
name = "github"
command = "npx"
args = ["@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"]

# HONE.md (in your project)
## Skill: Testing

Always run pytest after making changes.

## Skill: Code Review

Check for unwrap() calls without justification.

docs.title: 1. Install Hone
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/anthropics/hone.git
cd hone
cargo build --release
sudo cp target/release/hone /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: 2. Copy Your Goose Config to Hone Config
docs.text:
Goose config location: .goose/config.yaml or ~/.goose/config.json

Hone config location: ~/.config/hone/config.toml

Example migration (Goose YAML → Hone TOML):

Goose: 

providers:
  default: anthropic
  anthropic:
    api_key: sk-ant-...
    model: claude-opus-4-5
mcp_servers:
  - name: github
    command: npx
    args:
      - "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"
    env:
      GITHUB_TOKEN: ghp_...

Hone: 

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "sk-ant-..."

[agent]
default_model = "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5"

[[mcp_servers]]
name = "github"
command = "npx"
args = ["@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"]
env = { GITHUB_TOKEN = "ghp_..." }

docs.title: 3. Migrate Your Recipes
docs.text:
Copy Goose recipes to Hone:

cp .goose/recipes/* ~/.config/hone/recipes/

Update tool names if needed: - Goose extensions → Hone MCP tools (names may differ) - Goose providers → Hone providers (same names)

docs.title: 4. Create HONE.md for Project Conventions
docs.text:
If you had Goose system prompts or guidelines:

# Project Skills

## Skill: Testing

Always run pytest after changes. Example:
  pytest -v tests/

## Skill: Commit Messages

Use conventional commits:
  fix: resolve race condition in cache
  feat: add async batch processing

docs.title: 5. Migrate Custom Extensions (Optional)
docs.text:
If you built Goose extensions in Python or Node:

Option A: Use MCP (recommended) - Wrap your extension as an MCP server (same as Goose) - Register in config.toml (same format as Goose)

Option B: Contribute to Hone (advanced) - Implement in Rust as a Layer 2 native tool - Add to hone-tools crate - Submit a PR (see Contributing guide)

docs.title: 6. Test Your First Session
docs.text:
cd /your/goose/project
hone

Hone should work with your recipes and MCP servers immediately.

docs.title: Can I use my Goose recipes in Hone?
docs.text: Yes, mostly. Recipe syntax is similar. Tool names may differ (check Layer 1 MCP tool names). Copy recipes over and test.

docs.title: Do my Goose MCP servers work in Hone?
docs.text: Yes, 100%. Hone is MCP-compatible. Register them in config.toml exactly as you did in Goose.

docs.title: What about my Goose extensions?
docs.text: If they're MCP servers, they work as-is. If they're language-specific plugins, you can either: 1. Wrap them as MCP servers 2. Contribute them to Hone as Layer 2 tools (Rust)

docs.title: Can I run both Goose and Hone?
docs.text: Yes. They're independent. Keep Goose until you're fully comfortable with Hone.

docs.title: How do I debug MCP servers in Hone?
docs.text:
Same as Goose. Enable logging in config:

[logging]
level = "debug"
mcp_trace_file = "/tmp/hone-mcp.log"

docs.title: Is Hone backward-compatible with Goose recipes?
docs.text: Mostly. Recipe syntax is similar; tool names may differ. Test your recipes and adjust as needed.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Install: Follow step 1 above
  2. Config: Migrate your Goose config to HONE.toml
  3. Recipes: Copy your recipes and test
  4. Test: Run hone --recipe your-recipe.yaml
  5. Extend: Read Tools and MCP for advanced integrations
  6. Team: Read Server and Remote for remote daemon setup

Questions about Goose → Hone migration? Open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Migrating from OpenCode to Hone
docs.text: You know OpenCode. You're comfortable with 75+ providers, LSP integration, client-server architecture, and web UI. Here's how Hone relates—and what's different.

docs.title: Concept Mapping
docs.text: OpenCode Hone Equivalent Notes 75+ provider support 75+ providers (same breadth) Full compatibility OpenCode LSP bridge LSP bridges (same approach) Embedded in Hone OpenCode web UI hone TUI + honed daemon TUI instead of web (faster) OpenCode client-server hone CLI + honed daemon HTTP/2 + SSE instead of WebSocket OpenCode cost tracking Real-time cost tracking Per-turn granularity Custom integrations MCP + ACP + Layer 2 tools More modular OpenCode recipes YAML recipes (same format) 100% compatible

docs.title: OpenCode Workflow
docs.text:
# Start web UI
opencode serve --port 3000
# Open http://localhost:3000

# In UI:
# 1. Select provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.)
# 2. Select model
# 3. Type prompt
# 4. View LSP diagnostics on the side
# 5. Agent makes changes
# 6. Review in web diff viewer

docs.title: Hone Workflow
docs.text:
# Start daemon
honed --port 7070

# Option 1: TUI (faster, no web browser needed)
hone --remote localhost:7070

# Option 2: Web UI (planned, not yet)
# hone serve --port 3000

# In TUI:
# 1. Select provider and model (or use default)
# 2. Type prompt
# 3. View LSP diagnostics (integrated)
# 4. Agent makes changes
# 5. Review diffs (git-native, not custom viewer)

Key difference: Hone uses TUI + daemon (faster) instead of web UI (more familiar).

docs.title: 1. Kernel Sandboxing
docs.text:
OpenCode has process isolation. Hone adds kernel-level confinement:

OpenCode: 

Process isolation: Parent container, restricted subprocess
Risk: Determined attacker could escape via kernel bugs

Hone: 

Kernel sandboxing: OS-native restrictions (Seatbelt/Landlock)
Risk: Attacker must exploit kernel itself (much harder)

Example: Agent tries to read /etc/passwd
  1. Hone syscall intercept (kernel level)
  2. Policy check: deny_read = ["/etc/*"]
  3. Error returned to process: Permission denied

On macOS, Hone uses the same sandbox API as Safari.

docs.title: 2. Adaptive Memory
docs.text:
OpenCode has basic session memory. Hone learns patterns:

OpenCode: 

# Session history stored in JSON
# No cross-session learning

Hone: 

# Encrypted SQLite with pattern learning
# Hone remembers:
#   - Which tools succeed most often
#   - Which models work best for each task type
#   - Common workflows and their steps
#   - Frequently-used file patterns

Example: 

You: (first session) Run the tests
Hone: [runs pytest]

You: (second session) Fix the failing test
Hone: Based on your pattern, should I run pytest after fixing?

docs.title: 3. Recipes with Conditional Logic
docs.text:
OpenCode recipes are linear. Hone recipes support branching:

OpenCode recipe: 

steps:
  - find_files: "tests/**/*.py"
  - agent: "Run pytest and fix failures"
  - commit: "fix: test failures"

Hone recipe: 

steps:
  - tool: file_search
    pattern: "tests/**/*.py"

  - agent:
      prompt: "Run pytest"
      model: openai:gpt-4o

  - condition: "if test_results.failed > 0"
    steps:
      - agent:
          prompt: "Fix failing tests"
          model: openai:gpt-4o

      - tool: shell
        cmd: "pytest -v"

  - condition: "if all tests pass"
    steps:
      - tool: git_commit
        message: "fix: test failures"
      - tool: slack_send
        message: "Tests passing. Ready to merge."

Conditional logic enables smarter automation.

docs.title: 4. Better LSP Integration
docs.text:
OpenCode embeds LSP bridges. Hone standardizes and extends them:

Both support: - Hover information (types, docs) - Diagnostics (errors, warnings) - Code actions (quick fixes)

Hone adds: - Workspace symbols (search code by meaning) - Semantic indexing (cross-file understanding) - Cost accounting for LSP calls

hone -i "What's the return type of authenticate()?"
# Agent calls: lsp_hover(file="auth.rs", line=42, col=10)
# Hone tracks: 1 LSP call (no cost, local)

hone -i "Find all calls to the deprecated API"
# Agent calls: semantic_search(query="deprecated API")
# Hone returns: 12 matching locations

docs.title: 5. Team Governance (RBAC)
docs.text:
OpenCode has basic permissions. Hone has fine-grained RBAC:

OpenCode: 

# Basic: authenticated or not
# Limited team features

Hone: 

# Roles: admin, operator, viewer
# Per-user budgets
# Audit logging (who did what, when)
# Cost tracking per user/team

[team.users]
alice = { role = "admin", budget = "unlimited" }
bob = { role = "operator", budget = "$500/month" }
charlie = { role = "viewer" }

Audit log: 

2026-04-05 12:34:56 [user=alice] Tool: edit_file, path=/src/main.rs
2026-04-05 12:34:57 [user=alice] Tool: shell, cmd=cargo test
2026-04-05 12:34:58 [user=bob] Tool: read_file, path=/src/main.rs

docs.title: 6. ACP Protocol (Standardized Custom Agents)
docs.text:
OpenCode has custom integrations. Hone standardizes via ACP:

ACP (Agent Client Protocol): - Persistent bidirectional connection - Full tool support (not limited to JSON-RPC) - Better for complex integrations

# config.toml
[providers.acp]
server_path = "/path/to/my-custom-agent"
server_args = ["--port", "9000"]

# CLI
hone --model acp:my-service

Your custom agent can implement complex logic, not limited to tool schemas.

docs.title: 1. TUI Instead of Web UI
docs.text:
OpenCode: Web UI in browser (familiar, but slower, requires port forwarding)

Hone: TUI in terminal (faster, lower latency, easier SSH access)

In comparison: - Web UI: Better for non-technical users, remote collaboration - TUI: Better for developers, lower latency, no browser overhead

Web UI is planned for Hone (not yet implemented).

docs.title: 2. Daemon Architecture
docs.text:
Both OpenCode and Hone have client-server. But different protocols:

OpenCode: WebSocket (stateless, polling)

Hone: HTTP/2 + SSE (stateful, push-based)

Benefits of Hone's approach: - Lower latency (push vs. poll) - Less network traffic - Better streaming (SSE) - Easier debugging (HTTP inspector)

docs.title: 3. TOML Config Instead of JSON
docs.text:
OpenCode: JSON config (UI-editable)

{
  "providers": {
    "default": "anthropic",
    "anthropic": { "api_key": "sk-ant-..." }
  },
  "lsp": { "enabled": true }
}

Hone: TOML config (human-editable)

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "sk-ant-..."

[agent]
default_model = "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5"

[lsp]
enabled = true

TOML is easier to edit manually and supports comments.

docs.title: 4. Git-Native Diff Review
docs.text:
OpenCode: Custom diff viewer in web UI

Hone: Git diff (standard tool)

# In Hone session
git diff          # See changes
git diff --cached # See staged changes
git status        # See file status

Why? Standard git tools are more powerful and integrate with your existing workflow.

docs.title: 1. Install Hone
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/anthropics/hone.git
cd hone
cargo build --release
sudo cp target/release/hone /usr/local/bin/
sudo cp target/release/honed /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: 2. Migrate Your OpenCode Config
docs.text:
OpenCode location: ~/.opencode/config.json or environment variables

Hone location: ~/.config/hone/config.toml

Example migration:

OpenCode: 

{
  "providers": {
    "default": "anthropic",
    "anthropic": {
      "api_key": "sk-ant-...",
      "model": "claude-opus-4-5"
    }
  },
  "lsp": { "enabled": true },
  "cost_tracking": { "enabled": true }
}

Hone: 

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "sk-ant-..."

[agent]
default_model = "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5"

[lsp]
enabled = true

[pricing.anthropic]
"claude-opus-4-5" = { input_per_mtok = 3.00, output_per_mtok = 15.00 }

docs.title: 3. Start the Daemon
docs.text:
# If running locally
honed --port 7070

# In another terminal
hone --remote localhost:7070

# Or remotely on a server
ssh myserver
honed --config ~/.config/hone/config.toml

# From your laptop
hone --remote myserver:7070

docs.title: 4. Test Your First Session
docs.text:
cd /your/opencode/project
hone --remote localhost:7070

Try a familiar task: 

Refactor the authentication module

Hone will: 1. Find related files via semantic search 2. Read them 3. Make changes 4. Show diffs 5. Commit (if you approve)

docs.title: 5. Create HONE.md (Project Conventions)
docs.text:
If you had OpenCode system prompts or guidelines:

# Project Skills

## Skill: Code Review

Before committing:
1. Run tests with pytest
2. Check for error handling
3. Review with `git diff`

## Skill: Refactoring

When refactoring:
1. Write tests first (if not present)
2. Make changes incrementally
3. Run tests after each change
4. Commit per logical unit

docs.title: 6. Migrate Your Recipes (If Any)
docs.text:
If you had OpenCode recipes, copy them over:

cp ~/.opencode/recipes/* ~/.config/hone/recipes/

Hone recipes are YAML (same format as OpenCode). Update tool names if needed.

docs.title: Can I still use the web UI?
docs.text: Not yet. Hone currently has a TUI. Web UI is planned.

docs.title: Do my OpenCode recipes work in Hone?
docs.text: Mostly. Recipe syntax is similar. Tool names may differ. Copy recipes and test.

docs.title: How do I set per-user budgets like OpenCode?
docs.text:
In config.toml:

[team.users]
alice = { budget = "unlimited" }
bob = { budget = "$500/month" }

Or enforce at daemon level:

honed --user-budget 500 --budget-period month

docs.title: Is Hone faster than OpenCode?
docs.text: For local use: yes (TUI is faster than web). For remote: similar (both use daemon).

docs.title: Can I use both OpenCode and Hone?
docs.text: Yes. They run independently. Keep both until you're comfortable with Hone.

docs.title: How do I export sessions like OpenCode?
docs.text:
In session: 

/export session.json

Sessions are also stored in memory database: 

~/.local/share/hone/memory.db

docs.title: What about the web UI? I prefer it.
docs.text:
Web UI is on the roadmap. For now, TUI is the primary interface. SSH tunneling works well for remote use:

ssh -L 7070:localhost:7070 myserver
hone --remote localhost:7070

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Install: Follow step 1 above
  2. Config: Migrate your OpenCode config to TOML
  3. Daemon: Run honed locally and connect via hone --remote
  4. Test: Try a familiar task
  5. Recipes: Read Recipes Guide for automation
  6. Team: Read Server and Remote for multi-user setup

Migrating from OpenCode? Questions? Open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: New User Walkthrough: AI Coding Agents Explained
docs.text: Welcome. If you've never used an AI coding agent before, this guide will walk you through the fundamentals, step by step. No assumptions about prior knowledge.

docs.title: What is an AI Coding Agent?
docs.text:
An AI coding agent is a conversational AI (like ChatGPT) that can read and modify your code. Instead of you copy-pasting code into a chat window and manually applying suggestions, the agent:

  1. Understands what you're asking (natural language)
  2. Reads relevant files from your project
  3. Writes or modifies code autonomously
  4. Runs tests to verify changes
  5. Commits changes to git

Example: 

You: Fix the null pointer exception in main.rs
Agent: [reads main.rs, identifies the bug, suggests a fix, shows you a diff, waits for approval]
You: Looks good, apply it
Agent: [applies the fix, runs tests to verify, commits to git]

Think of it as a very capable pair programmer who understands your codebase and can execute changes safely.

docs.title: Installing Hone
docs.text: Hone is built in Rust and runs entirely on your machine. Here's how to install it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You need: - Rust 1.85+ — the language Hone is written in - Git — for version control - A command-line terminal — bash, zsh, or similar

docs.title: Check What You Have
docs.text:
# Check Rust version
rustc --version
# Expected: rustc 1.85.0 or higher

# Check Cargo (comes with Rust)
cargo --version

# Check Git
git --version

If any are missing, install Rust from https://rustup.rs (it installs everything together).

docs.title: Build Hone
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/anthropics/hone.git
cd hone

# Build Hone (this takes ~3-5 minutes)
cargo build --release

# Install the binaries
sudo cp target/release/hone /usr/local/bin/
sudo cp target/release/honed /usr/local/bin/

# Verify installation
hone --version

That's it. Hone is a single, self-contained binary. No dependencies to manage.

docs.title: Your First Real-World Session
docs.text: Let's say you're working on a Python project and you have a failing test. Here's what happens step by step.

docs.title: Step 1: Start Hone
docs.text:
cd /path/to/your/python/project
hone

You'll see the TUI (terminal UI) load. Hone asks you to choose a model provider.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose a Provider
docs.text:
A provider is where the AI comes from. Hone supports many:

Select a provider:
1. Anthropic Claude (requires API key)
2. OpenAI GPT (requires API key)
3. Ollama (local, free, no API key)
4. Claude CLI (if you already have it installed)
... (70+ other options)

Choice:

For your first time: - If you have an OpenAI account, use OpenAI (GPT-4o) - If you have an Anthropic account, use Anthropic (Claude) - If you want free/private, use Ollama (see setup below)

docs.title: Setting Up Ollama (Free Option)
docs.text:
If you choose Ollama (local, free, private):

# Install Ollama from https://ollama.ai
# Then in a separate terminal:
ollama serve

# In your Hone session:
hone --model ollama:llama2

Ollama runs models on your machine. No internet, no API key, no cost. Trade-off: slower than cloud models (depends on your hardware).

docs.title: Step 3: In Your First Session
docs.text:
Once you've selected a model, you're in the chat loop. Type naturally:

You: There's a failing test in tests/test_auth.py. Fix it.

Hone: I'll help you fix the failing test. Let me start by reading the test file.

[Tool: read_file]
Input: tests/test_auth.py
Output: (file contents shown)

Now let me read the implementation to understand what needs fixing.

[Tool: read_file]
Input: src/auth.py
Output: (file contents shown)

I see the issue. The `authenticate()` function doesn't handle the case where the password is empty. Here's the fix:

[Tool: edit_file]
Input: src/auth.py, line 15-20
Old:
  def authenticate(username, password):
    user = db.find(username)
    return user.check_password(password)

New:
  def authenticate(username, password):
    if not password:
      raise ValueError("Password cannot be empty")
    user = db.find(username)
    return user.check_password(password)

[Show diff? (y/n)] y

At this point, you see a diff. Review it and type y to accept or n to reject.

docs.title: Step 4: Watch the Agent Work
docs.text:
After you approve, the agent continues:

[Tool: shell]
Input: pytest tests/test_auth.py -v
Output:
  test_auth.py::test_authenticate_valid ... PASSED
  test_auth.py::test_authenticate_invalid ... PASSED
  test_auth.py::test_authenticate_empty ... PASSED
  ===== 3 passed in 0.15s =====

Great! All tests pass. Let me commit this fix.

[Tool: git_commit]
Input: message="fix: handle empty password in authenticate()"
Output: [main a1b2c3d] fix: handle empty password in authenticate()
  1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)

Done. The agent: 1. Read the failing test 2. Read the implementation 3. Identified the bug 4. Showed you a diff 5. Got your approval 6. Ran tests to verify 7. Committed the change

Your role: Review and approve important changes. You're always in control.

docs.title: Token Streaming
docs.text:
You'll notice text appearing word-by-word:

Hone: I'm analyzing... your request... and will...

That's "token streaming." The AI generates text one word at a time, and Hone displays each word as it arrives. This makes it feel faster because you see progress immediately, rather than waiting for a full response.

docs.title: Tool Calls
docs.text:
Tool calls are actions the agent takes:

[Tool: read_file] src/main.py
[Tool: shell] cargo test
[Tool: git_commit] message="..."

Each tool call is visible, logged, and auditable. You see exactly what the agent is doing.

Built-in tools: - read_file — read a file from disk - write_file — create a new file - edit_file — modify a file (precise edits, not full rewrites) - shell — run a command (bash, python, cargo, etc.) - git_commit — create a commit - git_diff — show changes - git_checkout — switch branches - glob — search for files by pattern (e.g., *.py) - lsp_hover — get type information (language-aware)

docs.title: Cost Tracking
docs.text:
Each turn shows how much you're spending (if using a paid API):

Usage: 4521 input tokens, 312 output tokens
Cost: $0.019 USD (using openai:gpt-4o)
Session total: $0.24 USD
Budget remaining: $9.76 / $10.00

Tokens are the unit of text the AI processes. You're billed per token. Hone tracks this transparently.

If using Ollama (local): Cost is $0.00 (completely free).

docs.title: 1. Models
docs.text:
A "model" is the AI engine. Different models have different strengths:

Model Cost Speed Reasoning Best For Claude Opus (Anthropic) High Slow (20-30s) Excellent Complex tasks, design GPT-4o (OpenAI) Medium Medium (10-20s) Very good Balanced tasks Claude Haiku (Anthropic) Low Very fast (2-5s) Good Simple tasks, fast feedback Llama 2 (Ollama) Free Very slow (depends on hardware) Fair Testing, no cost

You can switch models mid-session with /model:

/model openai:gpt-4o  (switch to GPT-4o)
/model anthropic:claude-haiku  (switch to faster, cheaper Haiku)

Tip: Use fast/cheap models for simple tasks, powerful models for complex reasoning.

docs.title: 2. Tools
docs.text:
Tools are actions the agent can take. Layer 2 (native) tools are built-in and very fast:

  • File I/O — read, write, edit (< 1ms latency)
  • Shell — run commands (speed depends on command)
  • Git — commit, branch, diff (very fast)
  • LSP — language server (type info, diagnostics)

Layer 1 (MCP) tools extend Hone: - GitHub — create issues, manage PRs - Slack — send messages - Databases — query and insert - Custom tools (you can build them)

The agent chooses which tools to use based on your request.

docs.title: 3. Sandbox (Why It's Safe)
docs.text:
Hone runs code in a sandbox. If the agent tries to do something unsafe (delete system files, access the network without permission, etc.), the sandbox stops it:

# Show the sandbox policy
hone --show-sandbox-policy

# Output:
# Sandbox: Seatbelt (macOS)
#   Allow: Read files in /Users/you/project
#   Allow: Execute /bin/bash, /usr/bin/python3
#   Deny: Read /etc/passwd
#   Deny: Access the network (except api.openai.com, github.com)
#   Deny: Access /private/var, /tmp (except /tmp/.hone-*)

The sandbox uses your operating system's native security (Seatbelt on macOS, Landlock on Linux). It's the same technology Safari uses.

In practice: The agent can't do anything destructive. It can only modify code in your project, run tests, and commit to git.

docs.title: 4. Memory
docs.text:
Hone remembers your patterns:

First session: 

You: Run the tests
Agent: [runs pytest]

You: Commit this fix
Agent: [commits]

Second session: 

You: Fix this bug
Agent: (learns you typically run pytest after fixing, suggests it)
Agent: Should I run pytest to verify?

Memory is encrypted and stored locally on your machine. Hone never uploads your code to the cloud.

docs.title: Using Built-in Agents and Recipes
docs.text: Now that you understand the fundamentals, let's explore Hone's most powerful feature: built-in agents and recipes. These let you delegate specialized tasks to expert personas.

docs.title: What's an Agent?
docs.text:
An agent is a specialized AI persona. Instead of saying "fix this code," you can say "I want the security auditor to review this code." Each agent has:

  • A name (e.g., code-reviewer, debugger)
  • Specialized tools (file readers, shell, git, etc.)
  • Expert knowledge (system prompt encoded with best practices)
  • A preferred model (usually Sonnet for balanced speed/cost)

docs.title: Built-in Agents
docs.text:
Hone ships with 9 pre-trained agents:

Agent Use When code-reviewer You want a security/quality review debugger You're stuck on a bug security-auditor You need vulnerability scanning rust-expert You're writing Rust python-expert You're writing Python tdd-workflow You want to implement with TDD api-designer You're designing an API performance-optimizer You need to optimize code documentation-agent You need to write docs

docs.title: Using an Agent
docs.text:
# Use a specific agent
hone --agent code-reviewer -i "Review this code for security issues"

# Find an agent by keyword
hone --agent "test-driven" -i "Implement a new feature"
# This finds "tdd-workflow" automatically

# Use an agent in a recipe (we'll cover recipes next)
hone --recipe tdd-feature --agent rust-expert

During the session, you can also switch agents:

/agent debugger

docs.title: What's a Recipe?
docs.text:
A recipe is a structured workflow. Instead of manually running steps one by one, a recipe defines:

  1. What to do in each step
  2. The order to do them
  3. Whether to run tests at the end

Hone ships with 4 built-in recipes:

Recipe What It Does tdd-feature Implement a feature with Red-Green-Refactor bug-fix Fix a bug with a regression test code-review Comprehensive code review (5 steps) refactor Safely refactor with test verification

docs.title: Running a Recipe
docs.text:
# Run a built-in recipe
hone --recipe tdd-feature
hone --recipe bug-fix

Here's what a TDD feature run looks like:

Recipe: tdd-feature
Step 1/5: Understand
  Prompt: Read the relevant code and understand the current architecture...
  Agent: [reads files, summarizes the codebase]
  Continue? (y/n) y

Step 2/5: Red
  Prompt: Write failing tests that describe the desired behavior...
  Agent: [writes tests, runs them to confirm failure]
  Continue? (y/n) y

Step 3/5: Green
  Prompt: Write the minimum code to make tests pass...
  Agent: [writes implementation]
  Continue? (y/n) y

Step 4/5: Refactor
  Prompt: Refactor for clarity and quality...
  Agent: [improves code]
  Continue? (y/n) y

Step 5/5: Verify
  Prompt: Run all tests...
  Agent: [runs full test suite, reports success]

Test command: cargo test
Result: PASSED (all 12 tests)

Recipe completed successfully.

docs.title: Combining Agents and Recipes
docs.text:
You can use an agent with a recipe. For example, TDD in Rust:

hone --recipe tdd-feature --agent rust-expert

The rust-expert agent will apply Rust best practices (Arc, ownership, etc.) while following the TDD workflow.

docs.title: Creating a Custom Agent
docs.text:
If you find yourself doing the same type of work repeatedly, create a custom agent.

Create .hone/agents/my-agent.md:

---
name: my-agent
description: My custom agent for X
tools: [read, write, shell, grep, glob]
model: sonnet
---

You are a specialized agent for [your domain].

## Process

1. Understand the task
2. Take action
3. Verify results

[Your system prompt...]

Then use it:

hone --agent my-agent -i "Your task"

See Tools and MCP Guide for detailed examples.

docs.title: Bug Fixing with the Debugger
docs.text:
hone --agent debugger -i "The login form throws 'TypeError: cannot read password'. Fix it."

The debugger agent uses a systematic approach: 1. Reproduce the bug 2. Form hypotheses 3. Test hypotheses 4. Write the minimal fix 5. Verify with a regression test

You review and approve the fix.

docs.title: Code Review with Security Focus
docs.text:
hone --agent security-auditor -i "Review this code for vulnerabilities"

The security auditor scans for: - SQL injection, XSS, command injection - Hardcoded secrets - Authentication/authorization flaws - Cryptography issues - Known CVEs in dependencies

docs.title: Implement a Feature with TDD
docs.text:
hone --recipe tdd-feature --agent rust-expert

This combines the TDD workflow with Rust expertise. The agent: 1. Understands the architecture 2. Writes failing tests 3. Implements the minimum code to pass 4. Refactors for clarity 5. Verifies all tests still pass

docs.title: Refactor Code Safely
docs.text:
hone --recipe refactor

The refactor recipe enforces test verification at each step: 1. Establish a green baseline 2. Plan the refactoring 3. Execute changes one at a time 4. Run tests after each change 5. Report before/after metrics

You approve each step incrementally.

docs.title: Code Review (General)
docs.text:
hone --agent code-reviewer -i "Review this PR"

The code reviewer performs a systematic review: 1. Understand the scope 2. Check for correctness 3. Check for security issues 4. Check for performance issues 5. Report findings in a table

docs.title: Add Documentation
docs.text:
hone --agent documentation-agent -i "Generate API documentation"

The documentation agent can: - Generate API docs from code - Create architecture diagrams (Mermaid) - Write READMEs - Generate changelogs from git history

docs.title: 1. Be Specific About Paths
docs.text:
Bad: 

Fix the bug in the main file.

Good: 

Fix the null pointer exception in src/main.rs, around line 42.

Hone can search, but it's faster if you point it to the right file.

docs.title: 2. Describe the "Why" Not Just "What"
docs.text:
Bad: 

Add logging.

Good: 

Add structured logging to database query functions so we can debug slow queries.

With context about the why, the agent makes better decisions.

docs.title: 3. Use /model for Different Tasks
docs.text:
For complex reasoning (designing architecture, planning): 

/model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5
Design a caching layer for the API.

For simple, quick tasks: 

/model anthropic:claude-haiku
Add a comment to line 10 of main.rs.

This saves money and speeds up simple tasks.

docs.title: 4. Use /budget to Avoid Surprises
docs.text:
If you're trying a new model or expensive operation:

/budget 1.00  (stop after spending $1.00)

When you hit the budget, the session stops.

docs.title: 5. Request Incremental Changes
docs.text:
Bad: 

Refactor the entire database module.

Good: 

Refactor the database module incrementally. First, move the User model to a separate file. Then we'll handle relations.

Incremental changes are easier to review and revert if needed.

docs.title: 6. Use Slash Commands
docs.text:
Type /help anytime to see available commands:

/model <provider:model>   — switch models
/budget <usd>             — set spending limit
/compact                  — reduce output verbosity
/clear                    — clear conversation history
/export <path>            — save session to JSON
/context show             — show what files are loaded
/context add <path>       — add a file to context
/context drop <path>      — remove a file from context
/undo                     — undo last agent turn
/redo                     — redo last undo

docs.title: 1. Try Your First Session
docs.text:
Pick a real project. Start small: 

cd /your/project
hone

Ask it to fix a simple bug or add a small feature. See how it works.

docs.title: 2. Read the Tutorials
docs.text: Now that you understand the fundamentals: - Getting Started — More detailed setup guide - Model Providers — Deep dive into provider selection and cost - Tools and MCP — How tools work, agents, how to extend them - Recipes Guide — Full recipe syntax and writing custom recipes

docs.title: 3. Set Up a Configuration
docs.text:
Create ~/.config/hone/config.toml to customize defaults:

[agent]
default_model = "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5"
context_window_tokens = 16000
max_spend_usd = 10.00

[memory]
enabled = true

See Configuration for all options.

docs.title: 4. Create Project Conventions (HONE.md)
docs.text:
In your project root, create HONE.md:

# Project Skills

## Skill: Testing

Always run pytest after making changes:
  pytest -v tests/

## Skill: Commit Messages

Use conventional commits:
  fix: resolve race condition
  feat: add user authentication
  docs: update README

The agent learns these conventions (zero token cost).

docs.title: 5. Explore Recipes
docs.text:
When you find yourself doing the same workflow repeatedly, automate it with a recipe.

See Recipes Guide.

docs.title: 6. Join the Community
docs.text:
• Report bugs or ask questions on GitHub
  • Read the Architecture guide for deep dives
  • Check out Contributing if you want to extend Hone

docs.title: "API key not found"
docs.text:
Set your API key as an environment variable:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
# or
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

hone

Or add it to config:

# ~/.config/hone/config.toml
[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "sk-ant-..."

docs.title: "Model not supported"
docs.text:
List available models:

hone --list-models

Use one from the list.

docs.title: "Network error"
docs.text:
Check your internet connection and firewall. If behind a corporate proxy, configure it:

[http]
proxy = "http://proxy.company.com:8080"

docs.title: "Sandbox error"
docs.text: If you see a sandbox error, Hone is being extra safe. Check System Preferences > Security & Privacy on macOS. For Linux, ensure Landlock is available (kernel 5.13+).

docs.title: "Out of memory"
docs.text:
Your conversation got too long. Clear it:

/clear

Or reduce context size:

[agent]
context_window_tokens = 8000

docs.title: You're Ready
docs.text:
That's the fundamentals. You now understand: - What an AI coding agent is - How to install and run Hone - What happens in a real session - Key concepts (models, tools, sandbox, memory) - How to prompt effectively

Next: Pick a real task and give it a try. Hone is safest to learn by doing.

Questions? Open an issue on GitHub or read the full Getting Started guide.

docs.title: Hone Tutorials
docs.text: Welcome to the Hone tutorial documentation. These guides will help you get started, configure providers, integrate tools, and deploy Hone securely.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Start here if you're new to Hone:

  1. Getting Started — Install, build, and run your first session (20 min)
  2. Providers — Configure model providers and switch between them (15 min)

docs.title: For Users
docs.text:
• Getting Started — Prerequisites, building from source, first interactive session, one-shot mode, understanding output (token streaming, tool calls, cost tracking)

  • Providers — Configuring Anthropic API, OpenAI (and custom endpoints like DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Qwen), Ollama (local), CLI pass-through tools, ACP, hot-swapping providers, fallback chains, model routing rules, pricing tables, cost tracking, health checks, custom timeouts

  • Tools and MCP — Layer architecture (L0–L3), native tools (file, shell, git, LSP, semantic index), MCP integration (JSON-RPC, external tools), Code Mode (agent-generated orchestration), skills (HONE.md conventions), tool registry and dispatch, writing custom tools

  • Recipes — YAML recipe system, recipe format with annotations, conditional steps, TDD hook (test_cmd), running recipes interactively or in batch mode, recipe output and export, writing and sharing recipes

docs.title: For Operators
docs.text:
• Server and Remote — Starting the daemon (honed), REST API overview (sessions, turns, SSE events), real-time streaming with Server-Sent Events, tunnel support (Cloudflare, Ngrok), authentication (bearer tokens), collaborative sessions, health checks, running multiple daemons, systemd integration

  • Security — Hardened sandbox architecture (Seatbelt on macOS, Landlock on Linux, seccomp on containers), path traversal prevention, shell command classification, SandboxPolicy (file/network restrictions), network deny-by-default, RBAC roles and policies, audit logging, memory encryption (AES-256-GCM with Argon2id), ephemeral mode, threat model, best practices, troubleshooting

docs.title: Path 1: Interactive Agent (30 min)
docs.text:
1. Getting Started — Set up and run first session
  2. Providers — Switch between models

You can now use Hone interactively to ask questions, analyze code, and run shell commands.

docs.title: Path 2: Automated Workflows (45 min)
docs.text:
1. Getting Started — Set up
  2. Recipes — Define multi-step workflows
  3. Tools and MCP — Extend with custom tools

You can now automate complex tasks via YAML recipes.

docs.title: Path 3: Team Deployment (60 min)
docs.text:
1. Getting Started — Set up
  2. Server and Remote — Run the daemon
  3. Security — Configure sandboxes, RBAC, memory encryption, and audit logging
  4. Providers — Set up cost tracking, fallback chains, and custom endpoints
  5. Configuration — Fine-tune context optimization and budgets

You can now deploy Hone as a multi-user HTTP service with audit logging, access control, and encrypted memory.

docs.title: Path 4: Custom Integration (90 min)
docs.text:
1. Getting Started — Set up
  2. Tools and MCP — Integrate external tools
  3. Providers — Hot-swap providers based on task type
  4. Server and Remote — Expose via HTTP API

You can now build custom applications on top of Hone.

docs.title: Use Case: Code Review
docs.text:
Start with Getting Started, then use Recipes to automate the review process:

name: "Code Review"
steps:
  - name: "Analyze Changes"
    prompt: "Review the diff and identify issues"
  - name: "Suggest Improvements"
    prompt: "What are the top 3 improvements?"
  - name: "Generate Summary"
    prompt: "Write a review summary"
test_cmd: "cargo test"

Run it:

hone --recipe code-review.yaml

docs.title: Use Case: Semantic Code Search
docs.text:
Start with Getting Started, then use Tools and MCP to access the semantic index:

hone -i "Find functions that handle authentication"

The agent calls the semantic_search tool (Layer 2 native) to search by meaning.

docs.title: Use Case: Multi-User Team Workspace
docs.text:
Start with Server and Remote, then configure Security for RBAC:

honed --port 7777 --config /etc/hone/config.toml

Multiple users can now create sessions and collaborate via the REST API.

docs.title: Use Case: Custom Tool Integration
docs.text:
Start with Tools and MCP to write an MCP server:

# Your custom MCP server
python3 my-mcp-server.py

Then configure it in config.toml:

[[mcp_servers]]
name = "custom"
command = "python3"
args = ["my-mcp-server.py"]

The agent can now call your custom tools.

docs.title: File Structure
docs.text:
All tutorials live in this directory (docs/tutorials/):

docs/

docs.text:
• Architecture — System design, crate structure, data flows, trait definitions. Read after tutorials to understand how Hone works internally.
  • Implementation Plan — For contributors: TDD workflow, crate build sequence, test strategy, CI/CD pipeline.

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."

Or create ~/.config/hone/config.toml:

api_key = "sk-ant-..."
