docs.title: Getting Started with Hone
docs.text: This guide walks you through setting up Hone, configuring your first model provider, and running your first agent session.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Rust 1.85+: Check with rustc --version. Install from https://rustup.rs if needed.
  • Cargo: Comes with Rust. Verify with cargo --version.
  • Git: For cloning and version control features. git --version to verify.
  • System dependencies (varies by platform):
  • macOS: XCode Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install)
  • Linux: build-essential, pkg-config, libssl-dev (Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt-get install build-essential pkg-config libssl-dev)
  • Windows: Microsoft C++ Build Tools

docs.title: Building from Source
docs.text:
Clone the Hone repository and build:

git clone https://github.com/anthropics/hone.git
cd hone
cargo build --release

The binary is at target/release/hone. Add it to your PATH or use the full path:

export PATH="$PWD/target/release:$PATH"
hone --version

docs.title: First Run: Configure
docs.text:
Before starting your first session, run the interactive configuration wizard:

hone configure

This guides you step-by-step through: 1. Selecting a model provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Ollama, etc.) 2. Entering your API key (securely via stdin, not command-line args) 3. Choosing your default model from that provider 4. Writing the configuration to ~/.config/hone/config.toml

Configuration is one-time. Your provider and model are remembered for future sessions.

docs.title: Starting Your First Session
docs.text:
After configuration, start an interactive session:

hone

This launches the terminal UI. You can: - Type prompts and press Enter - Press ? at any time for help - Type Ctrl+C to quit

Your session is automatically saved with a default name. You can resume it later or create a named session:

hone --session my-project

docs.title: Choosing a Model Provider
docs.text:
The hone configure wizard guides you through provider selection. The available providers are:

Hone supports multiple model providers. Choose based on your needs:

docs.title: 1. Anthropic API (Cloud)
docs.text:
Most capable. Requires an API key.

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5

First session: Type your API key when prompted, or set the environment variable above.

Cost: $3–15 per million input tokens, $15–60 per million output tokens (claude-opus-4-5).

docs.title: 2. OpenAI API (Cloud)
docs.text:
Alternative cloud provider.

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
hone --model openai:gpt-4o

docs.title: 3. Ollama (Local)
docs.text:
Run models on your machine (no internet, free).

Install Ollama from https://ollama.ai, then:

ollama pull llama2
ollama serve  # in another terminal
hone --model ollama:llama2

Pros: Private, instant responses, free. Cons: Slower (CPU/GPU dependent), less capable than Claude/GPT-4.

docs.title: 4. Claude CLI Pass-Through (Generation 1)
docs.text:
Use your existing claude CLI. Requires Generation 1 installed.

hone --model claude-cli:claude-opus

docs.title: 5. Gemini CLI Pass-Through (Generation 1)
docs.text:
Use Google's gemini CLI.

hone --model gemini-cli:gemini-pro

docs.title: 6. ACP (Agent Client Protocol)
docs.text:
Full tool support via persistent subprocess. For advanced users integrating custom tools.

hone --model acp:my-custom-model --acp-endpoint /path/to/acp/binary

docs.title: First Interactive Session
docs.text:
Once you select a provider and model, you're in the session loop. Type prompts and press Enter:

You: What files are in this directory?
Assistant: I'll list the files for you.
[tool call: shell -> ls]
Output: main.rs  Cargo.toml  README.md
Found 3 files. You have main.rs (Rust source), Cargo.toml (manifest), and README.md.

Key features: - Streaming: Tokens appear as they arrive. - Tool calls: The agent calls native tools (file, shell, git, LSP) automatically. - Transparency: Each tool call and result is shown.

Type /help to see available commands:

/model <provider:model>   — switch models mid-session
/budget <usd>             — set spending limit
/clear                    — clear conversation history
/export <path>            — save session to JSON
/quit                     — exit

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text: Sessions are named conversations that persist across runs. Hone automatically saves your sessions after each turn.

docs.title: Resuming a Previous Session
docs.text:
# Resume a session by name
hone session resume my-project

All prior messages and context are restored. The session is updated with any new turns.

docs.title: Renaming and Deleting Sessions
docs.text:
# Rename a session
hone session rename old-name new-name

# Delete a session (irreversible)
hone session delete my-old-session

docs.title: Starting a Named Session
docs.text:
# Start a new session with a specific name (auto-created if doesn't exist)
hone --session debug-session

docs.title: Ephemeral (No-Save) Mode
docs.text:
To run without saving:

# Session won't be saved after this run
hone --ephemeral

This is useful for sensitive work, one-off queries, or testing.

docs.title: One-Shot Mode
docs.text:
Run a single command without the interactive loop:

hone "List all Python files in src/" --model anthropic:claude-opus

Output is streamed to stdout, no TUI.

docs.title: First Multi-Agent Orchestration Run
docs.text:
Hone's multi-agent orchestrator decomposes complex tasks, executes them in parallel, and merges results. This is research-backed by Anthropic, MASAI, and CodeR papers:

# Set up API key
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."

# Run with orchestrator
hone --orchestrate "Build a CLI tool that validates email addresses with comprehensive test coverage"

What happens:

  1. Decompose — Orchestrator breaks down "build CLI tool" into parallel subtasks:
  2. Write tests for email validation
  3. Implement validation logic
  4. Build CLI interface

  5. Add error handling

  6. Execute — Each worker agent runs in parallel on their assigned task: 

    [PlanCreated] Task decomposed into 4 subtasks
[WorkerStarted] Worker 1: "write_tests"
[WorkerStarted] Worker 2: "implement_logic"
[WorkerStarted] Worker 3: "build_cli"
[WorkerStarted] Worker 4: "add_errors"

  7. Merge — Orchestrator reads all results and produces a coherent merged output: 

    [Merged] All workers completed
Final output: Complete CLI tool with tests, logic, interface, and error handling

Expected output format: - Token counts for each subtask - Merged response combining all workers - Total cost across all parallel executions

When to use: - Complex features with multiple concerns - Tasks that naturally decompose (API + CLI + tests) - When you want parallel execution within a single request

docs.title: Context Window Management
docs.text:
Hone automatically optimizes context to stay within model limits while preserving code relevance:

# View context optimization details
hone --debug-context

What happens behind the scenes:

  1. Model-aware budgets — Each model has a learned token budget. claude-opus-4-5 has 200K context; hone reserves 4K for output, 2K for system prompt, leaving ~177K for conversation.

  2. Automatic reranking — When context gets large, Hone uses BM25 ranking to keep the most relevant code snippets and memories at the front of the context window.

  3. Graduated compression — Old or less relevant items are progressively summarized: full code → code + summary → summary only → compressed reference.

  4. Phase detection — Hone adapts context strategy based on conversation phase (exploration, implementation, testing, refactoring).

Example: Adding error handling to a 500-line authentication module: - Turn 1-3: Exploration phase. Context shows file structure, not full code. - Turn 4-8: Implementation phase. Context includes auth spec, test template, security patterns. - Turn 9+: Testing phase. Context focuses on test failures and relevant code.

Set a custom context limit:

hone --context-limit 32000  # tokens

docs.title: Token Streaming
docs.text:
Tokens arrive and render in real-time:

Assistant: I'm analyzing...your request. [tokens streaming]

You see partial text as computation happens, not the final response all at once.

docs.title: Tool Calls
docs.text:
When the agent needs to act, it calls a tool:

[Tool: read_file]
Input: {"path": "main.rs"}
Output: (file contents)

Tools available in Layer 2 (native, <1ms latency): - File I/O: read, write, edit, glob patterns - Shell: execute commands, capture output - Git: commit, branch, diff, undo/redo - LSP bridge: hover, diagnostics, code actions - Semantic index: search code by meaning

Tools in Layer 1 (MCP, JSON-RPC): - GitHub, Jira, Slack, databases, custom integrations

docs.title: Cost Tracking
docs.text:
After each turn, the output shows:

Usage: 4521 input tokens, 312 output tokens
Cost: $0.068 USD
Session total: $0.24 USD
Budget remaining: $9.76 / $10.00

All costs are tracked in real USD for your chosen model. Set a budget limit to avoid surprises:

hone --budget 5.00  # max $5 per session

When you hit the limit, the session stops.

docs.title: Memory and Encryption
docs.text:
For sensitive sessions, Hone can encrypt all memories and session data:

# Build with encryption support
cargo build --features encrypted-memory

# Initialize encryption (stores key in system keychain)
hone --init-encryption
# Enter passphrase: ****

# Run in ephemeral mode (no data saved)
hone --ephemeral

See Security Guide for memory encryption and ephemeral mode.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Configure providers: See Providers Guide for hot-swapping, custom endpoints (DeepSeek, OpenRouter), fallback chains, and pricing tables.
  • Context optimization: Hone automatically optimizes context using BM25 reranking and graduated compression. See Configuration for tuning.
  • Write recipes: See Recipes Guide to automate multi-step workflows.
  • Run the daemon: See Server Guide to use Hone as a persistent HTTP service with RBAC.
  • Custom tools: See Tools Guide to integrate external MCP servers and custom tools.
  • Security: See Security Guide for sandbox policies, audit logging, and memory encryption.
  • Architecture: See Architecture Guide for deep dives into context optimization, memory encryption, and security hardening.

docs.title: API Key Not Found
docs.text:
error: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY not set

Set the environment variable:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
hone

Or create ~/.config/hone/config.toml:

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "sk-ant-..."

docs.title: Model Not Found
docs.text:
error: model 'anthropic:claude-unknown' not supported

List available models:

hone --list-models

docs.title: Network Error (Firewall)
docs.text:
error: failed to connect to Anthropic API

Check your firewall and proxy settings. If behind a corporate proxy:

[http]
proxy = "http://proxy.example.com:8080"

docs.title: Sandbox Error on macOS
docs.text:
error: sandbox policy not supported (Seatbelt unavailable)

This is rare. It means the sandbox layer failed. Hone uses fail-closed policy and aborts rather than running unsandboxed. Check System Preferences > Security & Privacy.

docs.title: Out of Memory
docs.text:
error: context window exceeded maximum

The conversation history is too long. Clear the session:

/clear

Or reduce the context window in config:

[agent]
context_window = 32000  # tokens

docs.text:

  • Discussions: https://github.com/anthropics/hone/discussions
  • Documentation: See ../

docs.title: MCP Extensions Guide
docs.text: Hone supports 70+ community MCP (Model Context Protocol) extensions, allowing you to extend your agent's capabilities beyond native tools. This guide covers the most popular and useful extensions with copy-paste-ready configurations.

docs.title: Quick Start: Set Up Your First MCP Extension
1. Create a .hone/mcp.json file in your project
docs.text:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/workspace"]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: 2. Set environment variables (if needed)
docs.text:
Most extensions require API keys. Pass them via your shell:

export GITHUB_TOKEN="ghp_..."
export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://..."
hone

Hone will make these available to MCP servers automatically.

docs.title: 3. Start Hone and use the extension
docs.text:
hone
# Your agent now has access to filesystem operations beyond the working directory

That's it! The agent can now call the MCP server's resources and tools.

docs.title: How Hone Loads MCP Configs
docs.text:
Hone looks for MCP servers in two places (in order):

  1. Global config: ~/.config/hone/mcp.json — applies to all projects
  2. Project config: .hone/mcp.json — applies to this project only

When server names collide, project settings win. Files that don't exist or are malformed are silently skipped.

docs.title: 1. Filesystem
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem

Description: Read and write files outside the working directory, manage directory structures, and perform file operations beyond Hone's native sandboxed I/O.

What it enables: - Read files outside the current project - Write to system directories (e.g., /tmp, home directory) - Create symlinks and manage permissions - Recursively walk directory trees - Operations on large file sets

Installation: 

# No installation needed — npx fetches it automatically

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/workspace"],
      "timeout_ms": 10000
    }
  }
}

The argument /workspace is the root directory Hone's agent can access. Change it to restrict or expand access.

Example usage:

User: "Check for config files in my home directory and list them"

Agent calls filesystem MCP:
- list_dir(path="~/.config")
- read_file(path="~/.config/app.conf")
- Returns: file contents and directory structure

docs.title: 2. GitHub
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-github

Description: Create and manage GitHub issues, pull requests, branches, and inspect repository contents without git clone.

What it enables: - Read repo structure and file contents - Create/update issues and PRs - List and manage branches - Get commit history - Search repositories - Manage labels and milestones

Installation: 

# No installation — uses npx

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "github": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"],
      "env": {
        "GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"
      },
      "timeout_ms": 15000
    }
  }
}

Environment setup: 

# Create a Personal Access Token at https://github.com/settings/tokens
# Minimum scopes: repo, read:org
export GITHUB_TOKEN="ghp_..."
hone

Example usage:

User: "Create a GitHub issue in my-org/my-repo about fixing the auth bug"

Agent calls GitHub MCP:
- create_issue(
    owner="my-org",
    repo="my-repo",
    title="Fix authentication timeout issue",
    body="When idle for >30min, auth token expires...",
    labels=["bug", "auth"]
  )
- Returns: issue URL and number

Later:

User: "Show me open PRs in that repo"

Agent calls:
- list_pull_requests(owner="my-org", repo="my-repo", state="open")
- Returns: titles, authors, review status

docs.title: 3. PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres

Description: Query databases, inspect schemas, run migrations, and manage PostgreSQL instances.

What it enables: - Execute queries (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) - Inspect table schemas and indexes - Run migrations or raw SQL - Get query execution plans - Manage transactions

Installation: 

# No installation — npx handles it

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "postgres": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres"],
      "env": {
        "DATABASE_URL": "${DATABASE_URL}"
      },
      "timeout_ms": 30000
    }
  }
}

Environment setup: 

# PostgreSQL connection string (use a read-only user for safety)
export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://hone_user:password@localhost:5432/mydb"
hone

Example usage:

User: "Show me all tables in the current database with their column counts"

Agent calls Postgres MCP:
- query(sql="SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='public'")
- For each table: query(sql="SELECT COUNT(*) as columns FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name=$1")
- Returns: formatted table list with schemas

User: "Find slow queries (>100ms) from the last hour"

Agent calls:
- query(sql="SELECT query, calls, total_time FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE total_time > 100 AND query != '<insufficient privilege>'")
- Analyzes patterns and suggests indexes

docs.title: 4. Brave Search
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-brave-search

Description: Perform web searches and retrieve real-time information from the internet.

What it enables: - Full-text web search - News search - Image search - Real-time API data - Bypass information cutoff

Installation: 

# No installation — npx handles it

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "brave-search": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-brave-search"],
      "env": {
        "BRAVE_API_KEY": "${BRAVE_API_KEY}"
      },
      "timeout_ms": 10000
    }
  }
}

Environment setup: 

# Get a free key at https://api.search.brave.com
export BRAVE_API_KEY="..."
hone

Example usage:

User: "What's the latest React version and its key features?"

Agent calls Brave Search MCP:
- search(query="React latest version 2025")
- Returns: top 10 results with titles, snippets, URLs

Agent synthesizes: "React 19.1 includes Server Components, Actions, and..."

User: "Find recent articles about AI safety"

Agent calls:
- search(query="AI safety 2025", count=10)
- Returns: latest news with publication dates

docs.title: 5. Memory
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory

Description: Persistent key-value memory across sessions, enabling agents to remember context and decisions between runs.

What it enables: - Store and retrieve arbitrary data - Maintain project state across sessions - Track decisions and rationale - Cross-session learning - Session metadata

Installation: 

# No installation — npx handles it

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "memory": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory"],
      "timeout_ms": 5000
    }
  }
}

Example usage:

Session 1:

User: "We're using PostgreSQL 14. Remember this."

Agent calls Memory MCP:
- write_memory(key="db_version", value="PostgreSQL 14")
- write_memory(key="db_connection_pool", value="pgbouncer")

---

Session 2 (next day):

User: "Optimize the database queries"

Agent calls Memory MCP:
- read_memory(key="db_version")
- Returns: "PostgreSQL 14"

Agent: "I see you're on PostgreSQL 14 with pgbouncer. Let me optimize..."

docs.title: 6. Fetch
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-fetch

Description: Make HTTP requests, call APIs, and fetch web content for processing.

What it enables: - HTTP GET/POST/PUT/DELETE requests - Web scraping (fetch HTML) - API integration (REST, GraphQL) - Download files - Header and authentication management

Installation: 

# No installation — npx handles it

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "fetch": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-fetch"],
      "timeout_ms": 30000
    }
  }
}

Example usage:

User: "Fetch the pricing page from our API docs and extract the tier information"

Agent calls Fetch MCP:
- fetch(url="https://api.example.com/docs/pricing")
- Returns: HTML content

Agent parses and extracts:
- Tier names, prices, features

User: "Check the health of all our services"

Agent calls:
- fetch(url="https://service1.example.com/health", method="GET")
- fetch(url="https://service2.example.com/health", method="GET")
- Returns: status codes, response times
- Agent reports: "All services healthy, avg response 42ms"

docs.title: 7. SQLite
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-sqlite

Description: Query and manage SQLite databases stored locally or on disk.

What it enables: - Execute SQL queries on SQLite files - Inspect schemas - Create/modify tables - Run migrations - Analyze large datasets

Installation: 

# No installation — npx handles it

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sqlite": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-sqlite", "/path/to/data.db"],
      "timeout_ms": 15000
    }
  }
}

Example usage:

User: "How many users signed up last week? Show me by country."

Agent calls SQLite MCP:
- query(sql="SELECT country, COUNT(*) as signups FROM users WHERE created_at >= datetime('now', '-7 days') GROUP BY country ORDER BY signups DESC")
- Returns: country-wise signup counts

User: "Create a backup table of inactive accounts"

Agent calls:
- query(sql="CREATE TABLE inactive_backup AS SELECT * FROM users WHERE last_login < datetime('now', '-1 year')")
- Returns: success message with row count

docs.title: 8. Puppeteer
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-puppeteer

Description: Browser automation for testing, screenshots, interaction, and dynamic content rendering.

What it enables: - Take screenshots of websites - Interact with dynamic content (click, type, scroll) - Test web flows end-to-end - Extract rendered HTML (not just static) - PDF generation - Performance measurement

Installation: 

# Requires Node.js installed globally
npm install -g puppeteer

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "puppeteer": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-puppeteer"],
      "timeout_ms": 60000
    }
  }
}

Example usage:

User: "Take a screenshot of the login page at https://app.example.com"

Agent calls Puppeteer MCP:
- screenshot(url="https://app.example.com/login")
- Returns: PNG image base64-encoded

Agent: "The login form is visible with email and password fields"

User: "Test the forgot-password flow"

Agent calls:
- goto(url="https://app.example.com/login")
- click(selector="a[href='/forgot-password']")
- screenshot()
- fill(selector="input[type='email']", text="test@example.com")
- click(selector="button:contains('Reset')")
- waitForNavigation()
- Returns: success message with screenshot showing reset email sent

docs.title: 9. Slack
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-slack

Description: Send messages to Slack, read channels, manage threads, and integrate agent actions with Slack workflows.

What it enables: - Send direct messages to users - Post to channels - Read channel history - Manage threads and reactions - List channels and users - Upload files

Installation: 

# No installation — npx handles it

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "slack": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-slack"],
      "env": {
        "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN": "${SLACK_BOT_TOKEN}",
        "SLACK_APP_TOKEN": "${SLACK_APP_TOKEN}"
      },
      "timeout_ms": 10000
    }
  }
}

Environment setup: 

# Create a Slack app at https://api.slack.com/apps
# Generate tokens with scopes: chat:write, channels:read, users:read, files:write
export SLACK_BOT_TOKEN="xoxb-..."
export SLACK_APP_TOKEN="xapp-..."
hone

Example usage:

User: "Notify the dev team on Slack that the deployment is ready"

Agent calls Slack MCP:
- send_message(channel="#dev-team", text="Deployment ready for v2.1.0. Rollout starts in 10 minutes.")
- Returns: message timestamp

User: "Read the last 10 messages in #incidents"

Agent calls:
- read_channel(channel="#incidents", limit=10)
- Returns: messages with authors, timestamps

Agent summarizes: "3 open incidents, highest priority: database replication lag"

docs.title: 10. Sequential Thinking
docs.text:
Package: @modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking

Description: Structured reasoning and multi-step planning for complex problems.

What it enables: - Break complex queries into steps - Explicit reasoning chains - Verification and backtracking - Better error handling - Auditable decision-making

Installation: 

# No installation — npx handles it

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "thinking": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking"],
      "timeout_ms": 30000
    }
  }
}

Example usage:

User: "Design a database schema for a multi-tenant SaaS app"

Agent calls Sequential Thinking MCP:

thinking_start()

  Step 1: Identify core entities (users, teams, workspaces, data records)
  Step 2: Define relationships (users <-> teams, teams <-> workspaces)
  Step 3: Consider isolation (row-level security for tenants)
  Step 4: Plan for scaling (sharding, archiving strategies)
  Step 5: Design migrations (versioned schema changes)

thinking_end()

Agent outputs: Complete SQL schema with rationale for each design decision

User: "Audit this code for security issues"

Agent uses thinking to:
  1. Identify input vectors (URL params, form data, headers, cookies)
  2. Check for validation (length limits, type checks, encoding)
  3. Check for escaping (SQL injection, XSS, command injection)
  4. Check for auth/authz (permissions, token validation)
  5. Report findings with severity and fixes

Returns: actionable security report with prioritized fixes

docs.title: Finding More Extensions
docs.text: The MCP ecosystem is rapidly growing. Here's where to discover new extensions:

docs.title: Official Registry
docs.text:
• GitHub: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers
  • Monitored list of official and community extensions
  • Installation instructions and examples
  • Feature documentation

docs.title: Community Collections
docs.text:
• MCP.run: https://mcp.run (community registry with search)
  • Awesome MCP: https://github.com/pglombardo/awesome-mcp
  • Curated list of extensions
  • Categorized by use case

docs.title: Installing Custom MCP Extensions
docs.text:
Most extensions follow the same pattern:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "my-extension": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@scope/server-name", "arg1", "arg2"],
      "env": {
        "API_KEY": "${MY_API_KEY}"
      },
      "timeout_ms": 10000
    }
  }
}

For local or custom extensions:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "custom-tool": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["/path/to/server.py"],
      "env": {
        "CONFIG": "/path/to/config.json"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
Every MCP server in .hone/mcp.json has this structure:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "server-name": {
      "command": "string (required)",
      "args": ["array", "of", "arguments"],
      "env": {
        "ENV_VAR": "value or ${REFERENCE}",
        "API_KEY": "${MY_API_KEY}"
      },
      "disabled": false,
      "timeout_ms": 10000
    }
  }
}

Fields:

Field Type Default Description command string (required) Executable to run (e.g., npx, python, absolute path) args array [] Arguments passed to command env object {} Environment variables. Values can reference ${VAR} to use shell variables disabled boolean false Skip this server at startup timeout_ms number 10000 Per-request timeout in milliseconds

Environment variables: - ${VAR} syntax is expanded from your shell environment - Only variables set before hone starts are available - Use a .env file or shell profile to set them persistently

docs.title: Sandboxing
docs.text: MCP servers run in sandboxed subprocesses. Each server: - Runs with isolated file access (via args paths) - Cannot access Hone's memory or other servers - Is terminated if it hangs (via timeout_ms)

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text:
Do NOT hardcode secrets in .hone/mcp.json. Always use environment variables:

# Good: uses shell environment variable
export GITHUB_TOKEN="ghp_..."
hone

# Config references it safely:
"env": { "GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}" }

Do NOT commit .hone/mcp.json with real keys:

# Add to .gitignore
echo ".hone/mcp.json" >> .gitignore

# Create a template for teammates
cat > .hone/mcp.json.example << 'EOF'
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "github": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"],
      "env": {
        "GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}
EOF

docs.title: Principle of Least Privilege
docs.text:
• Use dedicated API keys with minimal scopes for each service
  • Revoke keys if a machine is compromised
  • Rotate keys periodically
  • Use read-only credentials when possible

Example for GitHub:

# Create a Personal Access Token with only these scopes:
# - repo (for public repos only, uncheck "Full control")
# - read:org
# - NOT: delete_repo, admin:repo_hook, workflow

export GITHUB_TOKEN="ghp_..."

docs.title: npx: command not found
docs.text:
Problem: Node.js/npx not installed.

Solution: 

# Install Node.js from https://nodejs.org
# Or via package manager:
brew install node          # macOS
sudo apt install nodejs    # Ubuntu/Debian
choco install nodejs       # Windows

Verify: 

npx --version

docs.title: Server crashes or returns errors
docs.text:
Problem: MCP server exited unexpectedly.

Debugging: 

# Check server output directly
npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /tmp

# Verify environment variables are set
echo $GITHUB_TOKEN

# Check server logs in Hone (if available)

Common causes: - Missing environment variables - Invalid arguments - Insufficient permissions (e.g., database user lacks query access)

docs.title: Timeout exceeded
docs.text:
Problem: timeout_ms expired before server responded.

Solution: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "slow-server": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-something"],
      "timeout_ms": 30000
    }
  }
}

Increase timeout_ms for: - Database queries on large tables - Complex web scraping - Slow network APIs

docs.title: Server not found by Hone
docs.text:
Problem: Configuration is correct but agent can't access server.

Solutions: 1. Verify .hone/mcp.json is valid JSON: 

cat .hone/mcp.json | jq .

  1. Check file location:
  2. Project-level: .hone/mcp.json (in your project root)

  3. Global: ~/.config/hone/mcp.json (home directory)

  4. Restart Hone after adding/changing config: 

    hone

docs.title: Agent can't find the tool
docs.text:
Problem: Server is running but agent doesn't know about its tools.

Solution: MCP servers expose tools that agents discover automatically. If discovery fails: - Check server logs for errors - Verify required environment variables are set - Increase timeout_ms if server is slow to respond

docs.title: Advanced: Writing Custom MCP Extensions
docs.text:
For team-specific tools, you can write custom MCP servers:

# Create a Python MCP server
mkdir my-mcp-server
cd my-mcp-server
pip install mcp

# Implement your server.py with resources and tools
# See https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/server/sdks for SDK docs

# Use it in Hone

Configuration: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "custom": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["./my-mcp-server/server.py"],
      "env": {
        "CUSTOM_CONFIG": "/path/to/config.json"
      }
    }
  }
}

For details, see the MCP specification.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Start small: Add one extension (e.g., Filesystem or GitHub) and test it
  2. Monitor usage: Watch agent logs to see which tools are called
  3. Expand gradually: Add more extensions as you discover use cases
  4. Share configs: Create .hone/mcp.json.example templates for your team
  5. Optimize timeouts: Adjust timeout_ms based on real performance

For more on Hone capabilities, see: - Tools and MCP Integration - Configuration Guide - Security Best Practices

docs.title: Model Providers
docs.text: Hone abstracts model access through the ModelProvider trait, allowing you to hot-swap providers mid-session, define fallback chains, and route different tasks to different models.

docs.title: Provider Overview
docs.text:
A provider is a concrete implementation of hone_providers::ModelProvider. It handles authentication, request formatting, streaming responses, and error handling for a specific model vendor.

flowchart TD
    Agent["hone-core: Agent"]
    Reg["ProviderRegistry"]
    Chain["FallbackChain"]
    Router["ModelRouter"]

    Agent -->|request| Chain
    Chain -->|try| Router
    Router -->|route by rule| Providers["Provider Pool"]
    Providers --> Anthro["Anthropic<br/>API"]
    Providers --> OAI["OpenAI<br/>API"]
    Providers --> Ollama["Ollama<br/>Local"]
    Providers --> CLI["Claude CLI<br/>Pass-through"]

docs.title: Provider Comparison
docs.text:
Hone supports 5 working providers + ACP. Here's how they compare:

Provider Tool Calling Streaming Cost Best For Anthropic API Yes Yes $$ Production (most capable) OpenAI API + compatible Yes Yes $ Budget-conscious teams, custom endpoints Ollama No Yes Free Local/offline work Claude CLI No Yes Subscription Existing CLI users Gemini CLI No Yes Free tier No API key setup ACP Yes Yes Subscription Custom tool servers

docs.title: Provider Auto-Detection
docs.text:
Hone automatically detects and prioritizes available providers in this order:

  1. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY env var → Anthropic API
  2. OPENAI_API_KEY env var → OpenAI API
  3. claude command available → Claude CLI
  4. gemini command available → Gemini CLI
  5. OLLAMA_HOST env var → Ollama
  6. Fallback → Mock provider (for testing)

Override with --model or config file.

docs.title: Anthropic API
docs.text:
Production-grade, most capable.

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
hone --model anthropic:claude-opus-4-5

Configuration:

[providers.anthropic]
api_key = "sk-ant-..."  # or env var ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
base_url = "https://api.anthropic.com"  # optional override
timeout_secs = 30

Available models: - claude-opus-4-5 — 200K context, best for complex tasks - claude-sonnet-4 — 200K context, fast general-purpose - claude-haiku-3-5 — 200K context, cheapest, good for simple tasks

docs.title: OpenAI API (and Compatible Endpoints)
docs.text:
Use OpenAI or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, OpenRouter, etc.).

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
hone --model openai:gpt-4o

For custom endpoints (DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, OpenRouter):

export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-api-key"
export HONE_OPENAI_BASE_URL="https://api.deepseek.com"
export HONE_OPENAI_MODEL="deepseek-coder"
hone

Configuration:

[providers.openai]
api_key = "sk-..."  # or env var OPENAI_API_KEY
base_url = "https://api.openai.com/v1"
timeout_secs = 30

OpenAI available models: - gpt-4o — Latest, most capable - gpt-4-turbo — Previous gen - gpt-3.5-turbo — Fast, cheap

Custom endpoint examples: - DeepSeek: https://api.deepseek.com, model deepseek-coder - Qwen (via DeepSeek): https://api.deepseek.com, model qwen-max - OpenRouter: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, any supported model - Self-hosted vLLM: http://localhost:8000/v1, your model name

docs.title: Ollama (Local Models)
docs.text:
Zero-cost local inference.

ollama pull llama2
ollama serve  # terminal 1
hone --model ollama:llama2  # terminal 2

Configuration:

[providers.ollama]
base_url = "http://localhost:11434"
timeout_secs = 300  # local models may be slower

Available models: Any model you ollama pull. Run ollama list to see installed models.

docs.title: Claude CLI Pass-Through (Generation 1)
docs.text:
Use your existing claude command-line tool.

# Requires: claude --version to work
hone --model claude-cli:claude-opus

Configuration:

[providers.claude_cli]
claude_path = "/usr/local/bin/claude"  # auto-detected if not specified

Why use this? You already have Claude CLI set up with credentials. Hone integrates with it directly.

docs.title: Gemini CLI Pass-Through (Generation 1)
docs.text:
Use Google's gemini command-line tool.

hone --model gemini-cli:gemini-pro

Configuration:

[providers.gemini_cli]
gemini_path = "/usr/local/bin/gemini"

docs.title: ACP (Agent Client Protocol)
docs.text:
Full tool support via persistent subprocess. Advanced integration for custom model servers.

hone --model acp:my-service --acp-endpoint /path/to/server/binary

Configuration:

[providers.acp]
server_path = "/path/to/acp/server"
server_args = ["--port", "9000"]
timeout_secs = 60

ACP allows you to: - Define custom tools in your own language - Implement complex logic (not limited to JSON-RPC) - Maintain a persistent connection to your service - Full bidirectional tool dispatch

For details, see Tools and MCP.

docs.title: Hot-Swapping Providers Mid-Session
docs.text:
Change providers without losing conversation history:

You: /model openai:gpt-4o
Assistant: Switched to gpt-4o (8192 token context). Conversation history preserved.

The context manager evaluates token count for the new model's limits and truncates if necessary.

When to hot-swap: - Switch to a cheaper model for simple tasks - Switch to a more capable model for complex reasoning - Test the same prompt across providers - Fall back to a backup provider if one fails

docs.title: Fallback Chains
docs.text:
Define a priority list of providers. If one fails, the next is tried automatically.

[[fallback_chains]]
name = "production"
providers = ["anthropic:claude-opus-4-5", "openai:gpt-4o", "ollama:llama2"]
retry_on = ["RateLimit", "Timeout", "ServiceUnavailable"]
retry_delay_secs = 5
max_retries = 3

The agent tries Anthropic first. If it rate-limits or times out, it retries after 5 seconds. After 3 failed attempts, it falls back to OpenAI. If OpenAI fails, it falls back to local Ollama.

Usage:

hone --fallback-chain production

Or set as default in config:

[agent]
default_fallback_chain = "production"

docs.title: Model Routing Rules
docs.text:
Route different task types to different models. Define rules by prompt pattern or turn count.

[[routing_rules]]
name = "quick_tasks"
condition = "input_length < 50"  # short prompts
provider = "anthropic:claude-haiku-3-5"

[[routing_rules]]
name = "complex_reasoning"
condition = "input_contains('analyze')"  # keyword match
provider = "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5"

[[routing_rules]]
name = "budget_conscious"
condition = "true"  # fallback: default
provider = "ollama:llama2"

The router evaluates conditions top-down and dispatches to the first matching provider.

Advanced condition syntax: - input_length < N — number of input characters - input_contains('keyword') — substring match - turn_count > N — number of turns in session - session_cost_usd > N — accumulated spend - true — always matches (use as default)

docs.title: Pricing Table and Cost Tracking
docs.text:
Hone tracks real-time costs. The pricing table maps model IDs to per-token rates:

[pricing.anthropic]
"claude-opus-4-5" = { input_per_mtok = 3.00, output_per_mtok = 15.00 }
"claude-sonnet-4" = { input_per_mtok = 3.00, output_per_mtok = 15.00 }
"claude-haiku-3-5" = { input_per_mtok = 0.80, output_per_mtok = 4.00 }

[pricing.openai]
"gpt-4o" = { input_per_mtok = 2.50, output_per_mtok = 10.00 }
"gpt-4-turbo" = { input_per_mtok = 10.00, output_per_mtok = 30.00 }
"gpt-3.5-turbo" = { input_per_mtok = 0.50, output_per_mtok = 1.50 }

[pricing.ollama]
# Local models are free; all rates are 0.00
"llama2" = { input_per_mtok = 0.00, output_per_mtok = 0.00 }

After each turn, Hone calculates cost:

Usage: 4521 input tokens, 312 output tokens
Cost calculation: (4521 / 1_000_000) * 3.00 + (312 / 1_000_000) * 15.00
Cost: $0.019 USD
Session total: $0.24 USD

Set a budget limit:

hone --budget 10.00  # stop after spending $10

docs.title: Provider Health Checks
docs.text:
The daemon performs periodic health checks on all configured providers. Use this to monitor uptime and detect issues early:

honed --health-check-interval 60  # every 60 seconds

Health check results are logged and available via the HTTP API:

curl http://localhost:7777/providers/health

Response:

{
  "anthropic:claude-opus-4-5": {
    "status": "healthy",
    "last_checked": "2026-04-05T12:34:56Z",
    "latency_ms": 45
  },
  "openai:gpt-4o": {
    "status": "rate_limited",
    "last_checked": "2026-04-05T12:34:55Z",
    "retry_after_secs": 120
  },
  "ollama:llama2": {
    "status": "unreachable",
    "last_checked": "2026-04-05T12:34:52Z",
    "error": "connection refused"
  }
}

docs.title: Customizing Timeouts
docs.text:
Each provider supports a timeout setting (default 30 seconds):

[providers.anthropic]
timeout_secs = 60  # increase for large requests

[providers.ollama]
timeout_secs = 300  # local models may be slow

If a request exceeds the timeout, it is cancelled and the fallback chain is triggered (if configured).

docs.title: Advanced: Provider Registry
docs.text:
Access the provider registry programmatically (for custom integrations):

use hone_providers::ProviderRegistry;

let registry = ProviderRegistry::from_config(config)?;

// List all available models
for provider in registry.all() {
    println!("{}: {}", provider.id(), provider.display_name());
    for model in provider.supported_models() {
        println!("  - {}", model.id);
    }
}

// Get a specific provider
let anthropic = registry.get("anthropic:claude-opus-4-5")?;
let response = anthropic.complete(request).await?;

See Architecture for the full ModelProvider trait definition.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Get started: See Getting Started to run your first session.
  • Recipes: Use providers in Recipes to automate workflows.
  • Server: Run the Server and Remote daemon to manage multiple sessions.
  • Tools: Extend providers with custom tools via Tools and MCP.

docs.title: Recipes: Automating Workflows with YAML
docs.text: Recipes are YAML files that define multi-step agent workflows. Each step runs a prompt through the model, and steps can depend on previous outputs.

docs.title: Built-in Recipes
docs.text: Hone includes 4 bundled recipes for common development tasks:

docs.title: tdd-feature
docs.text:
Implement a feature using Test-Driven Development (Red-Green-Refactor):

name: tdd-feature
description: Implement a feature using Test-Driven Development
steps:
  - name: understand
    prompt: "Read the relevant code and understand the current architecture. Summarize what you find."
  - name: red
    prompt: "Write failing tests that describe the desired behavior. Run them to confirm they fail."
  - name: green
    prompt: "Write the minimum code to make the tests pass. Do not add extra features."
  - name: refactor
    prompt: "Refactor the implementation for clarity and quality. All tests must still pass."
  - name: verify
    prompt: "Run all tests one final time. Report the results."
test_cmd: "cargo test"

docs.title: bug-fix
docs.text:
Fix a bug using systematic debugging with regression test:

name: bug-fix
description: Fix a bug using systematic debugging with regression test
steps:
  - name: reproduce
    prompt: "Read the bug report and reproduce the issue. Identify the failing behavior."
  - name: regression-test
    prompt: "Write a regression test that captures the bug. Verify it fails."
  - name: fix
    prompt: "Write the minimal fix. Do not refactor surrounding code."
  - name: verify
    prompt: "Run all tests. The regression test should now pass along with all existing tests."
test_cmd: "cargo test"

docs.title: code-review
docs.text:
Perform a comprehensive code review:

name: code-review
description: Perform a comprehensive code review
steps:
  - name: overview
    prompt: "Read the changed files. Understand the intent and scope of the changes."
  - name: correctness
    prompt: "Check for logical errors, edge cases, and off-by-one bugs."
  - name: security
    prompt: "Scan for injection vulnerabilities, secret leakage, and auth issues."
  - name: performance
    prompt: "Identify unnecessary allocations, N+1 queries, and hot-path issues."
  - name: report
    prompt: "Summarize findings in a table sorted by severity (CRITICAL > HIGH > MEDIUM > LOW > INFO)."

docs.title: refactor
docs.text:
Safely refactor code with test verification at each step:

name: refactor
description: Safely refactor code with test verification at each step
steps:
  - name: baseline
    prompt: "Run all existing tests to establish a green baseline. Report results."
  - name: plan
    prompt: "Analyze the code and create a refactoring plan. List each change and its purpose."
  - name: execute
    prompt: "Apply the refactoring changes one at a time. Run tests after each change."
  - name: verify
    prompt: "Run the full test suite. All tests must pass. Report before/after code metrics."
test_cmd: "cargo test"

docs.title: Using Built-in Recipes
docs.text:
# List all available recipes
hone --list-recipes

# Run a built-in recipe by name
hone --recipe tdd-feature
hone --recipe bug-fix
hone --recipe code-review
hone --recipe refactor

# Run in non-interactive mode (useful for CI/CD)
hone --recipe tdd-feature --non-interactive

# Override the test command
hone --recipe tdd-feature --test-cmd "pytest tests/"

The --list-recipes command shows all available recipes with descriptions:

Available recipes:
  tdd-feature           Implement a feature using Test-Driven Development
  bug-fix               Fix a bug using systematic debugging with regression test
  code-review           Perform a comprehensive code review
  refactor              Safely refactor code with test verification at each step

docs.title: What Are Recipes?
docs.text:
A recipe automates a sequence of agent turns. Instead of typing prompts manually, you define them once in YAML and run them repeatedly.

When to use recipes: - Multi-step workflows (e.g., analyze → improve → test) - Reproducible processes (e.g., code review, documentation generation) - Conditional branches (e.g., if test fails, retry) - TDD: define test before implementation

docs.title: Recipe YAML Format
docs.text:
Basic structure:

name: "Code Review"
description: "Review a code change and suggest improvements"

steps:
  - name: "Analyze Changes"
    prompt: "Review the changes in this pull request and identify issues"

  - name: "Suggest Improvements"
    prompt: "Based on your analysis, list the top 3 improvements we should make"
    when: true  # conditional: only run if condition is true

  - name: "Generate Summary"
    prompt: "Write a concise summary of the code review"
    when: true

test_cmd: "cargo test"  # optional: verify the recipe worked

docs.title: Recipe Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description name string Yes Recipe identifier description string No Human-readable description steps array Yes List of steps (see below) test_cmd string No Shell command to verify recipe success (TDD)

docs.title: Step Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description name string Yes Step identifier (used in logs, output) prompt string Yes The prompt to send to the agent when bool No Conditional execution (default: true)

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
Here's a realistic recipe for implementing a feature with TDD:

name: "TDD Feature Implementation"
description: "Implement a feature test-first: write test → implement → verify"

steps:
  - name: "Analyze Requirements"
    prompt: |
      I want to add a feature that validates email addresses. 
      Please outline:
      1. Test cases (valid/invalid formats)
      2. Edge cases (international domains, subdomains)
      3. Recommended library or algorithm
    when: true

  - name: "Write Tests"
    prompt: |
      Based on the analysis above, write comprehensive unit tests for email validation.
      Use Rust's standard testing framework.
      Don't implement yet — just the tests.
    when: true

  - name: "Implement Feature"
    prompt: |
      Now implement the email validation function to make the tests pass.
      Keep it simple and well-commented.
    when: true

  - name: "Review for Edge Cases"
    prompt: |
      Review the implementation. Did we handle all the edge cases from the analysis?
      Suggest any additions.
    when: true

  - name: "Optimize"
    prompt: |
      The implementation works. Can we make it faster or more readable?
      Suggest optimizations without breaking tests.
    when: true

test_cmd: "cargo test"  # Verify all tests pass

docs.title: Conditional Steps (when)
docs.text:
Control which steps run using the when field:

steps:
  - name: "Check Compilation"
    prompt: "Does the code compile? Run `cargo check`"

  - name: "Fix Compilation Errors"
    prompt: "Fix any compilation errors"
    when: false  # conditionally enable based on previous step
    # In future versions: when: "previous.step.failed"

  - name: "Run Tests"
    prompt: "Run the test suite with `cargo test`"
    when: true  # always run

Currently, when accepts boolean literals. Future versions will support expressions like: - when: "previous_step.success" - when: "output_contains('error')"

docs.title: TDD Hook: test_cmd and Test Verification
docs.text:
The test_cmd field automatically runs tests after each step and feeds test failures back to the agent for fixing. This creates a tight TDD feedback loop.

name: "Implementation Recipe"

steps:
  - name: "Write Implementation"
    prompt: "Implement the feature"

  - name: "Add Tests"
    prompt: "Write tests for the feature"

test_cmd: "cargo test && cargo clippy"  # Both must pass after each step

How test verification works:

  1. Agent executes a step (writes code, modifies files)
  2. test_cmd runs automatically: cargo test
  3. If tests pass: → move to next step
  4. If tests fail: → feed test output to agent and retry (up to 3 times)
  5. Agent sees the failure and fixes code based on error messages

Example output:

Recipe: TDD Implementation
Step 1: Implement Authentication Function
  Running: cargo test
  test auth::test_login ... FAILED
  error[E0308]: mismatched types

  [Retry 1/3] Agent re-runs step with test output as context...
  test auth::test_login ... PASSED ✓

Step 2: Add Documentation
  Running: cargo test && cargo clippy
  test result: ok. 5 passed ✓
  clippy: no warnings ✓

Recipe result: SUCCESS

Configuration:

name: "TDD Feature"
description: "Build a feature with automatic test verification"
test_cmd: "pytest tests/"  # Run after each step
steps:
  - name: write_tests
    prompt: "Write failing tests for the new feature"

  - name: implement
    prompt: "Implement the feature to pass tests"
    # test_cmd runs here automatically
    # If tests fail, agent retries with failure details

  - name: cleanup
    prompt: "Refactor for clarity"
    # test_cmd runs here too

Retry behavior:

  • Default: retry up to 3 times if tests fail
  • Each retry includes the previous test output as context
  • If max retries exhausted, recipe halts with error
  • Successful runs advance to next step immediately

When to use test verification:

  • Implementing features (TDD: red-green-refactor)
  • Bug fixes (regression test then fix)
  • Refactoring (tests ensure behavior preserved)
  • Complex algorithms (automatic validation)

Research: The TestVerificationLoop catches 40% more bugs than self-generated tests (AgentCoder study). The tight coupling between test failures and agent iterations significantly improves code quality.

docs.title: Interactive Mode
docs.text:
hone --recipe code-review.yaml

Hone runs each step, streaming output. Press y at each step to proceed, n to skip, or q to quit.

Recipe: Code Review
Step 1/3: Analyze Changes
Agent: I found 3 issues...
[pause] Continue to next step? [y/n/q]
> y

Step 2/3: Suggest Improvements
Agent: Top improvements are...
[pause] Continue to next step? [y/n/q]
> y

Step 3/3: Generate Summary
Agent: Summary of review...
[pause] Test command: cargo test
✓ All tests passed
Recipe completed successfully.

docs.title: Batch Mode
docs.text:
hone --recipe code-review.yaml --non-interactive

Runs all steps without pausing. Useful for CI/CD.

docs.title: With Model Override
docs.text:
hone --recipe code-review.yaml --model ollama:llama2

Use a specific model for all steps in the recipe.

docs.title: With Budget Limit
docs.text:
hone --recipe code-review.yaml --budget 5.00

Stop if the recipe exceeds $5 in API costs.

docs.title: Recipe Output and Export
docs.text:
Each recipe run produces a report:

hone --recipe code-review.yaml --export-to review-report.json

Report format:

{
  "recipe_name": "Code Review",
  "started_at": "2026-04-05T14:30:00Z",
  "completed_at": "2026-04-05T14:32:15Z",
  "steps": [
    {
      "name": "Analyze Changes",
      "output": "The pull request contains...",
      "skipped": false,
      "tokens_input": 1200,
      "tokens_output": 340,
      "cost_usd": 0.024
    },
    {
      "name": "Suggest Improvements",
      "output": "Top 3 improvements: ...",
      "skipped": false,
      "tokens_input": 2100,
      "tokens_output": 520,
      "cost_usd": 0.035
    }
  ],
  "test_result": {
    "cmd": "cargo test",
    "status": "passed",
    "output": "test result: ok. 5 passed"
  },
  "session_cost_usd": 0.059,
  "status": "success"
}

docs.title: Recipe Directory and Discovery
docs.text:
Hone looks for recipes in:

  1. Current directory (./*.yaml)
  2. ~/.config/hone/recipes/ (user recipes)
  3. /etc/hone/recipes/ (system recipes)
  4. Built-in recipes (bundled with Hone)

List all available recipes:

hone --list-recipes

Output:

Available recipes:
  user:
    code-review.yaml — Review a code change and suggest improvements
    tdd-feature.yaml — Implement a feature test-first
  system:
    documentation.yaml — Auto-generate API documentation
    refactor.yaml — Refactor code safely
  built-in:
    unit-test.yaml — Write comprehensive unit tests
    integration-test.yaml — Write integration tests

docs.title: Writing Your Own Recipe
docs.text:
Step-by-step:

  1. Create a .yaml file:
cat > my-recipe.yaml << 'EOF'
name: "My Workflow"
description: "What this recipe does"

steps:
  - name: "Step 1"
    prompt: "First prompt"

  - name: "Step 2"
    prompt: "Second prompt"

test_cmd: "echo 'All done!'"
EOF
  1. Test it locally:
hone --recipe my-recipe.yaml
  1. Share it: Commit to your repo or publish to the Hone marketplace.

docs.title: 1. Clear Prompts
docs.text:
Write prompts that give the agent specific direction:

# Good
prompt: |
  Write unit tests for the `validate_email` function.
  Use Rust's #[test] macro.
  Include at least 5 test cases.

# Vague
prompt: "Write tests"

docs.title: 2. Break Down Steps
docs.text:
Separate concerns into distinct steps:

# Good: each step has a clear focus
steps:
  - name: "Analyze"
    prompt: "Analyze the requirements"
  - name: "Design"
    prompt: "Design a solution"
  - name: "Implement"
    prompt: "Implement the design"

# Vague: too much in one step
steps:
  - name: "Do everything"
    prompt: "Analyze, design, and implement"

docs.title: 3. Reference Previous Steps
docs.text:
Prompts can reference outputs from earlier steps implicitly (the conversation history includes them):

steps:
  - name: "Identify Issues"
    prompt: "List all issues in the code"

  - name: "Fix Issues"
    prompt: "Fix the issues you identified above"
    # The agent sees the previous step's output in context

docs.title: 4. Use test_cmd for Verification
docs.text:
Always include a test command to catch regressions:

test_cmd: "cargo test && cargo clippy && cargo fmt --check"

docs.title: Marketplace
docs.text:
Share recipes with the community (future feature):

hone recipe-publish my-recipe.yaml

This publishes your recipe to the Hone marketplace. Others can then:

hone --recipe @username/my-recipe.yaml

docs.text:
